question: The opening line of the Daodejing is one of the most quoted in Chinese thought: the Dao that can be spoken is not the eternal Dao. Why start a book this way?
answer: Warning the reader that no string of words can fully capture what the book points at.
choices: Warning the reader that no string of words can fully capture what the book points at.
Promising that careful study of the text will at last deliver the true name of the Dao.
Arguing words are useless, so a wise person should give up speaking of philosophy.
Praising the older oral teachings the Zhou ritual masters preserved before writing.
context: Daodejing Ch. 1. The opening is not a counsel of silence — Laozi writes the rest of the book anyway. The move is closer to Wittgenstein's later distinction between showing and saying: language can point at the Dao, but the pointing is not the same as the thing. Distractors are real misreadings — the optimistic-mystic reading (full disclosure later), the linguistic-defeatist reading (give up speaking), and the antiquarian reading (the older oral way was better).

question: Around 520 CE, the Indian monk Bodhidharma arrived at the court of Emperor Wu of Liang — a ruler who had built temples, copied scriptures, and supported monks for years. The emperor asked: how much merit have I earned? What did Bodhidharma say?
answer: None at all — meritorious acts done for the sake of merit miss the point entirely.
choices: None at all — meritorious acts done for the sake of merit miss the point entirely.
Vast merit — your support has carried the dharma further than any other ruler's.
Equal merit — emperor and beggar both gain by the measure of what they offer.
Lasting merit — buildings and books outlive the body and so guard the dharma.
context: The encounter is recorded in The Blue Cliff Record (case 1) and other Chan compilations. Bodhidharma, who would become the legendary founder of Chinese Chan (Japanese Zen), refuses to play the merit-economy game the emperor expects. Action aimed at earning spiritual credit, in this reading, is still grasping — and grasping is what Buddhism is trying to undo. Distractors are real positions held within the broader Buddhist world: merit-transfer doctrine, equal-offering doctrine, longevity-of-works idea.

question: A Zen koan asks: what is the sound of one hand clapping? Beginners hear it as a trick riddle with a clever answer hidden somewhere. Rinzai teachers insist the hunt for a clever answer is exactly the wrong response. Why?
answer: The koan is meant to exhaust thinking, not to be solved — frustration is part of the method.
choices: The koan is meant to exhaust thinking, not to be solved — frustration is part of the method.
The koan has one correct logical answer, but the student must derive it without instruction.
The koan is mainly a memory aid, helping the student keep a doctrinal point in active mind.
The koan is a private signal between master and disciple, used to confirm a stage of training.
context: The one-hand koan is attributed to the eighteenth-century Japanese Rinzai master Hakuin. The Rinzai use of koans (kanna Zen) is to drive the student into a state of intense doubt — the great ball of doubt — until the conceptual mind exhausts itself and direct insight breaks through. Soto Zen tends to emphasize seated meditation (zazen) more than koan practice. Distractors are real but mistaken framings: koan-as-riddle, koan-as-mnemonic, koan-as-credential.

question: In the Chandogya Upanishad the sage Uddalaka teaches his son with simple lessons — salt dissolved in water, the seed of a fig, a clay pot. Each builds toward one short sentence Uddalaka repeats nine times. What sentence?
answer: Tat tvam asi — that thou art — the deepest self in you is the source of all things.
choices: Tat tvam asi — that thou art — the deepest self in you is the source of all things.
Neti neti — not this, not that — the deepest reality cannot be named by any description.
Aham brahmasmi — I am the source — the awakened sage alone is the cause of the world.
Om tat sat — om that is real — the chanted syllable contains all the seeker can need.
context: Chandogya Upanishad 6.8-16. Uddalaka's lesson is the classical statement of non-dual Vedanta: the atman (deepest self) and brahman (underlying reality) are not two things. Shankara built his entire philosophical system on it eight centuries later. Distractors are real Upanishadic and Hindu formulae used by other lineages: neti neti (Brihadaranyaka 2.3.6), aham brahmasmi (Brihadaranyaka 1.4.10), om tat sat (Bhagavad Gita 17.23). Each is canonical — only one is the line Uddalaka teaches.

question: The Bhagavad Gita opens with the warrior Arjuna freezing before a battle he no longer wants to fight — kin stand across the field. He drops his bow. Krishna, his charioteer, spends eighteen chapters answering him. What is the answer?
answer: Do the duty of your role with skill and detachment, leaving the fruits to a higher order.
choices: Do the duty of your role with skill and detachment, leaving the fruits to a higher order.
Refuse the duty of your role, since killing kin cannot be reconciled with enlightenment.
Withdraw from action entirely, since only inward meditation ends the cycle of rebirth.
Choose the duty that the named gods assign, since dharma is their direct command alone.
context: The Bhagavad Gita, set within the larger Mahabharata, is one of the most influential religious-philosophical texts ever written. Krishna's teaching to Arjuna — karma yoga, action without attachment to outcomes — became the keystone of Hindu philosophical practice and influenced Gandhi, Emerson, and many others. Distractors are real positions held by other Indian schools the Gita is in conversation with: Jain non-violence absolutism, ascetic-withdrawal Sramanism, theistic-ritual Vedism.

question: Each spring in Japan, crowds gather under cherry trees for hanami — flower-viewing. The blossoms last only a week. Poets have written about them for a thousand years, and the feeling has a name: mono no aware. What does the phrase point at?
answer: The tender ache of feeling something beautiful precisely because it is about to be gone.
choices: The tender ache of feeling something beautiful precisely because it is about to be gone.
The cheerful pleasure of an annual festival shared with neighbors, family, and friends.
The serious duty of remembering ancestors at the change of each major farming season.
The quiet pride of a culture in treating its native flora as the symbol of the land.
context: Mono no aware — literally something like the pathos of things — was named in the eighteenth century by the scholar Motoori Norinaga, who used it to describe a sensibility running through the Tale of Genji and older Heian poetry. It is not sadness, not nostalgia, not melancholy — it is the bittersweet alertness that the very thing making you happy will not last. Cherry blossoms became its emblem because they are so visibly transient. Distractors are real but flatter readings: social festival, ancestor ritual, nationalist symbol.

question: A tree in a forest, with no one looking, does not exist at that moment. Why did he say such a strange thing?
answer: Because to be is to be perceived — without a mind, there is nothing left for the tree to be.
choices: Because to be is to be perceived — without a mind, there is nothing left for the tree to be.
Because trees are too small to exist without a witness — only large things persist unobserved.
Because matter blinks in and out of being randomly, and only steady gaze can stabilize it.
Because language alone gives the tree existence — when no one names it, the tree dissolves.
context: Berkeley, an Irish bishop writing in 1710, was not joking. He thought 'Matter' was a confused idea: strip away color, shape, smell — all of which are perceptions in some mind — and nothing is left. To save the unobserved tree, he added that God perceives everything. Esse est percipi: to be is to be perceived.

question: The philosophy a person chooses depends on what kind of person they are. What was his striking claim from that idea?
answer: A lazy mind picks a system where things just happen; a free mind picks one where the self acts.
choices: A lazy mind picks a system where things just happen; a free mind picks one where the self acts.
A young thinker prefers freedom; an aging thinker drifts back to fate and acceptance of necessity.
A poor mind clings to materialism; only the rich can afford the luxury of idealist speculation.
A pious mind sees God in all things; a worldly mind sees only matter pushed about by causes.
context: Fichte, lecturing in Jena around 1797, refused to treat philosophical disagreement as just intellectual variation. To him, choosing dogmatism (the world acts on me) over idealism (I act) revealed something about a thinker's grip on freedom itself. The remark is striking; many readers still find it overreaching.

question: A baker doesn't bake your bread out of love for you. Yet you get bread anyway. What did he say made the system work?
answer: Each person pursues their own interest, and prices guide that effort into others' service.
choices: Each person pursues their own interest, and prices guide that effort into others' service.
Each person feels duty toward neighbors, and reliable bread reflects this widespread civic virtue.
Each person fears the magistrate's whip, and the law forces good behavior on every trader.
Each person learns by long custom, and tradition alone keeps the bakers turning out their loaves.
context: Adam Smith argued this. Smith's Wealth of Nations (1776) put the point plainly: 'It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.' He called the coordinating effect of self-interest meeting prices the 'invisible hand.'

question: In 1920s Vienna a group of scientists and philosophers met weekly in coffee houses to argue about what counts as real knowledge. They became known as the Vienna Circle. What was their guiding test?
answer: A claim has meaning only if some observation could in principle show it true or false.
choices: A claim has meaning only if some observation could in principle show it true or false.
A claim is trustworthy only if a recognized expert in that field has formally endorsed it.
A claim is meaningful only if the speaker is willing to act as though it were truly the case.
A claim is acceptable only if it agrees with the older traditions of the European universities.
context: The Vienna Circle (Schlick, Carnap, Neurath, Hahn, and others) gathered around 1924 in Vienna cafés and Schlick's seminar. The 'verification principle' was their slogan: meaning equals method of verification. Metaphysics, theology, and traditional ethics all came out (on their reckoning) as literally meaningless. The principle eventually broke on its own teeth — it could not verify itself — but it set the agenda for half a century.

question: Adorno coined the phrase 'the culture industry' for popular music, films, magazines, and radio shows. Why did he insist on the word 'industry' rather than 'culture'?
answer: The products are made the way cars are — to a pattern, for sale, on a schedule.
choices: The products are made the way cars are — to a pattern, for sale, on a schedule.
The artists involved hold formal degrees from universities in the industrial arts.
The audiences pay close attention as if they were workers learning a serious craft.
The critics treat each new film with the rigor that a scientist applies to research.
context: Adorno wanted to block a comforting assumption — that popular songs and Hollywood movies were the natural expression of 'the people.' He argued they were industrially produced consumer goods, designed to standard specifications by a few firms, marketed back to the audience as 'their' culture. The word 'industry' was the punch: an honest description of the production line behind the entertainment.

question: Jackson imagined Mary, a scientist who has lived her whole life in a black-and-white room knowing every physical fact about color. One day she steps outside and sees red for the first time. What did Jackson say happens?
answer: Mary learns something new — proving facts about experience that no physics captures.
choices: Mary learns something new — proving facts about experience that no physics captures.
Mary learns nothing new, since she already knew every physical fact about red.
Mary loses her science and must relearn color from scratch, as a child does.
Mary gains an ability — to imagine red — but acquires no new factual knowledge.
context: Jackson's 'Mary the colour scientist' (1982) attacked physicalism. If complete physical knowledge leaves something out — what red looks like — then the world contains facts beyond the physical. Dennett and Lewis reply that Mary gains ability or learns nothing new.

question: Someone says: 'This sentence is false.' If it is true, then it is false. If it is false, then it is true. What is this puzzle?
answer: The liar paradox — a sentence that can be neither consistently true nor consistently false.
choices: The liar paradox — a sentence that can be neither consistently true nor consistently false.
The sorites paradox — small unnoticed changes adding up to a clearly different situation.
Russell's paradox — a set containing exactly the sets that are not members of themselves.
Zeno's dichotomy — any motion must first cover half a distance, then half the rest forever.
context: Attributed to Epimenides in antiquity, the liar paradox forced 20th-century logic to rethink truth. Tarski concluded that a language cannot consistently contain its own truth-predicate. The distractors are three other famous paradoxes the player may have heard named together.

question: Leopold once shot a wolf and watched the 'fierce green fire' die in its eyes. The county killed the wolves; deer multiplied; the mountains were stripped bare. He called the lesson 'thinking like a mountain.' What did he mean?
answer: A piece of land has a long-term welfare that the eye, focused on immediate gain, misses.
choices: A piece of land has a long-term welfare that the eye, focused on immediate gain, misses.
Nature is a hierarchy with predators on top; removing one collapses the rank order beneath.
Wilderness has rights of its own that override any human claim to use or improve the land.
Ecology is a science, and political decisions about land belong to the trained ecologist.
context: Leopold's 1949 Sand County Almanac founded modern conservation ethics. The wolf-deer-mountain chain is its central image. Distractors are real rival positions: trophic-cascade ecology without ethics, deep-ecology rights talk, technocratic land management.

question: Across many Southern African languages runs the saying: 'A person is a person through other persons.' Tutu and Ramose called it Ubuntu and read it as a philosophical claim. What is the claim?
answer: A self comes into being through recognition by, and bond to, a surrounding community of persons.
choices: A self comes into being through recognition by, and bond to, a surrounding community of persons.
Each person holds inalienable rights from birth; community is a contract that adds nothing real.
The self is illusion; liberation is dissolving the ego into an impersonal cosmic order beyond ties.
Moral worth lies in autonomous rational willing; others matter only because reason commands respect.
context: Ubuntu, developed philosophically by Desmond Tutu and Mogobe Ramose among others, frames personhood relationally rather than individually. The distractors map onto Locke's individualist rights, Advaita Vedanta's dissolution of self, and Kant's autonomy — three real rival accounts of what makes a self.

question: Vine Deloria Jr. titled his 1973 book God Is Red and argued Western and tribal religions answer different opening questions. What did he say the difference was?
answer: Western religion organizes meaning around time and events; tribal religion around place and land.
choices: Western religion organizes meaning around time and events; tribal religion around place and land.
All religions express the same perennial truths in different wrappers; the wrappers vary, not the core.
Religion is the alienated form of social production; both Western and tribal religions cloak relations.
Genuine religion arises only from private mystical experience; ritual and community are later add-ons.
context: Deloria, a Standing Rock Sioux scholar, contrasted sacred time (Sinai, Easter) with sacred place (Bear Butte, Blue Lake). The distractors map onto Huxley's perennialism, Marx's religion-as-alienation, and James's experiential individualism — three real rival framings of what religion is.

question: Stoics and Buddhists, separated by centuries and continents, both diagnosed human suffering as rooted in a wrong relation with desire. Where did they agree on the root cause?
answer: Both blamed attachment to fleeting goods — clinging to what cannot last produces the suffering.
choices: Both blamed attachment to fleeting goods — clinging to what cannot last produces the suffering.
Both denied desire any role at all — the sage simply ceases to want, and cessation is wisdom.
Both treated suffering as illusion — the awakened person sees the pain as empty and unreal.
Both prescribed withdrawal from public life — only the monk or hermit attains the inward peace.
context: Epictetus held suffering comes from judgments about events, not events themselves. The Buddha named tanha — craving — as the second noble truth. They differ on technique: Stoics retrain judgment; Buddhists follow the eightfold path. The distractors are caricatures both schools would reject.

question: A politician's tax plan is criticized only by noting he once cheated on his own taxes. The plan itself goes unaddressed. This move has a Latin name. What is it?
answer: Ad hominem — attacking the arguer rather than the argument they made.
choices: Ad hominem — attacking the arguer rather than the argument they made.
Tu quoque — replying that you also fail rather than answering the point.
Red herring — dragging in something unrelated to distract from the issue.
Straw man — attacking a weakened version of the opponent's real claim.
context: Ad hominem attacks the person, not the argument. A flawed person can still be right; a saint can still be wrong. The argument's truth is independent of who makes it.

question: Someone says trade should be expanded gradually. Their opponent shouts back: 'So you want to ship every job overseas.' The opponent has replaced the real claim with a wilder one. What is this move?
answer: Straw man — attacking a distorted version of the opponent's claim.
choices: Straw man — attacking a distorted version of the opponent's claim.
Red herring — pulling discussion onto a different unrelated topic.
Slippery slope — claiming one step must lead to a disastrous result.
Loaded question — asking something that presupposes a disputed point.
context: A straw man is easier to knock down because you built it. The fix is the steel man: state the opponent's view in its strongest form, then engage that.

question: Atoms fall through the void. But if every atom fell in perfectly parallel lines, nothing could ever happen. What rescue did he propose?
answer: An unpredictable swerve — atoms now and then deviate slightly, so collisions, worlds, and choice become possible.
choices: An unpredictable swerve — atoms now and then deviate slightly, so collisions, worlds, and choice become possible.
A guiding intellect — some divine mind nudges atoms into the patterns the visible cosmos requires for order.
A primal vortex — the original whirling motion of matter explains why parallel paths could never have held.
A web of attractions — atoms pull on one another so parallel falling is broken by their natural affinities.
context: The clinamen, or swerve, was Lucretius and Epicurus's most controversial physics. Cicero mocked it as causeless motion. Defenders said it was what saved the universe from a frozen, pointless rain.

question: The Stoics held that the wise person aims at apatheia. Translators warn this is NOT what English speakers hear in the word. What did Stoics actually mean?
answer: Freedom from the destructive passions — fear, greed, rage — not the absence of love, joy, or rational concern.
choices: Freedom from the destructive passions — fear, greed, rage — not the absence of love, joy, or rational concern.
Withdrawal from civic life — the sage retires from politics entirely to attend solely to the inner citadel.
Total indifference to others — the wise person feels neither pity nor delight at what happens to anyone else.
Calm acceptance of ignorance — the sage suspends judgment on every question that reason cannot fully settle.
context: Modern 'apathy' is a Stoic word with the meaning sandblasted off. The Stoic sage felt friendship, civic duty, and 'good feelings' like rational joy; what they refused were the disordered passions that warp judgment.

question: Crates the Cynic gave away his fortune to live in rags. The aristocrat Hipparchia married him, then joined him sleeping and eating in the open agora. The marriage was a deliberate demonstration. Of what?
answer: That a virtuous life and a real marriage need no property, status, or privacy at all.
choices: That a virtuous life and a real marriage need no property, status, or privacy at all.
That a woman could match any man in argument — Hipparchia debating philosophers as proof.
That romantic love is the highest of human goods, exceeding every other claim on a life.
That children belong to all — Cynic adults would raise any offspring as a shared ward.
context: Crates and Hipparchia were ancient Athens's most scandalous philosophical marriage. They lived, ate, and conducted married life openly in the agora — putting Cynic shamelessness (anaideia) on display as a kind of moral demonstration.

question: Epicureans called wealth, fame, and political office 'natural but unnecessary' — or vain and dangerous. One good they treated as essential and worth the trouble. What was it?
answer: Friendship — a small circle of close, trusted companions who would stand by you when fortune turned bad.
choices: Friendship — a small circle of close, trusted companions who would stand by you when fortune turned bad.
Family — the household into which one is born sets the lifelong limits of duty, affection, and honor.
Citizenship — the engaged civic life remains the highest training the city offers a soul that wants joy.
Solitude — only the philosopher who withdraws from human company can master the discipline fortune demands.
context: Epicurus's Garden was a community. He wrote that of all the goods wisdom provides for the happy life, by far the greatest is friendship. The garden welcomed women and slaves at a time when neither was welcome in most schools — a fact Romans found suspicious for centuries.

question: A clay pot, a wheel hub, and an empty room share one feature that makes each one useful. What did he say it was?
answer: The empty space inside — usefulness comes from absence, not from the material surrounding it.
choices: The empty space inside — usefulness comes from absence, not from the material surrounding it.
The skilled craft of the maker who shapes raw material into a precise and functional form.
The natural function of clay, wood, and stone, which determines the purpose each can serve.
The harmony between maker and material, achieved when neither dominates the creative act.
context: Daodejing Chapter 11. Thirty spokes share one hub: the empty space at the center is what makes the wheel turn. Clay is molded into a vessel: the empty space inside is what holds the water. Doors and windows are cut in a wall: the empty space is what makes the room livable. Laozi was making a general philosophical point — what is absent is often what does the work, and a culture that fixates on what is there will miss what is not there.

question: The Grand Inquisitor confronts a silent Christ in 16th-century Seville. The Church, he says, has fixed Jesus's mistake. What was the mistake?
answer: Christ gave humans freedom of conscience — a burden most cannot bear, when bread, miracle, and authority would content them.
choices: Christ gave humans freedom of conscience — a burden most cannot bear, when bread, miracle, and authority would content them.
Christ refused to found an institution — leaving only sayings, when a hierarchy with sacraments was needed to preserve faith.
Christ taught nonviolence — disarming a faith that had to win territory if its message was to outlast a generation.
Christ idealized poverty — embarrassing a Church that needed wealth to feed the poor and build the schools to teach them.
context: Ivan Karamazov's poem within The Brothers Karamazov (1880). The Inquisitor accuses Christ of overestimating humanity. The three temptations in the wilderness — bread, miracle, authority — were the three things Christ refused, and the three things the Inquisitor says the Church has restored, mercifully, against him. Dostoevsky lets the case land at full force; the rebuttal is not argument but the silent kiss Christ leaves on the old man's lips.

question: The sentence 'This sentence is false' looks innocent. If it is true, then it is false; if false, then true. What does the liar paradox specifically break?
answer: The classical assumption that every meaningful sentence has exactly one stable truth-value, true or false.
choices: The classical assumption that every meaningful sentence has exactly one stable truth-value, true or false.
The grammatical rule that a sentence cannot use the word 'sentence' to talk about its own internal structure.
The empirical principle that any claim worth examining must be checkable against some observation of the world.
The psychological habit of supposing that a careful reader will reach the same conclusion as any other reader.
context: The liar puts pressure on bivalence — the principle that every proposition is true or false. Tarski responded by banning self-reference: truth must live in a higher language than the sentences it judges. Dialetheists like Graham Priest answer instead that the liar is genuinely both, and logic must learn to live with it.

question: One grain is not a heap. Adding a grain to a non-heap cannot make one. So no number of grains is a heap. What does sorites expose?
answer: That many ordinary concepts have vague borders, and tiny changes cannot be ruled out where the borders fall.
choices: That many ordinary concepts have vague borders, and tiny changes cannot be ruled out where the borders fall.
That arithmetic itself is unreliable, because adding small numbers eventually fails to produce a large number.
That the senses are illusions, since a pile we can clearly see may turn out not to fit any concept we hold.
That language is purely a private code, so any two speakers may simply mean different things by 'heap.'
context: Sorites means 'heap' in Greek. Wang's paradox sharpens the move: if a number is small, its successor is small too — so every number is small. Some philosophers respond with epistemicism (there is a precise boundary, hidden from us), others with degree-theoretic logics where 'heap' admits values between 0 and 1.

question: A teacher promises a surprise exam next week — surprise meaning the day cannot be predicted. The students reason that no day works. What does this show?
answer: Self-referential predictions can undermine themselves: a claim about being unpredictable becomes predictable.
choices: Self-referential predictions can undermine themselves: a claim about being unpredictable becomes predictable.
Backward induction is invalid in any setting where future agents hold private information about each other's plans.
Promises about future actions never bind, because circumstances may always change before they come due in fact.
Teachers and students apply incompatible probability rules, so no shared expectation can ever form between them.
context: Rule out Friday — by Thursday night the students would know. So rule out Thursday — same reason. The chain rolls back to Monday, and no day is possible. Yet the exam happens on Wednesday and surprises everyone. The paradox sits at the joint of knowledge, prediction, and self-reference; Quine and Kripke both wrote on it.

question: A monk asked Zhaozhou whether a dog has buddha-nature. Zhaozhou replied, "Mu." Generations sat with this syllable. What were they meant to do with it?
answer: Press the question until conceptual thinking exhausts itself — the answer sought is the collapse of the yes-no frame.
choices: Press the question until conceptual thinking exhausts itself — the answer sought is the collapse of the yes-no frame.
Defend a measured no with scriptural citation — the trainee who could marshal sutras best had passed the test.
Settle the metaphysical fact about dogs — the student had to rule that buddha-nature was present or absent.
Recite the syllable as a protective formula — the chanted sound itself purifies karma over time.
context: Gateless Gate, Case 1. Mahayana doctrine says all beings have buddha-nature, so a flat yes would be correct and useless. Mu refuses the yes-no slot itself. The koan is not a riddle with a hidden answer; it is a wedge driven into the habit that questions like this admit clean propositional answers. The scholastic, metaphysical, and mantric distractors are real Buddhist uses of language Chan is pushing against.

question: Someone says: 'If we lower the drinking age to 18, next it'll be 16, then 14, then toddlers ordering beer.' Each step is treated as inevitable, with no reason given. What is this fallacy?
answer: Slippery slope — asserting one step must trigger a cascade without showing why each step must follow the previous one.
choices: Slippery slope — asserting one step must trigger a cascade without showing why each step must follow the previous one.
False dichotomy — framing only two options when the real range of positions available is in fact substantially wider.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping conclusion from a single case or a sample too thin to support the claim.
Appeal to consequences — claiming a position must be false because its truth would lead to unwelcome outcomes.
context: Slippery-slope arguments can be valid if you give reasons each step really does cause the next. The fallacy is asserting the chain without showing it.

question: A talk-show host says: 'Either you back our entire foreign policy or you hate this country.' Two options where the real range is much wider. What is this move?
answer: False dichotomy — framing only two options when the real range of positions is broader and includes serious alternatives.
choices: False dichotomy — framing only two options when the real range of positions is broader and includes serious alternatives.
Loaded question — asking something whose form presupposes a controversial claim the listener has not yet agreed to.
Equivocation — using one word in two senses inside one argument, so the inference depends on a hidden shift in meaning.
Begging the question — assuming the conclusion in one of the premises, so the argument moves in a small circle.
context: Also called the black-and-white fallacy. The cure: ask whether a third (or fourth) option has been hidden.

question: After a vaccine campaign expands, autism diagnoses rise. Headlines conclude the vaccine caused the rise. The two events did happen in sequence. What is this error?
answer: Post hoc ergo propter hoc — concluding B was caused by A just because B followed A, without ruling out other causes.
choices: Post hoc ergo propter hoc — concluding B was caused by A just because B followed A, without ruling out other causes.
Cum hoc ergo propter hoc — concluding one thing caused another because both happen together, when both share a third cause.
Texas sharpshooter — drawing the target around the bullet holes after firing, finding chance patterns and calling them real.
Hasty generalization — leaping to a sweeping conclusion from a single anecdote or sample too thin to support the claim.
context: Diagnostic criteria for autism widened in the same window vaccine programs expanded — the rise is real, but the cause is largely better identification. Correlation is not causation.

question: Someone argues God exists because the Bible says so, and the Bible is reliable because it is the word of God. The reasoning loops. The conclusion is buried inside the premise. What is this called?
answer: Begging the question — assuming what you are supposed to prove inside one of your premises, so the argument moves in a circle.
choices: Begging the question — assuming what you are supposed to prove inside one of your premises, so the argument moves in a circle.
Appeal to authority — backing a claim by citing an expert's say-so instead of the reasons the expert would give for it.
Equivocation — using one key term in two senses inside one argument, so a step that looks valid trades on shifting meaning.
False dichotomy — framing options as a forced choice between two when the actual range of positions is much broader.
context: Also called petitio principii. The phrase 'begs the question' in everyday speech now usually means 'raises the question' — but in logic it remains this circular move.

question: An opponent points out a cereal claiming to be healthy contains massive sugar. The reply: 'No true Scotsman cares about sugar.' The reply redefines the group. What is this?
answer: No true Scotsman — narrowing a general claim by redefining the category to exclude any counterexample, saving the claim by definition.
choices: No true Scotsman — narrowing a general claim by redefining the category to exclude any counterexample, saving the claim by definition.
Equivocation — sliding between two senses of one key word inside one argument, so a step that looks valid rests on a hidden shift.
Special pleading — exempting a favored case from a general rule without giving a principled reason why this case is different.
Tu quoque — replying to a criticism by pointing out the critic also fails, rather than engaging whether the criticism is correct.
context: Antony Flew named the move from an imagined Scotsman who insists no true Scot puts sugar in his porridge — then, faced with one who does, says no TRUE Scot would.

question: An argument runs: 'Feathers are light. What is light cannot be dark. So feathers cannot be dark.' The form looks tight, but one word shifts meaning between lines. What is this fallacy?
answer: Equivocation — using one key word in two senses across premises, so an argument looks valid only because the meaning quietly shifted.
choices: Equivocation — using one key word in two senses across premises, so an argument looks valid only because the meaning quietly shifted.
Composition — assuming what is true of each part of a whole must also be true of the whole, when wholes and parts can differ.
Amphiboly — exploiting a sentence's grammatical ambiguity, where one reading supports the conclusion and the other does not.
Division — assuming what is true of a whole must also hold of every part, when whole-properties need not transfer to pieces.
context: 'Light' shifts from 'low in weight' to 'bright.' Equivocation is the engine of most word-puzzle paradoxes and a surprising number of bad political arguments.

question: Oakeshott set the engineer who scraps the inherited machine and starts again against a different figure who refuses. What did he say that second figure prizes?
answer: The familiar, the workable, and the small adjustment over a perfect design that has never been tried in life.
choices: The familiar, the workable, and the small adjustment over a perfect design that has never been tried in life.
The authority of legitimate hierarchy and the duty of each rank to defer to the wisdom of the rank above it.
The unchanging moral law revealed in scripture and tradition over the shifting opinions of any human council.
The hard-won settlement of past struggles, which no living generation has any standing to revisit or to undo.
context: Oakeshott called this the conservative disposition — not a doctrine but a temperament. To be conservative was to prefer 'the tried to the untried, the actual to the possible, the convenient to the perfect.' Not because the present is good, but because it is ours.

question: Ordinary life is structurally unhappy, not by accident but by design. What was the structure of his case for pessimism?
answer: Will is endless wanting; each satisfaction breeds new lack, while contentment quickly slides into boredom.
choices: Will is endless wanting; each satisfaction breeds new lack, while contentment quickly slides into boredom.
Sin entered through one act; every later misery flows from a free will turned away from its true good.
History repeats the same cycle; ages of vigor decay into corruption, then collapse, then begin again.
Pleasure and pain balance on the ledger; lives feel poor only because losses weigh heavier than gains.
context: The argument is not a mood. Striving without an object is suffering, since wanting is a felt lack. Striving that reaches its object dissolves the wanting and leaves boredom, which is just the will hunting for a new lack. Between the two there is no third state where the will simply rests. Pessimism for Schopenhauer is the honest report of that swing, not a temperament that good fortune could cure.

question: Tastes, smells, and colors live in the perceiver, while shape, number, and motion live in the body itself. What did he say about a feather drawn across skin?
answer: The feather has shape and motion; the tickle exists only in the tickled animal, not in the feather.
choices: The feather has shape and motion; the tickle exists only in the tickled animal, not in the feather.
The feather and the tickle are equally real; both belong to the joint event, not to either party alone.
The feather has a hidden tickling power; sensitive bodies merely register a quality the feather carries.
The feather and the tickle alike are mental; matter is an inference, never appearing to any mind directly.
context: In Il Saggiatore (1623), Galileo used the feather-tickle to argue that secondary qualities are not in objects. Locke later named the primary/secondary distinction; Berkeley pushed further and denied primary qualities a mind-independent home too.

question: Vine Deloria Jr.'s God Is Red (1973) argued Western and tribal religions answer different opening questions. What was his core claim?
answer: Western religion orders meaning around time and events; tribal religion orders meaning around place and the land itself.
choices: Western religion orders meaning around time and events; tribal religion orders meaning around place and the land itself.
All religions encode the same perennial truths beneath surface symbols; only the cultural wrapping really varies between them.
Religion is the alienated form of social production; both Western and tribal forms mask the material relations beneath them.
Genuine religion arises from individual mystical experience; communal ritual is later scaffolding added on top of that core.
context: Deloria argued sacred history (Sinai, Calvary) frames Christianity as temporal, while sacred places (Bear Butte, Blue Lake) frame tribal religion as spatial. Distractors map onto Huxley, Marx, and James.

question: Condorcet, hiding from the Jacobins who would soon kill him, proved a theorem about juries voting independently on a yes-or-no question. What did the result show?
answer: If each voter is more than half likely right, the majority's accuracy rises toward certainty as the jury grows.
choices: If each voter is more than half likely right, the majority's accuracy rises toward certainty as the jury grows.
If voters reason independently, cycles among three options make no stable collective ranking possible at all.
If voters share information, larger assemblies converge on the median voter's view regardless of any truth.
If voters are evenly split, the lottery of a tiebreaker yields outcomes no worse than further debate would.
context: Condorcet's 1785 jury theorem is one of the first mathematical defenses of democracy: many fallible judges, voting independently, outperform any one expert. He wrote it while drafting a constitution. The Terror caught him in 1794; he died in a cell, having argued to the end for indefinite human progress through reason.

question: Aldo Leopold's *A Sand County Almanac* (1949) closes with the 'land ethic.' Ethics had governed person-to-person, then person-to-society. What was his next extension?
answer: The moral community widens to include soils, waters, plants, animals — the land as fellow member.
choices: The moral community widens to include soils, waters, plants, animals — the land as fellow member.
Wildlife policy must rest on scientific data alone, since aesthetic responses cannot ground real duties.
Private ownership of wild land is the only safeguard, since shared resources collapse under common use.
Conservation succeeds only when nature is shown to serve the long-run welfare of future human beings.
context: Leopold's move was structural: ethics had widened twice — kin, then citizens — and the next widening was to the biotic community. 'A thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community.' Land becomes member, not commodity.

question: Holmes Rolston III argued nature has 'intrinsic value' — but he meant something stronger than 'humans find it beautiful.' What was his actual claim?
answer: Living things pursue their own good objectively; that achievement carries value with or without a valuer.
choices: Living things pursue their own good objectively; that achievement carries value with or without a valuer.
Wild places trigger spiritual responses in humans that no manufactured environment can ever replicate.
Ecosystems aggregate the preferences of sentient creatures, and that sum grounds the value we ascribe.
Biodiversity is irreplaceable insurance for future humans, so present generations owe its preservation.
context: Rolston's claim is metaphysical, not psychological. A wild plant pursues its own telos — water, light, reproduction — and that 'good of its own' exists prior to any observer. Value is *discovered* in nature, not *projected* onto it. The strongest realist position in environmental ethics.

question: Douglass broke with Garrison over the U.S. Constitution. Garrison called it 'a covenant with death.' What did Douglass come to argue?
answer: Read by its plain words, the Constitution is a liberty document; slavery survives only by extra-textual compromise.
choices: Read by its plain words, the Constitution is a liberty document; slavery survives only by extra-textual compromise.
The Constitution was a pro-slavery bargain; the abolitionist's duty is to break the Union itself to be free of it.
The Constitution is neither pro- nor anti-slavery; the matter was left wholly to states and to private conscience.
The Constitution's natural-rights language was rhetoric for foreigners; its working clauses settled little of substance.
context: Garrison burned a copy of the Constitution on July 4, 1854, calling it a pact with slaveholders. Douglass, after long study of figures like Lysander Spooner, came to the opposite view: the document's plain language nowhere named slavery, and the Preamble's purposes were freedom's.

question: Calhoun rejected 'all men are created equal' as a dangerous Lockean abstraction. What did he say was true of human beings instead?
answer: No state of nature ever existed; humans are born into ranked societies, and liberty is a reward earned by advanced peoples.
choices: No state of nature ever existed; humans are born into ranked societies, and liberty is a reward earned by advanced peoples.
Natural rights are real, but only the states, not the federal Union, may translate those rights into binding civil law.
Equality is moral, never political; the framers wrote the Declaration as inspiration, not as binding civil doctrine.
Men begin equal in some natural sense, but the social compact trades that equality for the order any society needs.
context: Calhoun's Disquisition on Government (1851) argued the founders had imported a false abstraction from Locke. Men, he said, are never found in any 'state of nature' — only in societies, ranked. The bank holds the natural-rights tradition Calhoun rejected; his position is presented here in his own terms.

question: Sakharov designed the Soviet hydrogen bomb at twenty-nine, then became the regime most famous dissident. His 1968 essay Reflections explained the turn. What did he argue?
answer: The Soviet and Western systems were converging, and only mutual openness could prevent nuclear catastrophe.
choices: The Soviet and Western systems were converging, and only mutual openness could prevent nuclear catastrophe.
Socialism had been correct, and needed only the removal of the Stalin clique to flower as Lenin had meant.
Nuclear deterrence had failed, and unilateral Soviet disarmament was the one path to long-term survival.
Scientists owed loyalty to the state that trained them, but only within limits set by the laws of physics.
context: Reflections on Progress, Peaceful Coexistence, and Intellectual Freedom circulated in samizdat in 1968 and reached the West within months. Sakharov argued the two superpowers were borrowing each other's flaws and would either converge into something humane or destroy each other; the choice ran through openness. The price for saying so was internal exile to Gorky.

question: The Communist Manifesto opens by reading recorded history as the struggle of freeman and slave, lord and serf, master and journeyman. What kind of history is this?
answer: A history of the relations of production — each age defined by who owns the means of work and who works.
choices: A history of the relations of production — each age defined by who owns the means of work and who works.
A history of great men — each age defined by the legislator or general whose will set the course of his time.
A history of national spirit — each age defined by a particular people's gradual self-discovery in events.
A history of liberty's advance — each age defined by the rights successive generations gradually secured.
context: The Manifesto's opening was a deliberate provocation. Other readers of history saw kings, philosophers, providence, race, or the gradual expansion of freedom. Marx and Engels said: look at the productive arrangement first. Who owns the field, the workshop, the factory? The political stories then sit as expressions of an older quarrel beneath them.

question: No two genuinely distinct things can share every property in common. What follows if you ever found two leaves exactly alike in every respect?
answer: They would not be two leaves at all but one and the same leaf, however many times you tried to count them.
choices: They would not be two leaves at all but one and the same leaf, however many times you tried to count them.
They would still be two leaves, distinguished by the bare fact of occupying different places on the tree.
They would be two leaves only because the world has classed them so by long convention and naming custom.
They would be two leaves while the eye finds them apart; sameness only obtains when no observer is present.
context: The principle of the identity of indiscernibles. Leibniz argued you can search the gardens of Hannover all day; you will never find two leaves matching in every detail. Bare numerical difference, with no qualitative ground at all, was for him no difference worth the name.

question: Mixing your labor with unowned nature makes a thing yours — pick an apple, the apple is yours. But he attached a famous proviso. What did he require?
answer: You must leave enough, and as good, for others; appropriation cannot leave latecomers worse off than before.
choices: You must leave enough, and as good, for others; appropriation cannot leave latecomers worse off than before.
You must work the land productively; uncultivated holdings revert to the commons after a year of disuse.
You must obtain consent from a representative assembly; private claims need public ratification to count.
You must share with the poor; charity is a debt owed from any holding above bare subsistence levels.
context: Locke's proviso in the Second Treatise has shaped every modern theory of property. Nozick later argued the proviso is met whenever appropriation makes most people better off through trade; critics argue it has not been met where land was simply taken.

question: William Rowe pointed at a fawn burning slowly in a forest fire no one will ever know about. He used the case to press the problem of evil. What was his argument?
answer: Such suffering looks pointless; if it really is, a good God would have prevented it, so probably none exists.
choices: Such suffering looks pointless; if it really is, a good God would have prevented it, so probably none exists.
Such suffering shows nature is amoral; God may exist, but is not the moral agent religious tradition supposes.
Such suffering reveals logical inconsistency; the very concept of a good creator collapses on inspection.
Such suffering is mystery, not problem; one consents to it as one consents to a hard saying of revelation.
context: Rowe's 1979 fawn case is the canonical evidential problem of evil: not that God and evil are inconsistent, but that gratuitous-seeming suffering is evidence against God. Skeptical theists reply we are in no position to judge what reasons God might have. The exchange has shaped contemporary philosophy of religion for forty years.

question: Al-Kindi worked in 9th-century Baghdad while caliphs paid translators to put Greek thought into Arabic. He was first to write philosophy as an Arab Muslim. What core move enabled this?
answer: Treating reason and revelation as one truth — what Greeks proved and what the Quran taught had to agree.
choices: Treating reason and revelation as one truth — what Greeks proved and what the Quran taught had to agree.
Treating Greek philosophy as preparation — pagan reason a stage the Quran would soon bring to closure.
Treating revelation as decoration — useful for the masses but unneeded by a philosopher reading Aristotle.
Treating reason as foreign — a tool the Muslim may use but never weigh against the scripture itself.
context: Al-Kindi worked in the Bayt al-Hikma, the House of Wisdom, where translations of Plato, Aristotle, Plotinus, Euclid, and Galen poured into Arabic. He argued in On First Philosophy that truth-from-wherever is welcome — adopting Greek philosophy in no way threatened the faith, since both reach the one God. The whole later falsafa tradition rests on this move.

question: British empiricists treated relations — 'next to,' 'before,' 'caused by' — as things the mind adds to bare sensations. James's radical empiricism reversed this. What did he insist?
answer: Relations between things are themselves directly experienced, not added after the felt items arrive.
choices: Relations between things are themselves directly experienced, not added after the felt items arrive.
Relations between things are mind-independent structures the senses gradually disclose to careful observers.
Relations between things are linguistic conventions that vary by culture and reshape what one can perceive.
Relations between things are forms imposed by the understanding, organizing an otherwise formless flux.
context: James's slogan: experience comes already strung together. You feel the 'and,' the 'with,' the 'next.' Hume had to construct continuity from discrete impressions; James said continuity was there in the stream from the start — the 'stream of thought.'

question: Subjects may resist a government, but only under specific conditions. What did he say was required to justify resistance?
answer: The rulers must act against the trust, attacking the people's lives, liberties, or properties under colour of law.
choices: The rulers must act against the trust, attacking the people's lives, liberties, or properties under colour of law.
A majority of qualified citizens must vote, in lawful assembly, that the present magistrates have lost their office.
An evident tyrant must rule, against whom any private man may rise in arms once conscience is fully convinced.
A long train of distant abuses must occur, such that no improvement could reasonably be hoped from petition.
context: Locke's right of resistance (Second Treatise, chapter 19) is narrower than later 'whenever I dislike them' caricatures. The government must breach its fiduciary trust; the resort is to the people as a whole, not to private judgment. Jefferson borrowed Locke's 'long train' phrasing, but the principle is Lockean trust-violation.

question: If you do an outwardly wicked deed believing it right, you are not guilty as you would be knowingly. What does that imply about where moral guilt sits?
answer: Guilt sits in inward consent to what one believes is wrong; the external act adds nothing morally on its own.
choices: Guilt sits in inward consent to what one believes is wrong; the external act adds nothing morally on its own.
Guilt sits in the external act itself, regardless of intent; the deed alone determines the moral weight.
Guilt sits in the consequences produced; an act is wrong in proportion to the actual harm it causes.
Guilt sits in violation of divine command; only direct contradiction of God's will makes an act sinful.
context: Abelard's *Scito te ipsum* ('Know Thyself,' c. 1140) located sin in the interior act of consent, not the external deed. A persecutor convinced he is doing God's work in killing apostles is not guilty as guilt is usually understood; one who consents to evil knowingly is. The thesis scandalized contemporaries and was condemned at the Council of Sens (1141), but it pushed Western ethics decisively toward intention — a line running through Kant and modern criminal law's *mens rea*.

question: Nyaya, founded by Gautama, asked how many sources of valid knowledge — pramanas — actually exist. Their answer set the agenda for centuries. What was it?
answer: Four — perception, inference, comparison, and reliable testimony — each with its own characteristic failure modes.
choices: Four — perception, inference, comparison, and reliable testimony — each with its own characteristic failure modes.
Two — perception and inference — since the others reduce to these or simply fail to deliver knowledge at all.
Six — perception, inference, comparison, testimony, non-perception, postulation; nothing less covers the field.
One — perception alone — since inference and testimony are chains of perception under close logical analysis.
context: Nyaya Sutras 1.1.3. Gautama's four are pratyaksha, anumana, upamana, and shabda, each with named failure modes — illusion ruins a perception, an ill-formed middle term ruins an inference. Distractors are the rival counts: Buddhist Dignaga at two, Mimamsa at six, Charvaka at one.

question: Samkhya, one of the oldest Hindu schools, gave a dualist analysis of existence. What were its two ultimate categories, and how related?
answer: Purusha (silent witnessing awareness) and Prakriti (active matter); bondage is awareness mistaking itself for matter.
choices: Purusha (silent witnessing awareness) and Prakriti (active matter); bondage is awareness mistaking itself for matter.
Brahman as the one source and maya as its appearance; bondage is mistaking the appearance for the source.
Soul and body as distinct substances within the human; bondage is the soul becoming attached to bodily pleasures.
God and creation as utterly different orders; bondage is human effort to bridge them, release the divine grace.
context: Samkhya-Karika of Ishvara Krishna (c. 4th c.). Samkhya is non-theistic — it gets along without a creator god — and provides Yoga with its metaphysical framework. Distractors: Advaita's brahman/maya (which sounds similar but is monist), Cartesian/scholastic substance-dualism, and a Christian-Augustinian grace frame.

question: The Mimamsa school defended a startling thesis about the Vedas that looks like piety but is sharper underneath. What did Mimamsa actually argue?
answer: The Vedas are eternal, uncreated, and authorless — no god stands behind them; ritual obligation is built into reality itself.
choices: The Vedas are eternal, uncreated, and authorless — no god stands behind them; ritual obligation is built into reality itself.
The Vedas were dictated by a creator god to ancient sages, and the school's task is to defend divine authorship.
The Vedas were composed once at the start of each cosmic age by a wise sage chosen at the dawn of that age.
The Vedas hold authority only for ritual; metaphysical claims must be tested against perception and inference.
context: Mimamsa, systematized by Jaimini's sutras and later Kumarila Bhatta and Prabhakara (7th–8th c.). The school is famously non-theistic — Kumarila wrote detailed arguments against a creator god — and grounds Vedic authority in the apaurusheya (non-human-authored) doctrine. The surprise: rigorous scripture-defense ends in atheism. Distractors: the popular divine-author view, Puranic cyclic-author view, Charvaka materialism.

question: Tooby and Cosmides gave the same logic puzzle in two forms. Abstract symbols: 25% solve it. 'If drinking, must be 21': 75% solve it. What did they argue the gap shows?
answer: Mind is not a general logic engine; an evolved module fires to detect cheaters in social-exchange rules.
choices: Mind is not a general logic engine; an evolved module fires to detect cheaters in social-exchange rules.
Mind is a general logic engine; abstract puzzles just take longer for lacking concrete handles to grasp.
Mind learns logic from culture; societies that drill rule-following raise scores on abstract Wason puzzles.
Mind is bottlenecked by working memory; concrete framings free resources that logic problems consume.
context: The puzzle is Wason's selection task. Tooby and Cosmides argued the cheater-detection result is hard to square with a domain-general reasoner: the same logical form is easy in one wrapping, near-impossible in another. Their conclusion — the architecture of mind is a kit of specialized tools — became a founding claim of evolutionary psychology.

question: Twin studies put adult-height heritability near 0.80. Reading this as 'height is 80% genetic in me' is a basic mistake, behavioral geneticists insist. What does the figure actually measure?
answer: Share of trait variance in a population that tracks genetic variance — not any individual's trait.
choices: Share of trait variance in a population that tracks genetic variance — not any individual's trait.
Share of trait variance fixed at conception — the part no environment or upbringing could later move.
Share of trait variance explained by named gene variants identified in genome-wide association studies.
Share of trait copied directly from parent to child — read off the simple parent-offspring correlation.
context: Heritability is a population statistic indexed to a given environment. The same trait can have heritability near zero in one setting and near one in another — change the variance in environments and the ratio moves. The number cannot be applied to a single person, and it cannot tell you whether a between-group difference is genetic or environmental.

question: Logicians distinguish valid from sound arguments. An argument can be one without the other. What does soundness demand that mere validity does not?
answer: Validity means the conclusion follows from the premises; soundness adds that the premises themselves are true, so the conclusion is guaranteed true.
choices: Validity means the conclusion follows from the premises; soundness adds that the premises themselves are true, so the conclusion is guaranteed true.
Validity means a reasonable audience would accept it; soundness adds hard evidence backing, so soundness layers empirical support on persuasion.
Validity means true premises and conclusion; soundness adds that the form alone carries the inference, so soundness layers structure on truth.
Validity is informal and compelling; soundness adds strict deductive-system rules, so soundness layers formal rigor on informal persuasion.
context: Validity is about form: IF the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be. Soundness adds the further condition that the premises actually are true. Aristotle's Prior Analytics distinguished form from content. Validity is purely about form (does conclusion follow from premises). Soundness adds: are the premises actually true?

question: Kahneman called it one of the most stubborn errors in reasoning. A disease affects 1 in 1000. A test is 99% accurate. You test positive. Untrained guesses say 99%. The real answer is far lower. What is the error?
answer: Base-rate neglect — ignoring how rare the underlying condition is, so the prior gets dropped and the test result gets all the weight.
choices: Base-rate neglect — ignoring how rare the underlying condition is, so the prior gets dropped and the test result gets all the weight.
Confirmation bias — seeking information that supports a belief already held, while overlooking evidence pointing the other way.
Gambler's fallacy — thinking past independent events shape future ones, like expecting tails because a coin keeps landing heads.
Anchoring — letting an early irrelevant number drag your final estimate toward itself by a measurable systematic margin.
context: Bayes's theorem fixes this. With a 1-in-1000 prior, 99% accurate test, 1% false-positive rate, the actual probability you have the disease given a positive result is about 9%.

question: The Founders shared a 'tragic' picture of human nature, while Godwin and Condorcet shared its rival. What did the tragic picture insist on?
answer: Self-interest and bias are built into human beings, so good policy works by tradeoffs, not by perfecting the citizen.
choices: Self-interest and bias are built into human beings, so good policy works by tradeoffs, not by perfecting the citizen.
Most people are decent at heart, so wise institutions need only remove the corrupting influences keeping virtue down.
Human beings are radically free, so any picture of fixed nature is a refusal of the agency real politics presupposes.
Human beings are mostly products of their class position, so changing the economy will change every other moral fact.
context: Sowell called this the 'constrained vision' in A Conflict of Visions. He thought most political disagreements between left and right trace back to whether people read human nature as tragic and fixed or as plastic and improvable. The disagreement is older than the political camps that inherit it.

question: Kuhn used the famous duck-rabbit picture to illustrate something about paradigm shifts. What was the analogy meant to convey?
answer: Once you see one figure, you see different shapes — the same evidence now reads differently because the categories themselves have changed.
choices: Once you see one figure, you see different shapes — the same evidence now reads differently because the categories themselves have changed.
Once you see one figure, you cannot see the other — the categories of one paradigm are not simultaneously available with another's.
Once you see one figure, you can switch at will — paradigms are toolkits scientists choose pragmatically for the task at hand.
Once you see one figure, you know everything in the image — paradigms gather all the facts an inquiry will ever need under one frame.
context: Kuhn's duck-rabbit captured what he called the gestalt-switch of revolutions. The world had not changed; the scientists had. What counted as data, what called for explanation, what counted as a good answer — all had shifted together, and the new figures of the field could not always be reduced to the old.

question: Anthropologists once thought emotional expressions might vary radically across cultures. Paul Ekman ran a study with the Fore people of New Guinea. What did he find?
answer: Six basic facial expressions — happiness, sadness, anger, fear, disgust, surprise — were recognized across a culture with no prior contact with Western faces.
choices: Six basic facial expressions — happiness, sadness, anger, fear, disgust, surprise — were recognized across a culture with no prior contact with Western faces.
Most expressions were culturally specific, with only one universal — the smile of greeting common to all human groups studied.
Recognition rates varied with exposure to outside media — groups with no media access had no reliable ability to identify Western expressions.
Expression was largely learned through childhood imitation — Fore children raised in isolation showed no spontaneous emotional faces at first.
context: Ekman's mid-1960s fieldwork tested a long-running anthropological debate: are emotional expressions cultural conventions or human universals? His New Guinea results, replicated since, supported a universalist conclusion against the cultural-relativist orthodoxy of the period. Some facial expressions, it turns out, predate language and travel across all known human groups.

question: Haidt and Lukianoff in The Coddling of the American Mind diagnosed three 'great untruths' shaping a generation. They argued each contradicted ancient wisdom. What were they?
answer: What does not kill you makes you weaker; trust your feelings; life is a battle between good people and evil people — each false, each widely taught.
choices: What does not kill you makes you weaker; trust your feelings; life is a battle between good people and evil people — each false, each widely taught.
Hard work has no payoff; only structure matters; group identity exhausts the analysis — each false, each widely taught in higher education.
Reality is socially constructed; objective inquiry is a power play; lived experience trumps argument — each false, each common in current curricula.
Knowledge is private to subgroups; cross-cultural dialogue is harmful; tradition is bondage — each false, each circulated in contemporary discourse.
context: Haidt and Lukianoff drew the title's images from Nietzsche, Buddha, and Solzhenitsyn — three traditions saying the opposite of each modern teaching. Children raised on the three untruths, they argued, will be fragile, emotionally dysregulated, and prone to seeing politics as Manichaean. The book's argument was empirical (rising mental health statistics in young people) and philosophical at once.

question: Pythagoreans heard the cosmos as music. Each planet's orbit, they said, made a tone, and the tones formed a heavenly harmony. Why, they asked, can humans not hear it?
answer: We have been immersed in it since birth — like the smith deaf to his hammers, our ears have lost the contrast that would let it register.
choices: We have been immersed in it since birth — like the smith deaf to his hammers, our ears have lost the contrast that would let it register.
We lack the right purifying rites — initiates who completed Pythagorean training could in fact hear the music, but kept the reports closely guarded.
We hear only the lowest tones of the cosmic scale — the higher pitches belong to outer spheres beyond what the human ear can ever pick up.
We perceive the music as ordinary thought rather than sound — the harmony enters the mind directly as the rational order of reasoning.
context: Aristotle, De Caelo II.9. The image runs through Cicero's Dream of Scipio, Boethius, Kepler's Harmonices Mundi, and Shakespeare's Lorenzo on the moonlit lawn in Merchant of Venice.

question: The Pyrrhonian Skeptics aimed at tranquility through suspended judgment. To suspend judgment, they used a technique called isostheneia. What did it actually involve?
answer: Setting equally strong arguments on opposing sides of any question — once the cases balance exactly, the mind cannot tilt either way and urgency lifts.
choices: Setting equally strong arguments on opposing sides of any question — once the cases balance exactly, the mind cannot tilt either way and urgency lifts.
Cultivating indifference to worldly goods through long meditation — once nothing in the world holds value, the question of choosing no longer arises.
Submitting every belief to systematic doubt by hypothetical demons — once no belief survives the strongest challenge, the mind rests from claims.
Practicing bodily detachment through fasting and physical hardship — once the senses are weakened by ascetic training, conflicting reports cease.
context: Sextus Empiricus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism I. Equipollence produces epoche (suspension), and epoche reportedly produces ataraxia (tranquility) — which the Skeptic, having sought nothing, finds has come.

question: McMahan asked a sharper version of the abortion/euthanasia question. Most bioethics asks whether the being is a person — yes/no — and lets that settle the case. McMahan said no: what matters is how strongly your current self is psychologically tied to your future. He called these its time-relative interests. What follows?
answer: Wrongness of ending a life scales with the present psychological link to the future. Embryos and the deeply demented lose far less by dying than middle-aged adults.
choices: Wrongness of ending a life scales with the present psychological link to the future. Embryos and the deeply demented lose far less by dying than middle-aged adults.
Killing any sentient being is the same wrong, since loss of subjective experience cannot be ranked by quantity without slipping into arbitrary speciesism.
Ending a life is wrong only when the being can presently form a verbal preference to continue existing — the preference-utilitarian line McMahan rejects.
Wrongness depends only on the future experiences a being is deprived of, with no extra weight given to whether a present self is psychologically tied to it.
context: In *The Ethics of Killing* (2002), McMahan rejected the all-or-nothing personhood framework that drives most bioethics debates. His time-relative interests account asks how strongly the present subject is psychologically bound to its own future. A late-term fetus has weak ties; a demented adult has lost them. Death takes less from beings whose grip on their own future is thin. The view delivers unusually graded verdicts on abortion, euthanasia, and animal killing alike. Utilitarianism (Bentham, 1789; Mill, 1861) — actions are right insofar as they produce the greatest happiness for the greatest number. Mill refined Bentham by ranking higher and lower pleasures.

question: Warhol's 'Brillo Box' looked identical to the cardboard boxes in any supermarket. The supermarket boxes were not art; Warhol's were. Arthur Danto built a theory around the puzzle. What did he conclude?
answer: What makes something art is not its visible properties but its place in a theory and history — the 'artworld' of practices that lets an object count as art.
choices: What makes something art is the artist's sincere expression of an inner emotion in the object, which the indifferent factory worker never gives to ordinary goods.
What makes something art is the arrangement of formal qualities — line, color, mass — that produces aesthetic emotion regardless of subject matter or origin.
What makes something art is not its visible properties but its place in a theory and history — the 'artworld' of practices that lets an object count as art.
What makes something art is craft excellence relative to a tradition — fine joinery makes a chair art, and a printed carton fails by showing no comparable skill.
context: Danto's 1964 essay 'The Artworld' asked the obvious question: if two things look identical and one is art, the difference cannot be perceptual. He argued artworks live inside an 'atmosphere of theory' without which the category does not apply. George Dickie later formalized this as the 'institutional theory': art is whatever the relevant institutions confer that status on. Critics from Scruton onward argue this collapses art into power.

question: Gersonides faced a dilemma: if God foreknows every free choice, choice is not free; if not, omniscience cracks. He chose. What did he conclude God does not know?
answer: Future contingents — not-yet-settled choices of free agents — though He knows all general orders.
choices: Future contingents — not-yet-settled choices of free agents — though He knows all general orders.
Particular material things — only their universal forms, since matter is the principle of imperfection.
The acts of evil agents — for God turns away from sin and does not behold the deeds of the wicked.
Anything outside Himself — God knows only Himself, and the world follows as a side effect of that.
context: Levi ben Gershon (1288–1344), in *The Wars of the Lord* III, argued that genuine contingency is built into the world; God knows the order of things as ordered, but the not-yet-actualized branch of a free choice is not yet a fact for anyone, including God. Crescas attacked this fiercely, defending full foreknowledge with compatibilist freedom. Aquinas had taken a third route: God sees all time at once eternally. Gersonides' move was the boldest of medieval theism.

question: Hakuin Ekaku revived Rinzai Zen in eighteenth-century Japan by systematizing koan study. He gave students an opening koan he had devised himself. What does 'the sound of one hand clapping' aim to do?
answer: Defeat the discursive mind's attempt to find a referent — there is no answer to fetch, and exhausting the search is where the practice begins.
choices: Defeat the discursive mind's attempt to find a referent — there is no answer to fetch, and exhausting the search is where the practice begins.
Test the student's familiarity with classical Chinese — the koan only makes sense in its original Tang-dynasty context, which Hakuin used as an entry exam for serious study.
Train the imagination to visualize impossible objects vividly — the meditative skill that Hakuin held was required for the more advanced visualizations later in the curriculum.
Convey the inseparability of action and inaction — the right hand cannot clap alone, just as conventional life cannot proceed without the support of monastic discipline.
context: Hakuin's 'sekishu no onjo' (the sound of one hand) was constructed to replace the older Mu koan as a fresh barrier for beginners. The point is not that there exists some hidden right answer that a clever student can deduce — koan practice in Rinzai uses such barriers to bring the discursive intellect to a halt, opening a different mode of seeing. The Soto school under Dogen emphasized shikantaza (just sitting) over koan work, marking a real intra-Zen split.

question: Daoism shares with Confucianism the term de — usually rendered 'virtue' or 'power.' But Daoist de means something different from Confucian de. What is the contrast that the Daodejing presses?
answer: Confucian de is cultivated character that earns moral standing; Daoist de is the inherent power a thing has when it is fully itself, without effort to be anything other than what it is.
choices: Confucian de is cultivated character that earns moral standing; Daoist de is the inherent power a thing has when it is fully itself, without effort to be anything other than what it is.
Confucian de belongs to humans only and to humans only after deliberate training; Daoist de is the property of any natural object whatsoever and lacks any specifically moral content at all.
Confucian de is taught through ritual practice in the village school; Daoist de is acquired through ascetic discipline practiced in the mountains far from the corrupting influence of cities.
Confucian de is a public reputation built across many years; Daoist de is the inner felt sense of one's own goodness that requires no outside witness or acknowledgement in any form.
context: Daodejing chapters 38, 51, and 65 develop Daoist de. The line in chapter 38 — 'The highest de is not de, and so it has de; the lowest de does not lose de, and so it has no de' — pokes directly at the Confucian project of self-conscious cultivation. Daoist de is more like what a sharp knife or a clear stream has: it is the way that thing works when nothing obstructs its functioning. Confucian de is a moral inheritance accumulated through effort; the two readings of the same word run on different rails.

question: Vine Deloria Jr. in God Is Red (1973) argued that Christian thought treats history as the primary stage of revelation while Indigenous American thought treats place as the primary stage. What does the contrast generate?
answer: Sacred history happens to a people across time and travels with them; sacred place happens to a particular landscape and cannot be transplanted — uprooting a people severs them from revelation itself.
choices: Sacred history happens to a people across time and travels with them; sacred place happens to a particular landscape and cannot be transplanted — uprooting a people severs them from revelation itself.
Sacred history is a linear sequence with a beginning and end; sacred place is cyclical and renews itself in spring — the contrast is between progressive and recurrent visions of time alone.
Sacred history is recorded in scriptures that travel; sacred place is recorded in oral traditions that fade — the contrast is methodological rather than reflecting any deeper metaphysical commitment.
Sacred history concerns events that did happen; sacred place concerns events that could happen — the contrast is between actual and possible, with each tradition prioritizing one of them.
context: Deloria (Standing Rock Sioux, 1933-2005) wrote God Is Red as a sustained comparison of Christian and Indigenous religious thought. His core claim — that the sacred geography of Indigenous traditions is not a primitive prefiguring of universalist religion but a genuine philosophical alternative — has shaped subsequent Indigenous philosophy. The implication for federal land policy is direct: removing a people from their landscape destroys what cannot be moved with them, in a way unintelligible to a religion that travels through history rather than dwelling in place.

question: Even an absolute sovereign cannot demand one specific thing of a subject. Where did he draw the limit?
answer: A subject is never bound to submit to his own immediate killing — the contract was for self-preservation, and that limit holds.
choices: A subject is never bound to submit to his own immediate killing — the contract was for self-preservation, and that limit holds.
A subject is never bound to confess a religious belief he does not hold — Hobbes treated conscience as outside the sovereign's reach.
A subject is never bound to surrender his property — Hobbes anticipated Locke in giving property a foundation prior to the state.
A subject is never bound to obey an unjust law — the sovereign loses authority over any command demonstrably contrary to reason.
context: Hobbes was surprisingly clear on this. Even the absolute sovereign cannot demand that a man cooperate in his own death. The contract was rational only because it secured self-preservation; a command to die ran against the very reason for entering the contract. Religion, property, and justice — all could be regulated. Life itself could not be required.

question: Sidgwick saw a 'dualism of practical reason' that he never resolved. What was the deep tension he diagnosed?
