answer: Rational egoism and rational universalism each seem self-evident, yet neither can be reduced to the other on any defensible footing.
choices: Rational egoism and rational universalism each seem self-evident, yet neither can be reduced to the other on any defensible footing.
Pleasure and pain are commensurable in the agent but not across persons, so no aggregate calculation can ever be coherent.
Common-sense morality and utilitarian calculation diverge at the margins, so utilitarianism must absorb common-sense rules wholesale.
Higher and lower pleasures are incommensurable, so Mill's qualitative move collapses the calculus into incomparable rankings.
context: Sidgwick's Methods of Ethics (1874) is the most rigorous utilitarian work in English. He could find no rational refutation of someone who said 'Why should I care about others?' yet also found the impartial standpoint self-evident. The two axioms together generate no contradiction in any particular case — yet neither is a theorem of the other. Utilitarianism (Bentham, 1789; Mill, 1861) — actions are right insofar as they produce the greatest happiness for the greatest number. Mill refined Bentham by ranking higher and lower pleasures.

question: Mereology is the study of part-whole relations. A famous puzzle: is a statue identical to the clay it's made of? They share every part, yet you can destroy one without destroying the other. What follows?
answer: Either identity is not what we thought, or the statue and the clay are two distinct things sharing the same matter at the same time.
choices: Either identity is not what we thought, or the statue and the clay are two distinct things sharing the same matter at the same time.
The statue is a property of the clay, not a separate object — what looks like coincidence is just clay arranged statue-wise.
The puzzle is verbal — 'statue' and 'clay' name the same object, so destruction of one entails destruction of the other.
The puzzle dissolves under four-dimensionalism — both are space-time worms, and they happen to share their current slice but not others.
context: The statue-clay puzzle drives a wedge into modal metaphysics. The statue could not survive crushing; the clay could. If they have different modal profiles, Leibniz's law says they are different things — yet they occupy the same space, with the same atoms. Some bite the bullet; some deny coincidence; some say the right view is four-dimensionalism's. Each carries costs.

question: Galen Strawson revived panpsychism by arguing that experience must be present at the bottom of matter, since you cannot build it from utterly non-experiencing parts. Critics fired back with the combination problem. What did they ask?
answer: How tiny experiences in particles could ever fuse into the single unified experience a person actually has at a moment.
choices: How tiny experiences in particles could ever fuse into the single unified experience a person actually has at a moment.
How experience at the bottom could causally influence behavior, given that physics already explains every motion.
How we could ever know experience went all the way down, since the inner life of an electron leaves no trace.
How a theory committed to experience everywhere could avoid attributing moral standing to rocks, rivers, and stars.
context: William James first pressed the worry in 1890: a hundred feelings clustered together are still a hundred feelings, not one feeling of a hundred parts. If a person's unified moment of experience cannot be added up from particle-experiences, panpsychism faces its own version of the gap it tried to close. Goff and others have spent two decades trying to answer.

question: Three positions on time. Presentism: only the present is real. Eternalism: past, present, and future are equally real. The growing-block view splits the difference. What does that theorist hold?
answer: Past and present are real and fixed; the future does not yet exist, and the universe grows as each present is added to the block of what has happened.
choices: Past and present are real and fixed; the future does not yet exist, and the universe grows as each present is added to the block of what has happened.
Future and present are real while the past has ceased to be; reality moves forward by leaving each present moment behind as a new one arrives.
All three times exist, but only the present has determinate properties; past and future events are real but their features stay indeterminate until observed.
Only the present is real, as presentism says, but its extent is wider than an instant — covering all events causally linked within the specious moment.
context: C. D. Broad defended the growing block in the 1920s and Michael Tooley revived it. Presentism honors how time feels, eternalism fits special relativity, the growing block tries to keep an open future without losing the fixed past.

question: Sleeping Beauty is woken once if a coin lands heads, twice if tails, memory wiped between. On waking, what credence should she give to heads? Thirders and halfers agree on the math. What divides them?
answer: Whether self-locating uncertainty about which waking this is should shift credence in the original coin toss at all.
choices: Whether self-locating uncertainty about which waking this is should shift credence in the original coin toss at all.
Whether the betting odds she would accept must match her stated credence under conditions of guaranteed memory loss.
Whether conditional probability is properly defined for events where the agent cannot identify her own temporal position.
Whether the coin should be modeled as fair given that the experimenter chose the protocol after knowing the outcome.
context: Adam Elga argued for 1/3 using indifference over centered worlds; David Lewis defended 1/2, holding that no new evidence arrives on waking. Nick Bostrom, Joseph Halpern, and Sarah Moss have all written on it. The split tracks a deeper question — does anthropic information count as evidence — that recurs in cosmology and the Doomsday argument.

question: Two envelopes hold money; one has twice the other. You pick one and consider switching. Calculation: if yours holds X, the other has either 2X or X/2, giving expected 1.25X — so always switch. What goes wrong?
answer: Using your envelope's value as the conditioning variable double-counts the prior; 'X' refers to different sums in the two branches.
choices: Using your envelope's value as the conditioning variable double-counts the prior; 'X' refers to different sums in the two branches.
The argument depends on a uniform prior over all positive real values, which is improper and yields a divergent expected value.
Expected utility theory fails here, since rational agents must use a bounded utility function rather than raw dollar amounts.
Symmetry between the envelopes breaks once you observe the contents, so the pre-opening calculation cannot apply unchanged here.
context: David Chalmers, Frank Jackson, and James Chase have all written resolutions. Some pin the error on the improper prior, some on the variable-binding sleight of hand, some on bounded utility. The diagnoses do not all agree, which is why the puzzle keeps appearing in decision theory seminars — different solutions teach different lessons about expectation.

question: The Doomsday argument. List every human who will ever live, in birth order; note your spot — your birth rank. If humans go extinct soon, you sit in a short list. If humans last millions of years, you are astonishingly early. Treat yourself as a typical draw; probability tilts toward short lists. What do critics attack?
answer: Treating your birth rank as a random draw from all humans who will ever live — Nick Bostrom's Self-Sampling Assumption, the rule that you should reason as a random sample from your reference class.
choices: Treating your birth rank as a random draw from all humans who will ever live — Nick Bostrom's Self-Sampling Assumption, the rule that you should reason as a random sample from your reference class.
Conflating epistemic probability — degrees of belief — with objective chance — real frequencies in the world — when actual extinction frequencies remain wholly unknown.
Applying Bayes' theorem to a hypothesis space including scenarios in which the reasoner herself does not exist — a coherence problem about reasoning from inside one's existence.
Reasoning from your evidence to the world's overall structure without ruling out radical Cartesian skeptical scenarios about whether evidence reflects the world at all.
context: John Leslie and Brandon Carter built the argument; Nick Bostrom systematized the assumptions. Critics like Dennis Dieks and Ken Olum attack the Self-Sampling Assumption directly. Bostrom's Self-Indication Assumption rival cancels the doomsday boost but creates new problems. The dispute connects Sleeping Beauty, fine-tuning, and simulation arguments — same machinery throughout.

question: Chrysippus the Stoic held that every event is fated by the divine logos, yet that we are still responsible for our actions. He answered the lazy argument with a famous distinction. What did he say does the work?
answer: External causes start a sequence, but our own character determines how we assent — fate works through us, not around us.
choices: External causes start a sequence, but our own character determines how we assent — fate works through us, not around us.
External causes fix bodily motion, but the rational soul is uncaused and stands free of the chain of physical events.
External causes are fated, but human futures contain genuine alternative branches that the agent selects between.
External causes determine outcomes, but the gods reward effort regardless of whether the effort changes anything.
context: Chrysippus distinguished principal causes (a cylinder's shape, which makes it roll) from antecedent ones (the push). Fate supplies the push; what we are supplies the rolling. Modern compatibilists from Frankfurt to Dennett rediscover the move; libertarians like Kane reject it as merely rebranding the puzzle. Susanne Bobzien's reconstructions made the dispute live again. The Stoics (Zeno, Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius, Seneca) taught that virtue is the only true good and that we should focus on what we control: our choices.

question: When we say God is good, we do not mean good in the same sense as a good knife, nor in a wholly unrelated sense. What is the analogical predication strategy meant to avoid?
answer: Univocity would make God a member of a common genus; equivocity would make all theology mere noise — analogy threads between them.
choices: Univocity would make God a member of a common genus; equivocity would make all theology mere noise — analogy threads between them.
Univocity would import sensory content into theology; equivocity would import nothing at all — analogy supplies a felt likeness.
Univocity would commit one to seeing God; equivocity would leave God unknown — analogy provides a middle visual grasp.
Univocity would imply finite creation in God; equivocity would deny all creation — analogy lets creation share his nature partly.
context: Scotus replied that without some univocity the argument cannot get started; Cajetan refined Aquinas's distinction into analogy of proportionality. Twentieth-century retrievals by Burrell, McCabe, and most recently the analytic Thomism of Eleonore Stump and Brian Davies wrestle with whether analogy is finally a real third option or a name for the puzzle. The Scotist/Thomist split still divides Catholic schools.

question: Sidgwick, at the close of The Methods of Ethics, confessed he could not reconcile two principles each of which seemed to him self-evident. He called the failure a dualism. What were the two principles?
answer: That each person should maximize his own good, and that each should maximize the good impartially — reason supports both, yet they diverge in practice.
choices: That each person should maximize his own good, and that each should maximize the good impartially — reason supports both, yet they diverge in practice.
That utility should be summed across persons, and that distributions should be equal — yet maximization and equality recommend different actions.
That pleasure is the only good, and that some pleasures are higher than others — yet pure quantity and Millian quality conflict in cases.
That the right is what maximizes happiness, and that motives must be virtuous — yet act and motive can come apart in clear cases.
context: Sidgwick's dualism — egoism and impartial benevolence both rational, yet pulling apart — was Bernard Williams's exhibit A against the project of impartial ethics. Derek Parfit's three-volume On What Matters is essentially a reopening of the case. Contemporary writers from Phillip Pettit to Roger Crisp to Susan Wolf are still arguing whether the dualism can be dissolved or must be lived with.

question: The 'crude' reading of perspectivism: any view as good as any. The 'sophisticated' reading rejects this. What does it say marks a better perspective?
answer: Reach and self-awareness — it sees more, holds rivals inside its account, knows its own conditions. A poor stance is parochial and naive about itself.
choices: Reach and self-awareness — it sees more, holds rivals inside its account, knows its own conditions. A poor stance is parochial and naive about itself.
Internal coherence alone — its component claims fit together without contradiction, whatever its scope or its relation to standpoints outside its own frame.
Practical fitness — it strengthens the holder against suffering. Truth-talk is a separate matter the strong adopt or drop as the moment requires of them.
Long-run convergence — other careful thinkers, working in good faith from independent starting points, eventually arrive at the same view as the holder.
context: Crude perspectivism is the sophomore reading. Nehamas's Life as Literature, Clark's Nietzsche on Truth, and Leiter's Routledge guide argue Nietzsche meant something stronger: perspectives are evaluable for what they let a thinker integrate and acknowledge.

question: Rolston III says nature has intrinsic value humans discover. Callicott says intrinsic value is real but always projected by a valuer. What does the dispute actually settle?
answer: Whether nature would retain value if no minds ever existed — Rolston says yes, Callicott says intrinsic value requires a valuer though the value remains real.
choices: Whether nature would retain value if no minds ever existed — Rolston says yes, Callicott says intrinsic value requires a valuer though the value remains real.
Whether ecosystems or only individuals count morally — Rolston grounds duties in the biotic whole, Callicott grounds them in the species member alone.
Whether wilderness preservation requires legal personhood — Rolston endorses giving rivers standing, Callicott calls the move category-confused legalism.
Whether duties to nature override duties to humans in conflict — Rolston accepts the override, Callicott insists human duties always retain priority.
context: Rolston's objectivism (Environmental Ethics, 1988) holds that a species or ecosystem has value independently of any observer — a 'value-in-itself' the way matter has mass. Callicott's Humean turn (In Defense of the Land Ethic) holds that all value requires a valuer, but rejects the easy slide from there to mere subjectivism: values can be grounded in valuers and still bind us. The dispute is whether anthropocentric and non-anthropocentric ethics can really be reconciled.

question: Eubulides refined an old puzzle into the sharpest paradox in logic: 'This sentence is false.' If true, false; if false, true. What lesson did Tarski draw for any formal language strong enough to talk of its own truth?
answer: No consistent formal language can contain its own complete truth predicate — to say which sentences of L are true demands a metalanguage above L, producing a hierarchy.
choices: No consistent formal language can contain its own complete truth predicate — to say which sentences of L are true demands a metalanguage above L, producing a hierarchy.
No consistent formal language can contain its own complete proof predicate — to say which sentences of L are provable demands a metalanguage above L, producing a hierarchy.
No consistent formal language can specify all its own well-formed sentences — to say which strings of L are grammatical demands a metalanguage above L, producing a hierarchy.
No consistent formal language can express its own complete semantic content — to give the meaning of each sentence of L demands a metalanguage above L, producing a hierarchy.
context: Tarski's hierarchy was a deep response to the Liar. Kripke and later truth theorists tried to allow languages to contain their own truth predicate using paraconsistent or partial-logic moves.

question: Four-dimensionalism says people are extended through time the way they are extended through space — slices of a single elongated worm. What does this dissolve?
answer: The puzzle of how I can be the same person as my five-year-old self — both of us are time-slices of one worm, like two ends of a hallway.
choices: The puzzle of how I can be the same person as my five-year-old self — both of us are time-slices of one worm, like two ends of a hallway.
The puzzle of why I am located in space at all — extension in time provides the resources to explain extension in space derivatively.
The puzzle of why I cannot return to the past — extension in time means my earlier slices are still real, so the asymmetry needs further explanation.
The puzzle of whether I will exist tomorrow — extension in time guarantees my future slices, making personal survival trivially secure.
context: Four-dimensionalism (or 'perdurantism,' developed by Quine, Lewis, and Heller) treats objects as spread out in time like a hallway is spread out in space. Personal identity through change becomes no more puzzling than spatial extension — the doorway is the same hallway as the back room, even though they are not in the same place. Whether this *helps* with the original puzzles is contested.

question: Newcomb's problem pits two decision principles against each other. The two-boxer takes both boxes since the prediction is fixed. The one-boxer takes only the opaque box since one-boxers walk away rich. What distinct principle does each side follow?
answer: Two-boxing follows causal decision theory: act on what your choice causes. One-boxing follows evidential decision theory: act on what your choice indicates, since one-boxers correlate with riches.
choices: Two-boxing follows causal decision theory: act on what your choice causes. One-boxing follows evidential decision theory: act on what your choice indicates, since one-boxers correlate with riches.
Two-boxing follows dominance reasoning always, while one-boxing follows expected-value calculation — the dispute reduces to which rational-choice principle gets priority in mixed cases that arise.
Two-boxing follows ordinary common-sense rationality, while one-boxing follows special logic for cases involving an infallible predictor — the split is over how unusual cases should be treated by us.
Two-boxing follows narrow individual self-interest, while one-boxing follows long-run cooperative reasoning — the dispute mirrors the prisoner's dilemma between defection and cooperation entirely.
context: Robert Nozick popularized Newcomb's problem in 1969. Gibbard and Harper (1978) developed causal decision theory; Jeffrey's evidential decision theory came earlier. Recent functional decision theory (Soares, Yudkowsky) tries to capture what is right about each.

question: The Golden Rule says treat others the way you want to be treated. If you love loud music but your sister hates it, what does the rule really ask you to do?
answer: Think about what your sister wants, not what you want.
choices: Think about what your sister wants, not what you want.
Play loud music for her since you would enjoy that.
Only follow the rule with people just like you.
Skip the rule when you and another person differ.
context: The Golden Rule works best when you stop and imagine the other person's side, not when you assume they want what you want.

question: A bully says 'I would want someone to be tough with me, so I am tough with you.' What is wrong with how he is using the Golden Rule?
answer: He is forcing his own taste on you instead of asking what you want.
choices: He is forcing his own taste on you instead of asking what you want.
He should be tougher, because being tough is always good.
He should never have heard of the Golden Rule in the first place.
He should treat others worse than he treats himself, not better.
context: The Golden Rule asks for real care about other people. If you only ask 'what would I want?', you can miss what they would want.

question: Imagine you really want a friend to push you when you are scared, because pushing helps YOU. Does the Golden Rule mean you should push other scared people the same way?
answer: Not always, because other people may need patience, not a push.
choices: Not always, because other people may need patience, not a push.
Yes, because what works for you must work for everyone.
No, because the Golden Rule never works for scared people.
Yes, because pushing someone always helps them in the end.
context: The rule asks you to care about what the other person needs, even when their needs are different from yours.

question: Your friend hands out birthday cake. She gives a big piece to everyone EXCEPT one kid she does not like. Why does this break the Golden Rule?
answer: She would not want to be left out, so she should not leave others out.
choices: She would not want to be left out, so she should not leave others out.
She should have given the kid a smaller piece, not nothing.
She should have skipped the party because cake is unhealthy.
She should have given the cake only to the kid she likes most.
context: The Golden Rule means we treat others the way we would want to be treated, even when we don't like them.

question: Two kids argue over whose turn it is on the swing. One says 'I would let you have it if it was my turn, so you should let me have it now.' Why is this NOT a fair use of the Golden Rule?
answer: He is using the rule to get what he wants, not to help the other kid.
choices: He is using the rule to get what he wants, not to help the other kid.
He used too many words, so the other kid did not understand him.
He should not use the rule on swings, only on bigger problems.
He should have argued louder so the other kid had to give in.
context: The Golden Rule is for caring about other people. It is not a trick to win arguments.

question: Your friend asks you to lie for her. She says it is for a good reason. What is the FIRST thing to think about?
answer: Whether her 'good reason' is really a good reason, or just convenient.
choices: Whether her 'good reason' is really a good reason, or just convenient.
Whether the lie will be fun to tell, since lies can feel exciting.
Whether you can get away with it without anyone noticing later.
Whether your friend will be mad if you do not lie for her.
context: People often dress up a lie as a 'good reason' when it is really just easier than telling the truth.

question: A kid breaks a window playing ball. He says 'I will say a stranger did it.' His sister says 'Tell the truth, even though you will get in trouble.' Why does his sister think honesty matters more than avoiding trouble?
answer: A lie hides what really happened, and other people deserve the truth.
choices: A lie hides what really happened, and other people deserve the truth.
She does not like her brother very much and wants him punished.
Lies never work out, but the truth always works out perfectly.
Strangers get blamed for too many things and have hurt feelings.
context: Honesty is not just about avoiding lies. It is about respecting other people enough to tell them what really happened.

question: Aunt Mary asks 'Do you LIKE my new green hat?' You think the hat looks silly. What is one HONEST thing you could say?
answer: You could say what you do like about the hat without lying.
choices: You could say what you do like about the hat without lying.
You could say the hat is the most beautiful hat in the world.
You could pretend you cannot see the hat at all, that solves it.
You could shout that the hat is silly so everyone hears you.
context: Being honest does not mean being mean. You can find true things that are also kind to say.

question: Some people say a 'white lie' (a small fib to be polite) is fine. Others say even small lies are wrong. What is one good reason a person might worry about white lies?
answer: Small lies can make telling bigger lies feel easier later on.
choices: Small lies can make telling bigger lies feel easier later on.
White lies are illegal and you could be arrested for telling one.
White lies only work if you have white skin, which is unfair.
White lies make your tongue turn white, which doctors can see.
context: Some thinkers worry that getting used to small lies, even kind ones, can change what we are willing to lie about later.

question: A boy on the playground tells everyone he has a pet tiger at home. It is not true. Why might this kind of brag-lie hurt HIM in the end?
answer: Other kids will stop trusting him, even when he tells the truth.
choices: Other kids will stop trusting him, even when he tells the truth.
Tigers are protected animals so it is illegal to even pretend.
The other kids will think tigers are real and become scared.
He will get in trouble for owning a tiger he does not own.
context: When people catch you in a lie, they wonder what ELSE you have lied about. Trust is hard to rebuild.

question: Your dad asks 'Did you brush your teeth?' You did not. Why does even a tiny lie like 'yes I did' matter?
answer: Your dad cannot help you take care of yourself if he can't trust you.
choices: Your dad cannot help you take care of yourself if he can't trust you.
Teeth are not important, so the question was not worth asking.
Your dad will never know whether you really brushed your teeth.
Lies about teeth lead to lies about everything else by tomorrow.
context: Honesty in small things is what makes honesty in big things possible. Trust is built one little moment at a time.

question: A friend tells a secret and asks you to keep it. Later, you find out the secret is that he stole from someone. Why is THIS different from a normal secret?
answer: Keeping the secret means letting the harm continue, which is wrong.
choices: Keeping the secret means letting the harm continue, which is wrong.
Stealing is fun to talk about, so you should tell everyone.
All secrets are bad and you should never agree to keep one.
His secret is not really a secret unless you tell strangers too.
context: Promises matter. But a promise to hide harm from the person being hurt is not a promise we should keep.

question: Your sister says 'Be honest, am I funny?' You think her jokes are really not funny. What is the kindest honest answer?
answer: You could say which joke you DID like and ask about her favorites.
choices: You could say which joke you DID like and ask about her favorites.
You should say her jokes are the worst jokes ever invented.
You should pretend her jokes are funny so she keeps telling them.
You should say all her jokes are funny except the ones you hate.
context: Being honest is a skill, like riding a bike. You can learn to be truthful without being cruel.

question: Three kids share a pizza with eight slices. The biggest kid says 'I am bigger so I get four slices.' Why does this NOT feel fair?
answer: Being bigger is not a reason to get more, unless they all agreed.
choices: Being bigger is not a reason to get more, unless they all agreed.
It is fair, because bigger kids need more food to grow up.
It is not fair, because pizza should be cut into three slices.
It is fair, because the biggest kid is usually the smartest one.
context: Fairness usually means people get something for a real reason, not just because they are stronger or louder.

question: Two friends both worked hard on a school project. The teacher gives ONE friend the prize because she likes that friend more. What word describes what just happened?
answer: Unfair, because the prize went to a favorite, not to the best work.
choices: Unfair, because the prize went to a favorite, not to the best work.
Fine, because teachers can do whatever they want in their class.
Funny, because school projects are supposed to be just for fun.
Smart, because the teacher knew who would do the project better.
context: Favoritism is the opposite of fairness. Real fairness ignores who you like and looks at who earned it.

question: If you find a wallet on the playground, what is the right thing to do?
answer: Take it to a grown-up who can find the person who lost it.
choices: Take it to a grown-up who can find the person who lost it.
Keep it, because finders get to keep whatever they find.
Throw it away so no one can steal it from you later on.
Open it, take only the money, and leave the rest behind.
context: The wallet belongs to someone who is probably worried. Getting it back to them is what fairness asks of us.

question: Your teacher gives every kid in class the SAME number of pencils. But some kids already have lots, and some have none at all. Is this the most fair way to share?
answer: Maybe not — kids with nothing might need more than kids with lots.
choices: Maybe not — kids with nothing might need more than kids with lots.
Yes, because giving everyone the same is always the most fair.
No, because kids with lots should have to give their pencils away.
Yes, because nobody can complain when they all got the same thing.
context: Sometimes fair means 'everyone gets the same.' Sometimes fair means 'each kid gets what they need.' Which one fits depends on the situation.

question: Two kids race. One trained for weeks. The other did not train at all. The trained kid wins. Is this 'unfair' to the kid who lost?
answer: No, because the winner earned it with practice and effort.
choices: No, because the winner earned it with practice and effort.
Yes, because the kids should have gotten the same trophy at the end.
Yes, because training before a race is cheating, plain and simple.
No, because losing a race is good for kids and teaches them stuff.
context: Fairness includes letting people benefit from work they really did. Stopping the trained kid from winning would punish her effort.

question: A kid gets blamed for breaking a vase he did not break. Other kids saw who really did it. What should they DO if they care about fairness?
answer: Speak up and tell the truth, even if the real breaker is their friend.
choices: Speak up and tell the truth, even if the real breaker is their friend.
Stay quiet, because telling on people is always wrong, no matter what.
Wait a day or two and see what happens before doing anything bad.
Tell only HALF the truth so nobody gets in too much trouble at all.
context: Letting the wrong kid take the blame is itself unfair. Speaking up takes courage, but it is part of being fair.

question: A new kid from another country joins the class. Some kids tease her because she sounds different. What does fairness say about this?
answer: She is new to ENGLISH, not to being a person who deserves respect.
choices: She is new to ENGLISH, not to being a person who deserves respect.
Teasing her is fine since she does not understand what they say.
She should change how she sounds to match the other kids quickly.
Other kids should tease her back to show her how teasing feels.
context: Fairness reminds us that every person deserves the same basic respect, even when they look or sound new to us.

question: Two friends both want the last seat by the window. They both got to the seat at the SAME time. What is one fair way to decide?
answer: Take turns — one sits today, the other sits the next time.
choices: Take turns — one sits today, the other sits the next time.
The louder kid gets the seat, because being loud is more important.
Both kids should be sent to the back row as a punishment for arguing.
Whoever was born first should win, because age decides everything.
context: When two people want one thing and both have an equal claim, taking turns is one of the simplest fair answers.

question: A friend cheats on a test. You can stay quiet (kind) or tell the teacher (just). Why might these two things pull in different ways?
answer: Being kind to your friend would mean other kids get cheated out of fair grades.
choices: Being kind to your friend would mean other kids get cheated out of fair grades.
Being kind to your friend would also mean lying to your parents at home.
Being just to the teacher would get the teacher in trouble with the school.
Being just always feels nicer than being kind, because justice is fun.
context: Kindness asks 'What will hurt the person I am with?' Justice asks 'What will hurt all the people I am NOT with?' Sometimes they agree, sometimes they fight.

question: Your little brother breaks your favorite toy. Mom says he should give you his allowance until your toy is paid back. He cries. What is Mom doing — kindness or justice?
answer: Justice — making sure the harm gets repaired, even though it makes him sad.
choices: Justice — making sure the harm gets repaired, even though it makes him sad.
Kindness — she is being kind to him by helping him save his money.
Both — because making your brother cry is just AND kind in this case.
Neither — because parents are supposed to fix everything themselves.
context: Justice often costs the person who did the harm. That can feel unkind in the moment, but it is how we restore what was broken.

question: Two kids are in trouble for the same thing. One says 'Sorry, I won't do it again.' The other does not say sorry. The grown-up gives them the SAME punishment. Is this fair?
answer: Maybe — saying sorry matters, but breaking the rule still has costs.
choices: Maybe — saying sorry matters, but breaking the rule still has costs.
No — the sorry kid should get a reward for being polite.
Yes — saying sorry is a trick and should not be trusted ever.
No — the not-sorry kid should be allowed to leave with no punishment.
context: An apology is not the same as undoing the harm. Justice can still ask for a consequence even when someone is genuinely sorry.

question: A homeless man takes bread from a shop because he is hungry. The shopkeeper is upset because the bread cost money to bake. Both things are TRUE — what makes this hard?
answer: The man's hunger is real, AND the shopkeeper's loss is real, all at once.
choices: The man's hunger is real, AND the shopkeeper's loss is real, all at once.
The man should have stolen from a richer shop instead of this one.
The shopkeeper should bake bread he is willing to give away for free.
The man cannot really be hungry if he had energy to reach for bread.
context: Real life often gives us situations where two true things pull us in different directions. Thinking about which thing matters more, and when, is part of growing up.

question: A judge has to decide a punishment for a person who stole bread to feed her children. Is the judge's job easier or harder than a friend's job in the same situation?
answer: Harder — the judge has to think of everyone, not just one person.
choices: Harder — the judge has to think of everyone, not just one person.
Easier — judges can just look up the answer in a big book of rules.
Easier — judges only have to decide once, but friends decide every day.
Harder — judges have to write everything down and friends do not.
context: A friend can care about ONE person. A judge has to care about the person AND the shopkeeper AND every future person tempted to steal bread. That is what makes the job hard.

question: A rule at your school says you cannot leave class. One day a kid is choking in the hallway and needs help. What does this show about rules?
answer: Rules are made for normal cases; sometimes doing right means breaking them.
choices: Rules are made for normal cases; sometimes doing right means breaking them.
Rules are always right and should never be broken for any reason at all.
Rules are always wrong and only fools follow rules someone made up.
Rules are about food and clothes, but never about helping other people.
context: Most rules exist for good reasons. But the people who made rules could not imagine every case. Doing right sometimes means using your judgment about when a rule does not fit.

question: Your friend says 'Rules are made to be broken!' Why might a thoughtful person disagree?
answer: Most rules protect someone — breaking them often means hurting someone.
choices: Most rules protect someone — breaking them often means hurting someone.
Rules are written down, so they cannot be broken even if you try.
Rules are not made by people, they are made by computers and lawyers.
Friends should never disagree with each other, no matter what the topic.
context: Rules can be silly. But the saying 'rules are made to be broken' hides who gets hurt when we break them — usually the people the rule was protecting.

question: A boy follows EVERY rule perfectly but is mean to his sister at home. Is he a good person?
answer: Following rules is not enough — being good means caring about people too.
choices: Following rules is not enough — being good means caring about people too.
Yes — following all the rules is the whole point of being good.
No — boys cannot be good people, only girls can really be good.
Yes — what happens at home does not count as part of being good.
context: A rule-follower can still hurt people the rules do not mention. Real goodness goes beyond just doing what you are told.

question: A girl never follows the rules, but she is kind to everyone and helps people who are hurt. Is she a good person?
answer: Maybe — kindness counts, but breaking rules can hurt people in ways she misses.
choices: Maybe — kindness counts, but breaking rules can hurt people in ways she misses.
Yes — kindness is the only thing that matters, and rules are nothing.
No — only people who follow all the rules can ever be good people.
Yes — breaking rules is always a sign that you are very smart inside.
context: Being kind and breaking rules can BOTH be true. A wise person asks 'Which rules?' and 'why is breaking them part of being kind?'

question: Long ago in America, the LAW said that some people could be slaves. Many people followed the law. Was following the law the right thing to do?
answer: No — following a law that hurts people does not make the hurting okay.
choices: No — following a law that hurts people does not make the hurting okay.
Yes — laws are made by the government and the government is always right.
Yes — slavery was so long ago that the rules of right and wrong were different.
No — laws never really mattered, so there was no law to follow in the first place.
context: Some of the bravest people in history broke unjust laws. They knew that what is LEGAL is not always what is RIGHT.

question: A little kid asks 'Why is the sky blue?' Her mom answers, and the kid says 'But WHY?' Mom answers that, and the kid says 'But WHY?' again. What does this show about questions?
answer: Every answer can open a new question — the world is deeper than it looks.
choices: Every answer can open a new question — the world is deeper than it looks.
Little kids are annoying and should stop asking after one question only.
Mom did not know the answer and was making things up the whole time.
The sky is not really blue, it just looks that way to little children.
context: Asking 'why?' over and over is something philosophers have always done. It is not annoying — it is the start of real thinking.

question: Two kids see a rainbow. One says 'It is beautiful.' The other says 'What makes it bend like that?' Which kind of thinking is more important?
answer: Both — you can wonder about a thing AND be amazed by it at the same time.
choices: Both — you can wonder about a thing AND be amazed by it at the same time.
Only the second — asking how things work is the only real thinking.
Only the first — asking how things work ruins the magic of the world.
Neither — rainbows are nothing special and people should ignore them.
context: Wondering 'why?' and feeling 'wow!' are not enemies. The biggest thinkers in history did both — they were amazed at things AND wanted to understand them.

question: A boy is sure he knows everything about dogs because he has one. What might a thoughtful person say to him?
answer: Knowing one dog is not the same as knowing all dogs everywhere.
choices: Knowing one dog is not the same as knowing all dogs everywhere.
He is right — owning one dog teaches you everything about every animal.
He should stop talking about dogs and switch to talking about cats.
He should get more dogs until he has met every single kind in the world.
context: Saying 'I know everything about X' is usually a sign you have stopped learning. The wisest people stay curious.

question: Long ago, people thought the Earth was flat. Then some thinkers started asking 'how do we KNOW it is flat?' What changed?
answer: Asking the question opened the door to finding out it was actually round.
choices: Asking the question opened the door to finding out it was actually round.
The Earth used to be flat and slowly got rounder over many years.
People who asked the question were arrested and the question stopped.
Nothing changed — most people still think the Earth is flat today.
context: Questions can sound dangerous because they shake up what everyone 'just knows.' But that is how we ever find out anything new.

question: A grown-up says 'Because I said so.' Is this a good answer to the question 'why?'
answer: Sometimes — but it does not actually answer the question itself.
choices: Sometimes — but it does not actually answer the question itself.
Always — grown-ups know everything and should not have to explain.
Never — grown-ups should always explain every choice they ever make.
Always — children should not be allowed to ask 'why?' to begin with.
context: 'Because I said so' is sometimes what a grown-up says when they are tired or in a hurry. It is not a real answer, but it can be okay when time is short.

question: Two kids see the same dog. One says 'He is friendly.' The other says 'He is scary.' Both are looking at the same dog. What is going on?
answer: They have different past experiences with dogs, so they see different things.
choices: They have different past experiences with dogs, so they see different things.
One of the kids is lying, because a dog can only really be one way.
Dogs change their friendliness depending on who is looking at them.
The dog is actually both friendly and scary on different days of the week.
context: We do not just SEE the world — we see it through what has happened to us before. Two people can look at the same thing and notice different parts.

question: Your friend believes ghosts are real. You think they are not. Neither of you is being silly. What might be a good way to talk about this?
answer: Listen to her reasons, and share yours — try to learn from each other.
choices: Listen to her reasons, and share yours — try to learn from each other.
Tell her she is wrong and stupid until she changes her mind quickly.
Agree with her so she does not feel bad, even if you do not really agree.
Stop talking to her, because friends should believe the same things.
context: Disagreeing well is a skill. You can say 'I do not see it that way' without saying 'you are dumb.' Real friends can disagree.

question: Different families have different rules. Some kids have a bedtime at 8, some at 10. One family eats meat, another does not. What does this show?
answer: There can be many right ways to live, even when families do things differently.
choices: There can be many right ways to live, even when families do things differently.
Whichever family has the latest bedtime is the smartest family of all.
Families with different rules are all wrong except for one family.
Families should all do the exact same thing or nothing will work.
context: Many small life-choices are not 'right' or 'wrong' — they are just different. Knowing the difference between 'different' and 'wrong' is important.

question: Long ago, almost everyone in one part of the world thought the Sun moved around the Earth. They were wrong. What does this teach us?
answer: Even when MANY people believe a thing, they can still all be mistaken.
choices: Even when MANY people believe a thing, they can still all be mistaken.
We should trust whatever most people believe, because the crowd is wise.
The Sun used to move around the Earth and only stopped doing it recently.
Old people are always wrong and young people are always right about science.
context: 'Everyone thinks so' is not the same as 'it is true.' History has many stories of crowds being wrong and a few thinkers being right.

question: A kid is sure his favorite movie is the best movie ever. Why might other kids think a DIFFERENT movie is the best?
answer: We all bring our own taste, our own family, and our own friends to what we like.
choices: We all bring our own taste, our own family, and our own friends to what we like.
They are all wrong, because his favorite movie really is the best one.
They are lying about which movie they like to make him feel bad.
They have not watched his favorite movie yet, but they will agree later.
context: Taste is not the same as truth. Two people can like different things and BOTH be right, because they are not making a claim about the world.

question: Two kids disagree about whether a game is fair. They are about to fight. What is one good way to find common ground?
answer: Ask each kid to say what would make the game more fair, and listen.
choices: Ask each kid to say what would make the game more fair, and listen.
Tell the louder kid he wins the argument and the game both at once.
Stop playing forever, because two kids cannot ever agree on games.
Pretend nothing is wrong and play the game even though they hate it.
context: Common ground is what both people can agree on, even when they disagree about a lot. Finding it usually starts with listening.

question: A kid says all olives are gross. Another kid loves olives. Is there ANY common ground here?
answer: Yes — they can both agree that taste differs from person to person.
choices: Yes — they can both agree that taste differs from person to person.
No — they should fight about olives until one of them gives up.
Yes — only kids who hate olives can be right, so the lover should give in.
No — common ground is impossible when two people disagree about food.
context: Even on small things like food, people who disagree can usually agree on SOMETHING. The art is finding that thing.

question: Your friend and you both want to play, but you want kickball and she wants tag. You are stuck. What is one way to handle this?
answer: Play kickball first, then tag — or look for a third game you both like.
choices: Play kickball first, then tag — or look for a third game you both like.
Play whatever YOU want and tell your friend to deal with it.
Give up and play nothing, since you cannot both have your way.
Decide whoever cries loudest gets to pick the game today.
context: Stuck moments are normal between friends. Looking for a 'we both win' answer is usually better than 'one of us wins, one loses.'

question: Two countries disagree about where their border should be. Their leaders sit down to talk. What does common ground LOOK LIKE here?
answer: Finding a deal both sides can live with, even if neither gets everything.
choices: Finding a deal both sides can live with, even if neither gets everything.
One country admits the other was right about EVERYTHING all along.
Both countries refuse to talk and just keep arguing for many years.
Both countries shrink to nothing so the border problem goes away.
context: Real-world disagreements rarely end with one side admitting it was completely wrong. Common ground usually means each side gives a little.

question: Two friends argue about a movie. One yells 'You are stupid!' The other yells 'No, YOU are stupid!' What has gone wrong?
answer: They stopped talking about the movie and started attacking each other.
choices: They stopped talking about the movie and started attacking each other.
Nothing — yelling 'stupid' is how grown-ups settle most disagreements.
The first kid was right, because the second kid called names first.
They should switch what they are arguing about to something different.
context: Attacking the person instead of the idea is a kind of giving up. It feels like you are arguing, but you have actually stopped.

question: You see an ant crawling on the sidewalk. Should you avoid stepping on it? What kind of reasons might say YES?
answer: The ant is alive and wants to live, just like you want to live.
choices: The ant is alive and wants to live, just like you want to live.
Stepping on ants is illegal in most countries around the world.
Ants will bite back if you step on them, so you should not try.
Ants are made of glass and will shatter under your heavy shoe.
context: How we treat small creatures says something about what KIND of person we are. There are no rules saying you have to avoid the ant — but it is the kind of question worth asking.

question: Your dog wags her tail when you come home. She seems happy. But can we REALLY know what she is feeling, since she cannot tell us in words?
answer: We can guess from her body, but we cannot be totally sure what she feels.
choices: We can guess from her body, but we cannot be totally sure what she feels.
We can know exactly, because dogs feel the same things people feel.
Dogs do not feel anything, so the wagging tail does not mean a thing.
We can know because the wag of a tail is described in every dog book.
context: Other minds are mysterious — even other PEOPLE's minds. We guess based on their bodies, words, and history. We rarely know for sure.

question: You promise your sister you will play her game later. But then your favorite show comes on. What did your PROMISE actually mean?
answer: You agreed to do something even when you might not feel like it later.
choices: You agreed to do something even when you might not feel like it later.
You agreed to play only if your favorite show was not on at the time.
Promises are not real, so it does not matter what you said earlier.
Promises are real, but only if the other person remembers them clearly.
context: A promise made only when convenient is barely a promise. Real promises matter most exactly when they are HARD to keep.

question: A toddler hits another kid and says 'Sorry.' Five minutes later, she does it again. Why might her 'sorry' have not been enough?
answer: Saying sorry without changing what you do does not really fix the harm.
choices: Saying sorry without changing what you do does not really fix the harm.
Toddlers are not allowed to say sorry — only big kids can do it.
She should have said 'I apologize' instead of using shorter words.
Saying sorry twice would have fixed it, so she only needed to repeat.
context: 'Sorry' is a small word that gets bigger when it changes your behavior. A real apology comes WITH a change.

question: Your brother does something nice for you. Later, he expects you to do something nice for him. Is this fair, or is he ruining the niceness?
answer: It is fair to expect kindness back, but a real gift does not come with a bill.
choices: It is fair to expect kindness back, but a real gift does not come with a bill.
It is always ruined — kindness should never go in both directions ever.
It is always fair — kindness MUST come with a bill or it is not real.
It is fair — your brother should charge you money for every nice thing.
context: Helping others usually feels best when it is freely given. But real friendships and families ALSO depend on give-and-take over time.

question: Two kids both think they are the smartest kid in the class. What might a wise person tell them?
answer: Knowing how much you do NOT know is a sign of being truly smart.
choices: Knowing how much you do NOT know is a sign of being truly smart.
Have a fight, and whoever wins gets to be the smartest one in class.
They are both wrong, because the teacher is the smartest one of them all.
Whoever has the loudest voice during arguments must be the smartest of them.
context: Socrates said something like 'I am wise because I know how little I know.' Real wisdom usually comes with humble curiosity, not loud bragging.

question: A boy says 'I am SO unlucky.' But he has food, a home, friends, and a family. What is one good question to ask him?
answer: Compared to WHO are you unlucky — and what would lucky even look like?
choices: Compared to WHO are you unlucky — and what would lucky even look like?
Why do you not just buy more luck at the store like everyone else?
How dare you say that when other people have less than you do?
Should you stop trying altogether since you are unlucky already?
context: Lucky and unlucky depend on what we compare ourselves to. Slowing down to ask 'compared to what?' often changes how a thing looks.

question: A girl says 'I cannot help it — that is just how I am.' Is this a good reason for everything she does?
answer: Not always — some of who we are can change with effort over time.
choices: Not always — some of who we are can change with effort over time.
Yes — once you say 'that is how I am,' nothing can ever change you.
No — kids must not be allowed to talk about themselves in this way.
Yes — saying it makes the words come true automatically, like magic.
context: 'Just who I am' can be honest — some things really are hard to change. But it can also be an excuse. The wise person knows the difference.

question: Two kids are at the playground. One wants to play, one wants to swing alone. Are both kids RIGHT, or is one of them being weird?
answer: Both are fine — people have different ways of liking the same place.
choices: Both are fine — people have different ways of liking the same place.
The one who wants to play is right, because being alone is always weird.
The one who swings alone is right, because playing with others is bad.
Neither is right — kids should all want to do exactly the same thing.
context: Wanting to be alone is not weird. Wanting to play together is not weird either. People are different — and a wise place for kids has room for both.

question: Your friend made a mistake and feels really bad. You can say 'it is okay, forget it' or 'you messed up, but I still like you.' Which is more honest AND more kind?
answer: The second — because it tells the truth AND keeps loving him.
choices: The second — because it tells the truth AND keeps loving him.
The first — because forgetting is the only way to fix mistakes.
The second — because it makes him feel worse, which is a good lesson.
The first — because honesty hurts and kindness should never hurt.
context: Real kindness does not need lies. You can name the mistake and STILL love the person. Pretending nothing happened is not the same as forgiving.

question: A kid feels bad about losing his big game. His coach says 'You still played really well.' That is true — but the kid wanted to WIN. What might his coach also need to say?
answer: That losing hurts AND it is okay to feel sad about it for a while.
choices: That losing hurts AND it is okay to feel sad about it for a while.
That winning is the only thing that matters in any kind of game.
That losing means he should never play games like this ever again.
That his sadness is silly and he should just smile and forget about it.
context: Cheering up is good. But sometimes a person needs their hard feelings named first, before they can hear the cheerful part.

question: A boy says 'I would never steal — but only because I would get caught.' Is this REALLY being a good person?
answer: Not quite — a good person also chooses not to steal when no one is looking.
choices: Not quite — a good person also chooses not to steal when no one is looking.
Yes — what matters is the outcome, and he is not stealing right now anyway.
Yes — getting caught is the only reason anyone ever chooses to be good.
No — he should steal to find out what it really feels like to be caught.
context: Plato told a story called 'Ring of Gyges' about a magic ring that made you invisible. He asked: would you still be good if nobody could see you? That is the test of real goodness.

question: Your friend wants to copy your homework. You know she will get in trouble if you tell, but you also know she will not learn if you say yes. What is the LOVING thing to do?
answer: Say no, and offer to help her learn the answers herself instead.
choices: Say no, and offer to help her learn the answers herself instead.
Say yes, because friends help each other no matter what is asked.
Say nothing and run away from your friend so she cannot ask you again.
Say yes to her face, but later tell the teacher about everything.
context: Real friends help each other GROW. Sometimes the loving answer is the harder one — not the easier one.

question: A grown-up says 'When I was your age...' before telling a story. Why might it be worth listening, even if the story sounds old?
answer: Grown-ups remember problems you have not faced yet, and what worked.
choices: Grown-ups remember problems you have not faced yet, and what worked.
Old stories are always more interesting than anything kids say.
Kids should listen to every word from grown-ups without thinking.
Listening to a story means you have to agree with all of it later.
context: You do not have to AGREE with everything an older person says. But they have lived through things you have not yet. Listening costs nothing and sometimes pays a lot.

question: A girl finds out her best friend has been talking behind her back. She wants to do something MEAN back. Her grandmother says 'Wait one night, then decide.' Why this advice?
answer: Anger is hot, and big choices made in anger are usually ones we regret.
choices: Anger is hot, and big choices made in anger are usually ones we regret.
Anger always goes away after one night, and there is no need to act later.
Grandmothers always say wait one night, no matter what the trouble is.
Doing mean things back is only allowed after waiting one full week first.
context: Many traditions teach 'cool down before you act.' The Stoics, Buddhists, and Christians all noticed that hot anger makes us say and do things we did not really mean.

question: Your little cousin asks 'Why are people sometimes mean to each other?' What is one honest answer a thoughtful kid could give?
answer: People can be scared, hurting, or tired — and meanness sometimes leaks out.
choices: People can be scared, hurting, or tired — and meanness sometimes leaks out.
People are mean because they are simply born that way and cannot change.
Only kids are mean — grown-ups have grown out of it for the most part.
People are mean because the moon was full on the day they were born.
context: Mean behavior usually comes FROM something — fear, hurt, tiredness, jealousy. Naming that does not excuse meanness, but it helps us understand it.

question: Long ago a sailor was lost at sea and used the stars to find his way home. What does this story show about KNOWING things?
answer: Knowing something true can keep you safe when nothing else around you helps.
choices: Knowing something true can keep you safe when nothing else around you helps.
Sailors should never trust stars and should ask passing fish for help.
Stars move too much to be useful for anything besides being pretty.
Sailing should be avoided since the sea will always trick anyone on it.
context: Knowledge is not just for school. The stars guided sailors home for thousands of years. Real knowledge can save lives.

question: A boy thinks 'I will be HAPPY when I am rich.' His grandfather says 'I have been rich and I have been poor.' What might Grandpa say next?
answer: That being happy comes from inside, not from how much money you have.
choices: That being happy comes from inside, not from how much money you have.
That being rich is the only way to actually be happy in any life.
That being poor is fun and everyone should try it for many years.
That happiness depends on the kind of car you can afford to buy.
context: Many thinkers across history have pointed out that money buys comfort, but not joy. Joy comes from inside — from your habits, people, and choices.

question: Two friends play a board game. One wins by following the rules. The other wins by cheating when nobody is looking. Did both kids actually WIN?
answer: Only one of them — winning by cheating is not really winning at all.
choices: Only one of them — winning by cheating is not really winning at all.
Yes — winning is winning, no matter how it happens in any game.
Yes — if the cheating kid does not get caught, the cheating was fair.
No — neither of them won, because games never have real winners.
context: A win you got by cheating only LOOKS like a win. You did not really do the thing you say you did. Some thinkers call this an empty win.

question: Utilitarians say we should pick the choice that creates the most happiness for the MOST people. What is one problem with this rule?
answer: It can excuse hurting a few people if it makes more people happy.
choices: It can excuse hurting a few people if it makes more people happy.
It only works for groups of less than five people at any one time.
It says happiness does not actually matter and pain matters more.
It is too easy to follow, so philosophers usually pick harder rules.
context: Utilitarianism asks one simple question — what creates the most good? But the simplicity can hide tough cases. Five people's happiness should not always outweigh one person's real harm.

question: A young Stoic complains 'My friend insulted me!' His Stoic teacher would say something like: 'Is the insult IN you, or is it just in the air?' What does this teach?
answer: Words only hurt as much as we let them — the choice to be hurt is partly ours.
choices: Words only hurt as much as we let them — the choice to be hurt is partly ours.
Insults are made of magical material that can really physically wound you.
Insults are illegal under Roman law, so they should be reported to police.
Insults can only hurt people who are weak, so toughen up and ignore them.
context: The Stoics did not say insults felt nice. They said the STING comes partly from how we respond. Two people can hear the same insult; one shakes it off, the other carries it for a week. The Stoics (Zeno, Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius, Seneca) taught that virtue is the only true good and that we should focus on what we control: our choices.

question: Buddhism teaches the 'Four Noble Truths.' The first is that life involves SUFFERING — including aging, loss, and disappointment. Why start there?
answer: Honesty about pain is the first step toward dealing with it well.
choices: Honesty about pain is the first step toward dealing with it well.
If life is suffering, then nothing else matters and you should give up.
Buddhists love being sad and want everyone to feel sad along with them.
Buddhists are forced by law to start with the saddest part of the lesson.
context: Many traditions try to skip past pain or pretend it is not there. Buddhism starts by NAMING it — not because it loves suffering, but because pretending pain is not real never actually fixes anything.

question: The second Noble Truth says the CAUSE of much suffering is 'tanha' — a kind of clinging or craving. What is one way tanha shows up in everyday life?
answer: Wanting a thing so badly you cannot enjoy what you already have.
choices: Wanting a thing so badly you cannot enjoy what you already have.
Drinking lots of water during the day to stay healthy and hydrated.
Studying very hard for a test even when you do not feel like it.
Letting other people have things you do not need yourself anymore.
context: Tanha is not just 'wanting' — it is the white-knuckle grip on a want. A kid can want a toy AND enjoy his other toys. Tanha is when the wanting blocks out the having.

question: Philosophers argue about FREE WILL — whether your choices are really YOURS, or whether your brain was always going to pick what it picked. What is one reason this matters?
answer: If choices are never really free, blame and praise lose their meaning.
choices: If choices are never really free, blame and praise lose their meaning.
If choices are never really free, then nobody can ever go to school again.
If choices are never really free, then ice cream will stop tasting good.
If choices are never really free, then nobody can read books any more.
context: If your brain made you do it, can we really PUNISH you for doing it? Can we PRAISE you for being kind, if you had no real choice? The question is older than philosophy itself and still matters today.

question: Some thinkers say free will is COMPATIBLE with everything in the brain being caused. They are called 'compatibilists.' What do they say a 'free' choice is?
answer: A choice that flows from YOUR own thinking — not one forced from outside.
choices: A choice that flows from YOUR own thinking — not one forced from outside.
A choice that comes from nowhere at all and surprises even yourself.
A choice that is made without any thought, just a quick guess off the cuff.
A choice that follows a strict set of rules written down at your birth.
context: Compatibilists redefine 'free' to mean 'not coerced.' If your choice came from your own reasons (even reasons that came from genes and upbringing), that is free enough. Many disagree, but it is one of the main answers.

question: Carol Gilligan studied how PEOPLE think about moral problems. She noticed many WOMEN focused on relationships and care, while many MEN focused on abstract rules. What did she think this showed?
answer: Both approaches matter — care for people and respect for rules are both real ethics.
choices: Both approaches matter — care for people and respect for rules are both real ethics.
Women are usually wrong about ethics, while men are usually right about it.
Men should not be allowed to study ethics, since they only focus on rules.
Moral problems only have one correct answer, no matter who is thinking about them.
context: Gilligan pushed back against psychologists who said one moral style was more 'mature' than the other. She argued that an ethics of care — paying close attention to who gets hurt, and how — is just as serious as an ethics of rules.

question: The ancient Chinese book the Daodejing (Tao Te Ching) says 'The way that can be told is not the eternal way.' Why would a BOOK start with the line that the truth cannot really be put into words?
answer: To warn the reader at the start: words are pointers, not the whole truth.
choices: To warn the reader at the start: words are pointers, not the whole truth.
Because the writer had run out of ink and could not finish the introduction.
Because the book was supposed to be a riddle and not be read by anyone.
Because Chinese books always start with a line saying not to read them at all.
context: Daoism warns against thinking you have captured truth in a clever sentence. The 'Dao' (the way) is something you have to live, not just say. Other traditions — Zen Buddhism, mystical Christianity — share this caution.

question: Daoists talk about 'wu-wei' — usually translated 'effortless action' or 'non-doing.' It does NOT mean laziness. What does it actually mean?
answer: Acting in tune with how things naturally flow, instead of forcing things.
choices: Acting in tune with how things naturally flow, instead of forcing things.
Doing absolutely nothing on purpose, all day, every day, for your whole life.
Doing the opposite of whatever Chinese rulers told you to do every day.
Doing many things at once until you wear yourself out and have to stop.
context: Wu-wei is like a good swimmer who works with the river instead of fighting it. You are still ACTING — but the action does not feel like a battle, because you are not pushing against what is.

question: Philosophers ask: what IS a thought? Is it just brain cells firing, or something more? People who say a thought is JUST brain activity are called 'physicalists.' What is one argument FOR their view?
answer: Damage to the brain changes thoughts — pointing to a strong brain-mind link.
choices: Damage to the brain changes thoughts — pointing to a strong brain-mind link.
Thoughts can be photographed by a camera if you hold the camera close enough.
Thoughts cost money to make, so they must be small machines in the brain.
Thoughts are visible during medical X-rays, so they must be in the bones.
context: Strokes, drugs, and head injuries change what people think and feel. That seems like strong evidence the mind depends on the brain. Critics push back: 'Depends on' is not the same as 'is.'

question: If a powerful, all-knowing, all-good God exists, why is there evil and suffering in the world? This puzzle is called the 'problem of evil.' What is ONE attempted answer?
answer: A world with free choice must allow that people sometimes choose evil.
choices: A world with free choice must allow that people sometimes choose evil.
Evil does not really exist; people only imagine it during nightmares at night.
God does exist but does not actually know what is going on most of the time.
Evil happens because nobody asked God to stop it nicely in their daily prayers.
context: This is called the 'free will defense.' Critics ask: what about natural evils — earthquakes, diseases — that no one chose? The problem of evil has many proposed answers, none of them quick.

question: Other thinkers say evil is part of how SOULS GROW — without challenges, courage and kindness would never develop. This is called a 'soul-making' theodicy. What is one criticism of this view?
answer: Some suffering is so extreme it destroys, rather than builds, a person.
choices: Some suffering is so extreme it destroys, rather than builds, a person.
Souls do not grow at all; they are just balloons inside our bodies somewhere.
Soul-making is a kind of cheese, so the theory is about food, not evil.
Souls cannot be made by humans, so a theory of soul-making is impossible.
context: If suffering builds character, what about a child who dies in pain, with no chance to grow? Or a survivor whose trauma destroys him? The soul-making view answers part of the problem but not all of it.

question: Philosophers often define knowledge as 'justified true belief.' If you BELIEVE something, and it IS true, and you have REASONS, then you know it. What is one tricky case where this DEFINITION breaks down?
answer: You can believe something true for the wrong reason — and 'know it' by accident.
choices: You can believe something true for the wrong reason — and 'know it' by accident.
You can believe something only when you are watching a TV show about it.
You can only believe things that are true, since beliefs cannot be wrong.
You can never have reasons for any belief, so knowing is totally impossible.
context: Edmund Gettier wrote a famous short paper showing 'lucky' true beliefs that meet the definition but do not really feel like knowledge. Philosophers have been arguing about fixes ever since.

question: An ancient kind of philosopher called SKEPTICS asked: are you ever REALLY sure of anything? Maybe your senses lie. Maybe your memory tricks you. What did some skeptics recommend as a result?
answer: Suspend judgment — don't strongly believe OR disbelieve until you have to.
choices: Suspend judgment — don't strongly believe OR disbelieve until you have to.
Believe everything you hear from any speaker, no matter who is talking.
Believe nothing at all, so you can never be wrong about any single thing.
Stop using your senses, since they are dirty and full of tricks against you.
context: The ancient Greek skeptics thought certainty was usually impossible. Their answer was not despair — it was a kind of calm: hold your beliefs loosely, do not get worked up about every claim, live by what seems most reasonable.

question: Is BEAUTY a real property of things, or just in the eye of the beholder? Philosophers have argued about this for a long time. What is one good reason to think beauty is MORE than just personal taste?
answer: People across cultures often agree on what counts as beautiful — too often for pure taste.
choices: People across cultures often agree on what counts as beautiful — too often for pure taste.
Beauty causes physical pain, which is why nobody likes looking at it for long.
Beauty is illegal in most countries, so it cannot be just personal taste.
Beauty was invented by Aristotle, so before him nothing was beautiful at all.
context: Different cultures find similar things beautiful — symmetry, certain ratios, certain melodies. If beauty were pure taste, this overlap would be hard to explain. Critics reply: maybe humans just have similar brains.

question: Why should anyone OBEY the law? Some thinkers say it is because we agreed (a 'social contract'). What is one complication with that idea?
answer: Most of us never actually agreed to anything — we were born into our country.
choices: Most of us never actually agreed to anything — we were born into our country.
Most of us already obey every single law, so the question never comes up.
Most of us live in countries that do not have any laws to obey in the first place.
Most of us are born inside contracts, since babies are born holding contracts.
context: The 'social contract' idea is powerful but tricky. Locke, Rousseau, and others imagined people CHOOSING to leave a wild 'state of nature' for a society. But none of us were actually there for that choice.

question: Jamie says we should eat less candy because sugar harms our teeth. Mike replies: 'Don't listen to Jamie — she's bad at math!' What's wrong with Mike's reply?
answer: Ad hominem — Mike attacked Jamie's character instead of answering whether sugar really harms teeth.
choices: Ad hominem — Mike attacked Jamie's character instead of answering whether sugar really harms teeth.
Straw man — Mike rewrote Jamie's claim into a wilder version that was easier to mock or dismiss.
Red herring — Mike brought up math, a topic mostly unrelated to the sugar argument at hand.
Slippery slope — Mike claimed one cavity would lead to many cavities without giving reasons.
context: Ad hominem attacks the person, not the argument. Even a person bad at math can be right about sugar.

question: Mom says: 'If we let the dog on the couch, soon he'll sleep in our beds, then eat off our plates, then run the house.' What's wrong with her reasoning?
answer: Slippery slope — she claimed a chain of disasters without giving any reason each step must follow the last one.
choices: Slippery slope — she claimed a chain of disasters without giving any reason each step must follow the last one.
Hasty generalization — she drew a sweeping rule about all dogs from a single case she saw with this dog.
Ad hominem reasoning — she attacked the dog's character instead of giving an actual reason about couch behavior.
Bandwagon move — she claimed most families let dogs on couches, so this family should follow the popular crowd.
context: A slippery-slope argument can be valid if each step's link is shown. The fallacy is asserting the chain without showing it.

question: Your friend says: 'Come on, EVERYONE is making fun of the new kid — you should too.' Why isn't 'everyone is doing it' a good reason?
answer: Bandwagon fallacy — popularity is not evidence; many people can be wrong, and joining cruelty doesn't make it right.
choices: Bandwagon fallacy — popularity is not evidence; many people can be wrong, and joining cruelty doesn't make it right.
Ad hominem fallacy — the friend has attacked the new kid's character instead of arguing about ideas they hold.
Red herring fallacy — the friend has dragged in a topic that has nothing to do with the original question.
Strawman fallacy — the friend has invented a wilder version of your view in order to knock it back down.
context: The bandwagon move treats popularity as proof. Counting heads doesn't replace giving a reason.

question: Tara met two unfriendly cats this week. She now says, 'All cats are mean.' What's wrong with her conclusion?
answer: Hasty generalization — she made a sweeping rule about all cats from a tiny sample of only two unfriendly ones.
choices: Hasty generalization — she made a sweeping rule about all cats from a tiny sample of only two unfriendly ones.
Slippery slope reasoning — she claimed one mean cat would lead to all cats becoming mean later on.
Begging the question — she assumed her conclusion in her premise so the argument circles back on itself.
Appeal to authority — she cited a famous cat-expert who agrees, instead of showing real evidence for it.
context: Two cases isn't enough to support a claim about every cat. Hasty generalization is leaping from a thin sample.

question: You say: 'We should clean up after lunch.' Sam replies: 'So you want us to spend ALL DAY cleaning?!' What's wrong with Sam's reply?
answer: Straw man — Sam replaced your modest claim with a wilder version that was easier to mock instead of engaging it.
choices: Straw man — Sam replaced your modest claim with a wilder version that was easier to mock instead of engaging it.
Ad hominem move — Sam attacked your character or motives instead of dealing with the actual cleanup proposal.
Red herring move — Sam dragged in an unrelated topic to pull the discussion away from the cleanup question.
Bandwagon move — Sam claimed most kids never clean up after lunch, so we should follow the popular crowd.
context: A straw man is easier to knock down because the attacker built it. The cure: state the real claim, then engage that.

question: A TV ad says: 'Doctors recommend Choco-Crunch candy bars.' Even if that's true, why might it still not be a good reason to eat them?
answer: Appeal to authority — doctors are experts in health, not candy ads; their say-so isn't evidence about nutrition here.
choices: Appeal to authority — doctors are experts in health, not candy ads; their say-so isn't evidence about nutrition here.
Begging the question — the ad assumes its conclusion in its premise, looping the argument back on itself in a circle.
Hasty generalization — the ad rests on too small a sample of doctors to support a claim about all candy bars.
Equivocation move — the ad uses the word 'recommend' in two different senses across the message, shifting meaning.
context: Authority counts when the authority's training fits the question. A doctor recommending candy is the same as a chef recommending surgery.

question: Mom says: 'Either you finish your homework right now, or you're a total failure.' What's another possibility she's leaving out?
answer: False dilemma — she has framed only two options when many real ones exist: finishing later, taking a break, getting help.
choices: False dilemma — she has framed only two options when many real ones exist: finishing later, taking a break, getting help.
Genetic fallacy — she has rejected the homework idea based on its origin or source rather than its actual content.
Tu quoque fallacy — she deflected criticism by claiming you do the same thing she was just being criticized for.
Composition fallacy — she has assumed something true of each part of homework must also be true of the whole task.
