context: Also called the either/or or black-and-white fallacy. The cure: ask whether a third option has been hidden behind the choice.

question: 'Why is broccoli good for you?' 'Because it's healthy.' 'Why is it healthy?' 'Because it's good for you.' What's the problem here?
answer: Begging the question — Circular reasoning — the answer assumes the very claim it was supposed to prove, so the argument loops in a small circle.
choices: Begging the question — Circular reasoning — the answer assumes the very claim it was supposed to prove, so the argument loops in a small circle.
Equivocation reasoning — the word 'broccoli' is used in two senses across the answers, so a step looks valid by quiet shift.
Appeal to ignorance reasoning — the speaker argued from a lack of evidence against broccoli to a positive claim about it.
Hasty generalization reasoning — the speaker drew a wide conclusion about all vegetables from one tiny anecdotal example.
context: Also called begging the question. The premise and conclusion are really the same claim, just dressed up differently each time.

question: Liam says: 'I've never seen a ghost, and nobody can prove ghosts aren't real, so they must exist!' What's wrong with this reasoning?
answer: Appeal to ignorance — not having evidence against something is not evidence for it; an unanswered question stays unanswered.
choices: Appeal to ignorance — not having evidence against something is not evidence for it; an unanswered question stays unanswered.
Slippery slope reasoning — Liam claimed one unexplained event would lead to many supernatural events afterward.
Ad hominem reasoning — Liam attacked the character of ghost-doubters instead of giving real reasons for his own view.
Bandwagon reasoning — Liam relied on the popularity of ghost stories among other people as the basis for his own claim.
context: Sherlock Holmes had this right: absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence. The burden of proof falls on the one making the claim.

question: Coach replies to a player asking why she was benched: 'I'm the coach, that's why.' What kind of reasoning is this?
answer: Appeal to authority — the coach cited her role to end the argument instead of giving a real reason for the bench decision.
choices: Appeal to authority — the coach cited her role to end the argument instead of giving a real reason for the bench decision.
Appeal to popularity — the coach pointed to what most other coaches do, treating crowd-following as the basis for action.
Appeal to consequences — the coach claimed the bench decision must be right because its truth would lead to good results.
Appeal to ignorance — the coach argued that lacking evidence against the bench choice was proof it must have been right.
context: Authority can fit a question — but 'because I said so' is not a reason. A good coach can also give a reason.

question: Nina says: 'Have you stopped cheating on your tests?' Yes or no? Why is this question unfair, even if Nina just asked it?
answer: Loaded question — the question presupposes you were cheating; saying yes or no both seem to admit it, which is the trap.
choices: Loaded question — the question presupposes you were cheating; saying yes or no both seem to admit it, which is the trap.
Circular question — the question and its answer use the same exact words, so any reply you give just loops back to it.
Slippery question — the question claims one small admission will lead to a chain of further admissions you cannot stop.
Vague question — the question uses one key word in two senses, so an inference looks valid only by a hidden meaning shift.
context: A loaded question hides a disputed claim inside the wording. The cure: refuse the question and challenge the buried assumption.

question: Tom says: 'Owen wears glasses, and Owen is smart, so all glasses-wearers are smart.' What is Tom's mistake?
answer: Hasty generalization — Tom drew a broad rule about all glasses-wearers from a single example, far too thin a sample.
choices: Hasty generalization — Tom drew a broad rule about all glasses-wearers from a single example, far too thin a sample.
False dilemma — Tom framed only two options when many real positions on glasses-and-smartness exist between them.
Tu quoque fallacy — Tom deflected criticism by pointing out his critic does the same thing he was just accused of.
Bandwagon fallacy — Tom relied on the popularity of his view among classmates rather than giving any solid reasons.
context: One case can't carry a claim about all. A stronger argument needs many cases drawn from a wide and fair sample.

question: Riley says: 'It's been raining for three days, so it'll definitely rain forever.' What's wrong with Riley's reasoning?
answer: Hasty generalization — Riley used a short pattern as evidence for a much larger sweeping claim the data cannot carry.
choices: Hasty generalization — Riley used a short pattern as evidence for a much larger sweeping claim the data cannot carry.
Ad hominem reasoning — Riley attacked weather forecasters' character rather than dealing with the actual rainfall data.
Strawman reasoning — Riley replaced the original claim about three days with a wilder version about the entire season.
Begging the question — Riley assumed forever-rain as a premise and then concluded forever-rain, so the loop is tight.
context: Three days is real evidence, but it's not enough for 'forever.' Inductive jumps need many cases and care.

question: Alex says: 'You can't tell me not to lie — you lied last week!' Even if Alex is right the critic lied, why is this a bad reply?
answer: Tu quoque — pointing out the critic's own fault doesn't show the original claim is false; the criticism still has to be answered.
choices: Tu quoque — pointing out the critic's own fault doesn't show the original claim is false; the criticism still has to be answered.
Slippery slope — Alex argued one small lie will lead to many bigger lies without giving any reason each step follows.
Appeal to ignorance — Alex used the lack of evidence against lying as positive proof that lying must be acceptable.
Hasty generalization — Alex drew a broad conclusion about all lying from a single small example his critic gave him.
context: Tu quoque means 'you too' in Latin. It feels like a clever comeback but doesn't actually address whether the original point was right.

question: Coach asks why Jordan missed practice. Jordan replies: 'Did you know Coach Wilson has the best record in the league?' What is Jordan doing?
answer: Red herring — Jordan dragged in an unrelated topic about Coach Wilson to pull attention from the question being asked.
choices: Red herring — Jordan dragged in an unrelated topic about Coach Wilson to pull attention from the question being asked.
Strawman tactic — Jordan replaced the question about missing practice with a wilder version that was easier to escape.
Slippery slope — Jordan claimed one missed practice would lead to many further misses without any reason given.
Loaded question — Jordan asked a question whose form presupposes a controversial claim the coach has not yet agreed.
context: A red herring is a smelly distraction. The name comes from dragging a fish across a trail to throw hounds off the real scent.

question: Ben hears one bad review of a restaurant. He declares: 'This place must be terrible — never go there!' What's wrong with Ben's reasoning?
answer: Hasty generalization — Ben drew a sweeping verdict about the whole restaurant from one review, far too thin a sample.
choices: Hasty generalization — Ben drew a sweeping verdict about the whole restaurant from one review, far too thin a sample.
Circular reasoning — Ben assumed the restaurant was bad in his premise and then concluded it was bad, looping back.
Equivocation reasoning — Ben used the word 'bad' in two different senses across the argument, shifting its meaning.
Appeal to fear reasoning — Ben argued the restaurant must be bad because its truth would lead to unpleasant results.
context: One review is a single data point. Many reviews from different people give a fairer picture of how the restaurant really is.

question: Greta says: 'My grandpa smoked his whole life and lived to 95, so smoking can't really be bad for you.' What's the flaw?
answer: Hasty generalization — one lucky case can't outweigh huge studies; rare survivors don't show smoking is safe for everyone else.
choices: Hasty generalization — one lucky case can't outweigh huge studies; rare survivors don't show smoking is safe for everyone else.
Loaded question fallacy — Greta's claim presupposes a disputed point that the listener has not yet agreed to accept on faith.
Appeal to ignorance — Greta argued from lack of evidence against smoking to a positive claim it must be perfectly safe to do.
Slippery slope fallacy — Greta claimed one smoker living long would lead to all smokers living a long time too in a chain.
context: One person's outcome is anecdote, not evidence. Large studies trump single stories when the question is about populations.

question: Mr. Lee says: 'Either we ban all phones at school, or learning will collapse completely.' What's wrong with this framing?
answer: False dilemma — he has framed only two extreme options when many fair middle paths exist: limits, classroom rules, certain hours.
choices: False dilemma — he has framed only two extreme options when many fair middle paths exist: limits, classroom rules, certain hours.
Hasty generalization — he has drawn a sweeping conclusion about all phones from a small sample of cases he saw in his class.
Ad hominem reasoning — he has attacked the character of phone-users instead of addressing whether phones really harm learning.
Begging the question — he assumes his conclusion inside his premise, so the entire argument just loops in a very small circle.
context: Forcing a choice between extremes hides every middle path. Ask: is there really no third option?

question: Tu quoque (Latin: 'You too') deflects criticism by accusing the critic of doing the same thing. Why is this a fallacy, even when the accusation is accurate?
answer: Tu quoque — the critic's behavior doesn't change whether the original claim is true; even hypocrites can correctly identify wrong actions in others.
choices: Tu quoque — the critic's behavior doesn't change whether the original claim is true; even hypocrites can correctly identify wrong actions in others.
The critic's behavior shows the original claim must be false; once a critic is hypocritical, nothing they say can be true at all.
The critic's behavior is the only evidence that counts; if a critic is hypocritical, the original criticism is fully cancelled out.
The critic's behavior switches the burden of proof; once accused, the critic must defend themselves before any claim can stand.
context: Tu quoque is the schoolyard 'I know you are but what am I.' It feels like a clever comeback but doesn't engage the actual claim being made.

question: A red herring introduces something off-topic to pull attention from the real argument. Which case below is the clearest example of this move?
answer: Asked why she failed to pay rent, the tenant replies by listing all the times the landlord refused to fix the broken heater last winter.
choices: Asked why she failed to pay rent, the tenant replies by listing all the times the landlord refused to fix the broken heater last winter.
Asked why she failed to pay rent, the tenant replies that nobody has proven she lacked the funds, so she must have had them.
Asked why she failed to pay rent, the tenant replies that her brother also pays late, so the criticism doesn't really apply to her.
Asked why she failed to pay rent, the tenant replies that the landlord has called her dishonest before, so he cannot judge her.
context: Red herrings sound related but lead elsewhere. The cure: drag the conversation back to the original question and refuse to be diverted.

question: Post hoc ergo propter hoc (Latin: 'After this, therefore because of this') assumes that because B followed A, A caused B. Which of these cases makes this exact mistake?
answer: Every time the rooster crows, the sun rises right after; the farmer concludes the rooster's crowing is what causes the sun to rise.
choices: Every time the rooster crows, the sun rises right after; the farmer concludes the rooster's crowing is what causes the sun to rise.
Every time the rooster crows, the farmer attacks the rooster's character instead of asking what really triggers the rooster's crow.
Every time the rooster crows, the farmer claims one early-morning sound will lead to many disturbances throughout the rest of the day.
Every time the rooster crows, the farmer argues most farmers in the region also keep roosters, so keeping one must be a sound idea.
context: Sequence alone is not causation. Both events may share a third cause (here, the rotation of the Earth) that produces both at the same time.

question: Appeal to ignorance argues: 'Nobody has proven X is false, so X must be true' (or its mirror). What's the flaw at the heart of this move?
answer: Lack of evidence against a claim is not evidence for the claim; an open question remains open until positive evidence settles it.
choices: Lack of evidence against a claim is not evidence for the claim; an open question remains open until positive evidence settles it.
Lack of evidence against a claim makes the claim false by definition; without proof, no statement can ever count as true at all.
Lack of evidence against a claim shifts the burden onto the speaker; the listener must prove the claim true before doubting it.
Lack of evidence against a claim shows both sides are equally supported; truth and falsehood become a perfect tie in such cases.
context: The burden of proof falls on the one making a positive claim. 'You can't prove it isn't' doesn't replace 'here's why it is.'

question: Equivocation occurs when one key word shifts meaning across an argument. Which case below shows equivocation in action most clearly?
answer: Equivocation — 'A feather is light. What is light cannot be dark. So no feather can ever be dark in color.' The word 'light' shifts meaning between lines.
choices: Equivocation — 'A feather is light. What is light cannot be dark. So no feather can ever be dark in color.' The word 'light' shifts meaning between lines.
'A feather is light. So pillows full of feathers are light too.' The word 'feather' keeps one steady meaning across every premise.
'A feather floats in air. So all small objects must float in air.' The word 'float' keeps one steady meaning throughout the argument.
'A feather has a quill. Quills hold ink. So feathers hold ink.' The word 'quill' keeps one steady meaning throughout the argument.
context: Equivocation is the engine of word-puzzle paradoxes. 'Light' meaning low-weight and 'light' meaning bright are different concepts sharing one spelling.

question: No true Scotsman saves a general claim by redefining the category to exclude any counterexample. Which case shows this move most plainly?
answer: Critic: many vegans wear leather shoes. Reply: well, no TRUE vegan would wear leather; those people aren't actually vegans at all.
choices: Critic: many vegans wear leather shoes. Reply: well, no TRUE vegan would wear leather; those people aren't actually vegans at all.
Critic: many vegans wear leather shoes. Reply: most vegans I know don't, so the criticism rests on too small a sample base.
Critic: many vegans wear leather shoes. Reply: you've changed the original modest claim about food into a much wider one to mock.
Critic: many vegans wear leather shoes. Reply: that's just an attack on vegans' character, not a real argument about the diet itself.
context: Named by Antony Flew. The trick: face a counterexample, and rather than weaken the claim, redefine the term to expel the counterexample.

question: Composition fallacy assumes what is true of each part must be true of the whole. Which case below makes this mistake about parts and wholes?
answer: Every player on this team is highly skilled. So the team itself must therefore be one of the most skilled teams in the entire league.
choices: Every player on this team is highly skilled. So the team itself must therefore be one of the most skilled teams in the entire league.
Every player on this team trained hard last summer. So most players on the team will probably be ready when the season opens up.
Every player on this team wears a uniform. So each player wears a uniform during the matches that take place over the long season.
Every player on this team has a position. So the team has many positions filled by the players when the squad takes the field.
context: A team is more than the sum of its individuals. Stars can clash on the court; a less starry roster with good chemistry can outplay them.

question: Division fallacy is the mirror of composition: it assumes what is true of the whole must be true of each part. Which case below shows this mistake?
answer: This salad is healthy as a whole dish. So every single ingredient inside the salad must by itself also count as a healthy food choice.
choices: This salad is healthy as a whole dish. So every single ingredient inside the salad must by itself also count as a healthy food choice.
This salad is healthy as a whole dish. So most of the ingredients inside the salad will be reasonably nutritious on their own merits.
This salad is healthy as a whole dish. So a salad eaten regularly will probably contribute to better health over time for the diner.
This salad is healthy as a whole dish. So a chef preparing this salad must understand at least some basic principles of nutrition.
context: Salt is not a 'salad-healthy' ingredient on its own, even when a salad needs some salt to taste good. Whole-properties don't always transfer to parts.

question: Genetic fallacy judges a claim by its origin rather than its content. Which case below commits this mistake about where an idea came from?
answer: You can't trust this finding about vaccine safety because the company funding the study also sells the vaccine being tested in it.
choices: You can't trust this finding about vaccine safety because the company funding the study also sells the vaccine being tested in it.
You can't trust this finding about vaccine safety because the trial included only seventy patients, far too small a sample for the claim.
You can't trust this finding about vaccine safety because the study has not been peer-reviewed, so its methods have not been checked.
You can't trust this finding about vaccine safety because the lead researcher mishandled data on three earlier projects she conducted.
context: Conflict-of-interest is a reason to be careful, not to dismiss. The actual data and methods still have to be examined on their own merits.

question: Appeal to popularity (argumentum ad populum) treats wide agreement as proof. Which case below is the clearest example of this move in action?
answer: Most people in this country believe the moon landings happened, so they must have happened; majorities settle factual questions.
choices: Most people in this country believe the moon landings happened, so they must have happened; majorities settle factual questions.
Most people in this country believe the moon landings happened, but a few still doubt; the evidence rather than opinion must decide.
Most people in this country believe the moon landings happened because films and photos from Apollo missions survived in archives.
Most people in this country believe the moon landings happened, yet the doubters point at minor details rather than the main facts.
context: Numbers don't make truth. Galileo was right when nearly everyone disagreed with him; many a popular belief has turned out wrong over time.

question: Appeal to consequences argues that a claim must be false (or true) because its truth would lead to unwelcome (or welcome) results. What's wrong with this?
answer: Whether a claim is true is independent of whether its truth is convenient or pleasant for us; reality doesn't bend to our preferences.
choices: Whether a claim is true is independent of whether its truth is convenient or pleasant for us; reality doesn't bend to our preferences.
Whether a claim is true depends entirely on whether the consequences make us happy; comfort is the final test of any claim at all.
Whether a claim is true depends on whether the consequences are popular among most people; majorities settle factual questions for us.
Whether a claim is true depends on whether the consequences match what authority figures say; experts settle factual questions for us.
context: Wishful thinking is a poor compass. 'I don't like the conclusion' doesn't refute the argument. The argument has to be answered on its own.

question: Cum hoc ergo propter hoc (Latin: 'With this, therefore because of this') concludes one thing caused another from mere correlation. Which case shows this?
answer: Towns with more ice-cream shops have more drownings; the analyst concludes ice cream causes drowning, when summer heat causes both.
choices: Towns with more ice-cream shops have more drownings; the analyst concludes ice cream causes drowning, when summer heat causes both.
Towns with more ice-cream shops have more drownings; the analyst concludes most townspeople in such towns are particularly clumsy.
Towns with more ice-cream shops have more drownings; the analyst attacks the character of ice-cream sellers instead of the data.
Towns with more ice-cream shops have more drownings; the analyst claims the connection is only a chance pattern in small numbers.
context: Two things correlated can share a third cause. Statisticians say 'correlation is not causation' for exactly this reason: a lurking variable can drive both.

question: False dilemma frames only two options when more exist. The fix is to ask: is a third path being hidden? Which case below offers a false dilemma?
answer: 'Either we cut every public program right now or our entire economy will collapse this year' — middle paths are completely ignored here.
choices: 'Either we cut every public program right now or our entire economy will collapse this year' — middle paths are completely ignored here.
'Either we cut every public program right now or our entire economy will collapse' — said because a hostile critic of the speaker said so.
'Either we cut every public program right now or our entire economy will collapse' — because most economists agree with this position.
'Either we cut every public program right now or our entire economy will collapse' — because the speaker's plan circles back on itself.
context: Also called false dichotomy or the black-and-white fallacy. Real choices usually have a range of options between the two extreme poles offered.

question: Loaded question hides a disputed claim inside the wording, so any direct answer seems to admit it. Which case below shows a loaded question?
answer: 'When did you stop bullying the younger kids?' — accepting either 'last year' or 'never' both seem to admit you bullied them at some point.
choices: 'When did you stop bullying the younger kids?' — accepting either 'last year' or 'never' both seem to admit you bullied them at some point.
'When did you stop bullying the younger kids?' — the question is asked because the speaker dislikes you and wants to make you feel bad.
'When did you stop bullying the younger kids?' — the question is asked because three other kids have said you bullied them before recess.
'When did you stop bullying the younger kids?' — the question is asked because the assistant principal sent you to her office this morning.
context: The cure: refuse the question's form and challenge the buried assumption. 'I never started, so the question doesn't apply.'

question: Slippery slope claims one step must trigger a cascade without showing why each step follows. When does this argument become valid rather than fallacious?
answer: When the speaker actually shows each step in the chain has a real causal mechanism linking it to the next step in the sequence.
choices: When the speaker actually shows each step in the chain has a real causal mechanism linking it to the next step in the sequence.
When the speaker simply asserts the chain with enough rhetorical force, the audience will be moved to grant the conclusion as right.
When the speaker cites the popularity of the chain among many other people, the wide agreement will support the asserted result.
When the speaker attacks the character of those who doubt the chain, the doubters are silenced and the chain stands as established.
context: Slippery slopes can be valid: 'One drink leads to another' is supported by addiction biology. The fallacy is asserting the chain without giving the mechanism.

question: No true Scotsman saves a general claim by redefining the category to exclude any counterexample. Why is this a serious fallacy rather than just a quibble?
answer: It makes the claim unfalsifiable: any counterexample is expelled from the category by definition, so no evidence could ever count against it.
choices: It makes the claim unfalsifiable: any counterexample is expelled from the category by definition, so no evidence could ever count against it.
It makes the claim too narrow to be interesting: shrinking the category each time leaves a thin trivial group hardly worth defending here.
It makes the claim culturally biased: redefining a national category implies one group has the authority to decide who really counts in it.
It makes the claim emotionally manipulative: the speaker leans on the listener's identity with the category to extract their agreement.
context: Falsifiability matters: if no possible evidence could refute a claim, the claim isn't really telling us anything about the world.

question: Composition fallacy moves from each-part to whole; the opposite mistake moves from whole to each-part. Which case shows COMPOSITION (parts to whole) most clearly?
answer: 'Each cell in this organism is microscopically small. So the entire organism must also be microscopically small in its overall size.'
choices: 'Each cell in this organism is microscopically small. So the entire organism must also be microscopically small in its overall size.'
'This entire forest is several centuries old. So each tree in the forest must also be several centuries old in its own age too.'
'This entire choir sings beautifully. So each singer in the choir must by themselves also sing beautifully without any others.'
'This entire team is highly experienced. So each member of the team must by themselves have many years of experience too.'
context: Composition errs going up (parts to whole); division errs going down (whole to parts). Both forget that wholes have emergent properties parts may lack.

question: Genetic fallacy judges a claim by its origin rather than its merits. When does pointing to a source become a genetic fallacy and when is it legitimate?
answer: Genetic fallacy — Legitimate when the source's reliability bears on the claim's evidence; fallacious when the source's character is treated as itself disproving the claim.
choices: Genetic fallacy — Legitimate when the source's reliability bears on the claim's evidence; fallacious when the source's character is treated as itself disproving the claim.
Legitimate when the source is unpopular; fallacious when the source is widely respected, since popularity should never be used to support a claim.
Legitimate when the source agrees with your view; fallacious only when the source disagrees, since hostile sources are always suspect for that reason.
Legitimate when the source is named; fallacious only when the source is anonymous, since unnamed sources can never bear on a claim's evaluation.
context: A study funded by a tobacco company on smoking deserves extra scrutiny — that's not genetic fallacy. Dismissing the study because of its funding without examining its methods is.

question: Pundits often blur correlation and causation. A study finds students who eat breakfast score higher on math tests. What conclusion does the data actually support?
answer: That eating breakfast and scoring well are statistically associated, leaving open whether breakfast causes scores or a third factor causes both.
choices: That eating breakfast and scoring well are statistically associated, leaving open whether breakfast causes scores or a third factor causes both.
That eating breakfast causes higher math scores, since both rose together and one would not move without the other in the data set.
That higher math scores cause students to eat breakfast, since scores were measured before breakfast was tracked in the study design.
That eating breakfast has no relation to math scores, since correlation by itself can never establish any link of any kind between two factors.
context: Breakfast might cause scores; scores might cause breakfast (likely not); or family stability might cause both. The data shows a link, not a direction.

question: An economist says: 'Free trade has made some workers poorer in the short term, so free trade is bad policy.' What's the fallacy in this argument?
answer: Composition: it moves from harm to some workers to harm to the policy overall, ignoring gains to many other workers and to consumers more broadly.
choices: Composition: it moves from harm to some workers to harm to the policy overall, ignoring gains to many other workers and to consumers more broadly.
Strawman: it replaces a more modest claim about free trade with a wilder version that opponents of free trade had never actually defended.
Ad hominem: it attacks the character of free-traders rather than addressing the actual arguments they have made for the economic policy here.
Equivocation: it uses the word 'trade' in two different senses across the argument, so a step looks valid only because of a hidden shift.
context: Policy evaluations need to weigh effects across a whole population. The harm to some matters morally, but doesn't by itself settle the policy's worth.

question: An ad campaign says: 'Choose Brand X — our customers are the happiest in America.' Even if true, which fallacies might lurk in this slogan? Pick the most central concern.
answer: Bandwagon — Selection bias and the bandwagon move: 'Happiest customers' may reflect who bought the product, and the implied 'so should you' is a popularity appeal.
choices: Bandwagon — Selection bias and the bandwagon move: 'Happiest customers' may reflect who bought the product, and the implied 'so should you' is a popularity appeal.
Strawman and tu quoque: the slogan rewrites a critic's actual position and then accuses critics of doing the same thing they are accusing.
Affirming the consequent and post hoc: the slogan uses an invalid conditional form and assumes one event caused another because it followed.
Equivocation and division: the slogan uses one word in two senses and applies what is true of the brand to each separate customer alike.
context: Customer surveys filter for buyers. Happy people picked the brand; unhappy ones returned it. The implicit 'join them' is a bandwagon nudge.

question: An argument runs: 'Either climate change is a hoax, or it's the most urgent problem facing humanity.' Why is this framing fallacious whatever your view of the science?
answer: False dilemma: it presents two extreme options as exhaustive when many middle positions exist between hoax and most-urgent-problem-of-all here.
choices: False dilemma: it presents two extreme options as exhaustive when many middle positions exist between hoax and most-urgent-problem-of-all here.
Genetic fallacy: it judges the science of climate by the political origins of those who first raised concerns about the warming planet's state.
Tu quoque: it deflects criticism by pointing out that critics of climate policy also have inconsistencies in their environmental conduct.
Begging the question: it assumes its conclusion as a premise, so the entire argument circles back on itself in a tight little loop here.
context: Real policy debates live between extremes. 'Hoax' versus 'most-urgent' rules out countless serious positions: real but manageable, urgent but tractable.

question: A debate-coach asks: 'When does naming a fallacy NOT settle an argument?' Pick the best answer for your debate club's training session this week.
answer: When the named pattern is similar but not actually present, when context makes the move legitimate, or when the fallacy-naming itself becomes a deflection.
choices: When the named pattern is similar but not actually present, when context makes the move legitimate, or when the fallacy-naming itself becomes a deflection.
When the audience hasn't heard of the fallacy before, since naming it works only when the listeners already know the technical term being used.
When the opponent hasn't formally been trained in logic, since naming a fallacy works only when both parties share the same technical training.
When the fallacy is named in English rather than Latin, since names in English carry less rhetorical weight than the classical Latin forms do.
context: Knowing fallacy names is a tool, not a trump card. The other side may have a point you've mis-described; argue the substance, not the label.

question: A common school-debate trap: arguing against a position by attacking the WEAKEST version of it. Which of these is the proper antidote to that?
answer: The steel-man: state the opponent's view in its strongest form, with the best supporting reasons available, before raising any objections to it.
choices: The steel-man: state the opponent's view in its strongest form, with the best supporting reasons available, before raising any objections to it.
The straw-man: state a weaker version of the opponent's view so that knocking it down is easier and the audience is more readily persuaded.
The red-herring: introduce a related but distinct topic so the discussion drifts away from the weakest parts of the original argument made.
The tu-quoque: point out that the opponent attacks weak versions of YOUR view, so they cannot complain when you do the same to theirs.
context: Steel-manning forces real engagement and makes your own thinking stronger. If you can't refute the BEST version, you may have learned something.

question: The sorites paradox: one grain isn't a heap; adding a grain to a non-heap can't make one; so no number is a heap. Yet a million grains plainly IS a heap. Where do philosophers diagnose the fault?
answer: They diverge: epistemicists hold there is a sharp boundary we cannot know; supervaluationists posit truth-value gaps near the borderline; many-valued logicians abandon bivalence.
choices: They diverge: epistemicists hold there is a sharp boundary we cannot know; supervaluationists posit truth-value gaps near the borderline; many-valued logicians abandon bivalence.
They agree: the inductive premise is straightforwardly false, since each grain measurably increases volume and a sufficient number obviously crosses into heap status under any reasonable definition.
They agree: the base case is false, since a single grain already counts as a heap in the relevant sense, and the inductive premise correctly carries heaphood up through every addition.
They agree: the paradox is purely linguistic and dissolves on translation, since languages with different boundary-terms show no analogous puzzle and the problem is an English-usage artifact.
context: Sorites drives all vagueness puzzles. Williamson defends epistemicism. Fine and others defend supervaluationism. Lukasiewicz-style fuzzy logic abandons true/false for degrees. Each diagnosis carries serious cost — the puzzle is far from settled.

question: Base-rate fallacy (Tversky and Kahneman, 1973): a test has 99% sensitivity, 95% specificity. Someone tests positive. If base rate is 1 in 1000, the correct probability is much lower than the intuited 95%. What does the failure illustrate?
answer: Neglect of prior probability: when a condition is very rare, even a highly accurate test produces more false positives than true ones — false-positive rate acts on the huge healthy majority.
choices: Neglect of prior probability: when a condition is very rare, even a highly accurate test produces more false positives than true ones — false-positive rate acts on the huge healthy majority.
Confusion of correlation and causation: the test correlates with disease but doesn't cause it; concluding 'positive means disease' runs post-hoc reasoning in a sophisticated statistical dress.
Neglect of sample size: small-sample results don't support broad conclusions about disease prevalence; much larger samples are needed before any inference can be reliably drawn here.
Confusion of validity and soundness: the test's form yields valid inferences but premises about sensitivity and specificity are unsound where clinical measurement errors compound difficulties.
context: Bayes' theorem: P(D|+) = P(+|D) × P(D) / P(+). With 1000 people, 1 has the disease (truly positive: ~0.99); 999 are healthy (false-positive: ~50). A positive test is ~1 in 51 ≈ 2% likely real. Doctors get this wrong; juries hearing forensic evidence often do too. Aristotle's Prior Analytics distinguished form from content. Validity is purely about form (does conclusion follow from premises). Soundness adds: are the premises actually true?

question: The fallacy of composition is treacherous in economics. Keynes called this the 'paradox of thrift'. What does the paradox illustrate, and which broader fallacy does it instance?
answer: One household saving more gets wealthier; all saving more at once drops aggregate demand and incomes, leaving everyone POORER. Composition: a part-level truth fails at the system level due to feedback.
choices: One household saving more gets wealthier; all saving more at once drops aggregate demand and incomes, leaving everyone POORER. Composition: a part-level truth fails at the system level due to feedback.
One household saving more gets wealthier; thrift is bad at the individual level when properly examined, since prudent individuals miss investment returns. The fallacy is mistaking caution for wisdom.
One household saving more gets wealthier; government must always offset private saving with spending. The fallacy is failing to see public and private accounts must balance in macroeconomic terms.
One household saving more gets wealthier; monetary policy matters more than fiscal restraint. The fallacy is treating saving as a moral virtue when it is really just a technical economic variable.
context: Keynes: my saving is your reduced income; if all save at once, total income falls and total saving may decline. Whether this is genuine or a failure of his model is disputed (Hayek, Austrians, RBC theorists). The composition framing itself is uncontroversial.

question: Sam says 'We should eat raw meat because cavemen ate it that way.' What is the problem with his reason?
answer: Just because something is old or 'natural' does not make it a good idea.
choices: Just because something is old or 'natural' does not make it a good idea.
Cavemen ate the wrong kinds of meat for kids who are still growing up.
Sam should be vegan instead, since plants are better than any meat is.
Cavemen are not real and never ate any kind of food in the past at all.
context: Saying 'it is natural' or 'people used to do it' is not a real reason. Lots of natural things hurt us. Lots of new ideas are great.

question: An ad says 'This drink is 100% natural, so it must be healthy.' Why is this NOT a strong reason to drink it?
answer: Lots of natural things, like poison berries, are very bad for you.
choices: Lots of natural things, like poison berries, are very bad for you.
The drink might taste bad even though it is healthy in the end.
The drink should also be cold, not just natural, to be any good.
Most drinks in stores are made up of water, so the ad is lying.
context: 'Natural' on a label means almost nothing. Some natural things help you. Some hurt you. The word by itself is not a reason.

question: Lily has been in line for an hour. The line still has not moved. She says 'I waited so long, I can't leave now!' What is wrong with that thinking?
answer: Sunk cost — the hour she spent is already gone — staying longer will not bring it back.
choices: Sunk cost — the hour she spent is already gone — staying longer will not bring it back.
She should have brought a book, but it is too late to go grab one in every case that comes up.
She is correct — once you start a line, you can never leave at all in every case that comes up.
She is wrong because lines are bad and nobody should ever wait in any in every case that comes up.
context: This trap is called sunk cost. The hour is gone no matter what she picks. The real question is what is best to do NOW.

question: Ben starts a puzzle. After an hour, it is clear half the pieces are missing. He says 'I already started, so I HAVE to finish.' Is this good thinking?
answer: No — if the puzzle cannot finish, his time is better spent on something else.
choices: No — if the puzzle cannot finish, his time is better spent on something else.
Yes — once you start any puzzle, the rules say you have to finish.
No — he should keep trying because missing pieces will show up later.
Yes — quitting puzzles makes you weak at every other game in life.
context: Time you already spent is gone. The smart question is 'what is the best use of my time RIGHT NOW?', not 'how much did I already spend?'

question: A shirt is marked $100, then says 'ON SALE for $40.' You don't really need a shirt. Is $40 a good deal?
answer: Not really — if you don't need it, $40 is still $40 out of your pocket.
choices: Not really — if you don't need it, $40 is still $40 out of your pocket.
Yes — any sale is a good deal, no matter what the item really is.
Yes — saving $60 is the same as earning $60, so you are richer.
No — the shirt is still too cheap and the store is tricking you.
context: The big $100 'before' price is a trick to make $40 feel small. The right question is 'do I need this for $40?', not 'is it on sale?'

question: Pat thinks 'Dogs hate cats.' He sees one dog chase one cat and says 'See, I was right!' But he ignored three dogs that ignored cats yesterday. What is he doing?
answer: He is only counting what fits his idea and skipping what does not.
choices: He is only counting what fits his idea and skipping what does not.
He is right because once you see a dog chase a cat the rule is proved.
He is wrong because cats actually hate dogs, not the other way around.
He is being smart by ignoring boring days when nothing happened at all.
context: We tend to notice what fits our ideas and miss what doesn't. Real thinkers force themselves to look at what does NOT fit.

question: Maya is sure her lucky shirt helps her score in soccer. She lists the games she won wearing it. She forgets the games she lost in it. What is she doing?
answer: She is remembering only the wins that match her idea about the shirt.
choices: She is remembering only the wins that match her idea about the shirt.
She is being smart, because winning games is what matters to her.
She is wrong because the lucky shirt only works on rainy days too.
She is using her shirt to show off and the other kids are jealous.
context: If you only count the times your idea worked, you can prove almost any silly idea. You have to count the misses too.

question: You flip a coin five times and get tails every time. Does this mean heads is 'due' on the next flip?
answer: No — each flip is fresh. The coin does not remember what just happened.
choices: No — each flip is fresh. The coin does not remember what just happened.
Yes — five tails in a row is too much, so heads has to come next.
Yes — the coin owes you a heads after making you wait so long.
No — five tails proves the coin can only show tails from now on.
context: Coins, dice, and lottery balls have no memory. A run of one result does not change what comes next. Each flip is its own thing.

question: Asher rolls a die six times and never gets a 6. He says 'A 6 has to come up next, it is owed to me!' Is he right?
answer: No — the die does not know what just rolled. Each roll is the same chance.
choices: No — the die does not know what just rolled. Each roll is the same chance.
Yes — the die owes him a 6 since he has been waiting so long now.
Yes — six rolls without a 6 means the die is broken and needs fixed.
No — but only because he is using the wrong die for the game.
context: Dice do not 'owe' anyone. Past rolls do not change future rolls. The die is just as likely to roll any number every single time.

question: Two kids broke a window. One did it on purpose. One did it by accident. Should they get the same punishment?
answer: Probably not — what they MEANT matters when we decide what is fair.
choices: Probably not — what they MEANT matters when we decide what is fair.
Yes — broken is broken, and the result is the only thing that matters.
Yes — both kids are equally bad because windows are equal to each other.
No — the one who broke it on purpose should be sent home for one week.
context: Two things that LOOK the same can be very different when you ask 'what was the person thinking when they did it?' Same result, different cases.

question: Riley says 'I yelled at my sister, and Mom yelled at me. So we both did the same thing!' What is Riley missing?
answer: Mom was correcting Riley. Riley was being mean. Yelling is not always the same.
choices: Mom was correcting Riley. Riley was being mean. Yelling is not always the same.
Riley is right — any time two people yell, the yelling is exactly equal.
Riley is wrong because moms are not allowed to yell at kids at all.
Riley is right — because the louder yell is always the meaner one.
context: Two actions can LOOK the same on the outside but be very different in why they happened. Calling them equal hides what really went on.

question: The new kid used to live in another country. Some kids say his ideas don't count because 'he's not from here.' What is wrong with that?
answer: Where an idea CAME FROM does not tell you if the idea is right or wrong.
choices: Where an idea CAME FROM does not tell you if the idea is right or wrong.
His ideas don't count, because only kids from here can have good ideas.
His ideas count more, because new kids always know more than old kids do.
His ideas should be ignored until he learns to talk like the other kids.
context: An idea is good or bad on its own. Who said it, or where they came from, does not change whether it is true.

question: Jen says 'This rule was made by the boring teacher, so it must be a boring rule.' What is wrong with the way she is thinking?
answer: The rule could be smart or silly. WHO made it does not decide.
choices: The rule could be smart or silly. WHO made it does not decide.
She is right because boring people only make boring rules in their lives.
She is wrong because boring teachers cannot make rules at any school.
She is right but only on days when the teacher is feeling extra tired.
context: Judging an idea by who said it skips the real question: is the idea any good? Even people you don't like can have good ideas.

question: Lee broke a vase. When his sister tells Mom, Lee yells 'yes, but what about when SHE broke the lamp!?' Is that a good defense?
answer: Whataboutism — no — his sister's old mistake does not undo what Lee just did.
choices: Whataboutism — no — his sister's old mistake does not undo what Lee just did.
Yes — bringing up her past lamp means his vase does not count at all.
Yes — moms are only allowed to be mad at one kid each day, not two.
No — but only because his sister broke a more expensive lamp than his.
context: Pointing at someone else's mistake does not fix yours. This trick is called 'whataboutism' — it dodges the real question.

question: Mom asks Tim to clean his room. Tim says 'But my brother's room is messy TOO!' Is this a good reply?
answer: No — what his brother does is a different question from Tim's own room.
choices: No — what his brother does is a different question from Tim's own room.
Yes — if one kid is messy, no other kid has to clean their own room.
Yes — brothers must always be in the same trouble at the same time.
No — but only if his brother's room is way messier than Tim's is.
context: Pointing at another person to get out of doing your part is a classic dodge. The real question — 'is Tim's room messy?' — is still right there.

question: Carlos says 'Prove dragons aren't real.' You say nobody has ever found one. He says 'Well, maybe they hide.' You say there is no sign anywhere. He says 'Maybe they're invisible.' What is Carlos doing?
answer: Moving the goalposts — He keeps changing the test so nothing can ever count as proof.
choices: Moving the goalposts — He keeps changing the test so nothing can ever count as proof.
He is being very smart and asking great questions about dragons today in normal use.
He is right because we can never prove anything about anything at all in normal use.
He is wrong because dragons used to be real and only stopped recently in normal use.
context: When every answer you give gets met with a new excuse, the other person is 'moving the goalposts.' They never planned to be convinced.

question: Sara doubts her brother saw a deer in the yard. He shows a photo. She says 'Photos can be faked.' He shows hoof prints. She says 'A dog could make those.' What is Sara doing?
answer: She is changing what would count as proof every time he brings some.
choices: She is changing what would count as proof every time he brings some.
She is being smart by not believing everything she sees in life today.
She is right because deer are not real and her brother is making it up.
She is wrong because deer in yards is the most normal thing on Earth.
context: If no answer is ever good enough, you cannot really win the talk. Honest thinkers say upfront what would change their minds.

question: 'Why do we do it this way?' 'Because we have ALWAYS done it this way.' Is that a strong reason by itself?
answer: No — old habits can be smart, but 'we always have' is not a real reason.
choices: No — old habits can be smart, but 'we always have' is not a real reason.
Yes — old habits are always smart, just because they have lasted long.
Yes — only doing new things is for kids and silly people, never us.
No — we should only do brand-new things and skip every old habit.
context: Some old habits are wise. Some are silly. 'We always have' does not tell you which one this is. You still have to ask WHY.

question: A town has a rule that boys cannot bake. People say 'we have done it that way for 100 years.' Is the rule a good rule?
answer: Not just because it is old — old rules can still be wrong and unfair.
choices: Not just because it is old — old rules can still be wrong and unfair.
Yes — any rule that is 100 years old must be right by now today.
Yes — boys really cannot bake, no matter what they do or learn or try.
No — but only because we should also stop girls from baking too soon.
context: Old does not mean right. Lots of old rules turned out to be unfair. Lots of new ideas turned out to be better. Age is not the test.

question: Dad asks 'Have you stopped sneaking cookies before dinner?' You never DID sneak cookies. Why is this question tricky?
answer: Loaded question — Saying yes OR no makes it sound like you used to sneak cookies.
choices: Loaded question — Saying yes OR no makes it sound like you used to sneak cookies.
It is a normal question and you should answer yes very quickly in every case that comes up.
Dad is testing you and you should give him a hug to dodge it in every case that comes up.
The right answer is 'cookies,' since cookies were named in the question.
context: A loaded question hides a guess inside it. The fair move is to step out of the trap: 'I never sneaked cookies in the first place.'

question: A reporter asks the mayor 'why do you hate our schools so much?' The mayor does NOT hate the schools. Why is the question unfair?
answer: Loaded question — It sneaks in a claim — that he hates schools — before he can answer it.
choices: Loaded question — It sneaks in a claim — that he hates schools — before he can answer it.
Reporters are not allowed to ask any mayor any questions in any state in normal use.
The mayor should answer the question quickly with a yes or with a no in normal use.
Schools are boring and the question is not really about schools at all in normal use.
context: A loaded question forces the other person to either accept a claim or look like they're dodging. The right move is to call out the hidden claim first.

question: Tim met one rude kid from Oakville. He says 'I guess kids in Oakville are all rude!' What is wrong with this?
answer: One kid is not enough to make a rule about a whole town of people.
choices: One kid is not enough to make a rule about a whole town of people.
He is right — one kid is a perfect sample of every other person there.
He is wrong — kids in Oakville are very nice, not rude, you know.
He should meet two kids from Oakville before he is allowed to decide.
context: Judging a whole group by one person is a hasty leap. Even a few people are not enough to know what a whole group is like.

question: Jenna tried two video games last year and didn't like either. She says 'I HATE all video games!' What is wrong with this jump?
answer: Two games are not enough to know about every game in the world.
choices: Two games are not enough to know about every game in the world.
She is right — two tries is plenty to know what all games are like.
She is wrong — she liked one of them, so she is lying to herself.
She should try three more games and then say it loudly all again.
context: Two games out of thousands is a tiny sample. Saying 'all of them' after trying so few is a hasty jump.

question: Owen's plant died after watering it twice. He says 'I can't grow ANYTHING!' What might his big sister say?
answer: Two times is not enough to learn — give it more tries before you decide.
choices: Two times is not enough to learn — give it more tries before you decide.
She should agree, because two tries is plenty for any kid to learn.
She should say 'plants always die,' so he should not try again at all.
She should say he should never water plants and try only sunlight next.
context: Drawing a big rule from two tries is hasty. You usually need more tries — and to think about WHY each one went the way it did.

question: Dad says 'If I let you stay up ONE late night, soon you'll be up all night EVERY night and your grades will fail!' What is wrong with how he is thinking?
answer: Slippery slope — He is skipping all the small steps and jumping to the worst ending.
choices: Slippery slope — He is skipping all the small steps and jumping to the worst ending.
He is right — one late night really does ruin every school year ahead in normal use.
He is right — kids who stay up late always grow up to drop out fast in normal use.
He is wrong because late nights are great for kids and parents both in normal use.
context: A slippery slope says one small step leads straight to a terrible end, with no stops along the way. Most slopes are not that slick.

question: 'If we let kids wear hats in class, soon they'll wear costumes, then they'll bring pets, then nobody will learn anything!' What is the problem with this?
answer: Slippery slope — each step is treated like it must happen — but each step is its own choice.
choices: Slippery slope — each step is treated like it must happen — but each step is its own choice.
It is correct — once hats are allowed, costumes always follow soon after in every case that comes up.
It is correct — pets in class is one tiny step past hats in class in every case that comes up.
It is wrong because hats are great and pets in class would also be great in every case that comes up.
context: A slippery slope skips the brakes. In real life, we can stop at any step we want. The big bad ending is not a sure thing.

question: Every kid in class is wearing the new sneaker. Sara thinks the shoe is ugly. Her friend says 'Just get them, EVERYONE has them!' Is 'everyone has them' a good reason for Sara to buy?
answer: Bandwagon — no — what other kids do says nothing about whether the shoe is right for her.
choices: Bandwagon — no — what other kids do says nothing about whether the shoe is right for her.
Yes — once enough kids do a thing, every other kid has to do it too in every case that comes up.
Yes — fitting in is the only thing that ever matters in life at all in every case that comes up.
No — but only because she should pick shoes that are even more ugly in every case that comes up.
context: 'Everyone is doing it' is called the bandwagon. It can feel strong, but a big crowd doing something dumb does not make the thing smart.

question: A video has a million likes. Tom says 'A million people like it, so it MUST be good.' What is wrong with using likes this way?
answer: Lots of people liking a thing does not prove the thing is any good.
choices: Lots of people liking a thing does not prove the thing is any good.
He is right — once a video gets a million likes, the video is great.
He is right because likes are how truth gets measured online nowadays.
He is wrong because likes always mean the video is bad and dumb forever.
context: Crowds can be wrong. Lots of likes mean lots of people clicked — not that the thing is good. You still have to think for yourself.

question: Two kids talk about saving water. One says 'We should turn off the tap when we brush.' The other says 'Who CARES — your sneakers are ugly!' What just happened?
answer: He attacked the kid's shoes instead of answering the water idea.
choices: He attacked the kid's shoes instead of answering the water idea.
He made a great point about how shoes change how water works at home.
He won the argument by being the louder person in the room today.
He is right because kids with ugly shoes can never have good ideas.
context: Attacking the person instead of the idea is a dodge. It feels like winning, but it skips the real question.

question: A kid suggests a new lunch game. Another kid says 'We shouldn't play it — YOUR DAD is weird!' What did he just do?
answer: He attacked the kid's dad instead of saying anything about the game.
choices: He attacked the kid's dad instead of saying anything about the game.
He made a great point because weird dads cannot have good game ideas.
He told the truth, and the truth always wins any argument right away.
He is the winner because his own dad is less weird than the other dad.
context: Attacking someone's family, looks, or mood instead of their idea is a way of saying 'I can't beat your idea, so I'll dodge it instead.'

question: Liz tells a joke during class. The teacher says 'You laugh too much, so your joke wasn't funny.' Why is this a strange reply?
answer: Whether the joke was funny does not depend on how often Liz laughs.
choices: Whether the joke was funny does not depend on how often Liz laughs.
The teacher is right because kids who laugh a lot never tell good jokes.
The teacher is right because Liz should not have told a joke in class.
The teacher is wrong because teachers cannot ever talk about jokes today.
context: Attacking a person's habits or mood — instead of looking at the thing they said — sidesteps the real point.

question: Mia says 'Let's save some allowance.' Her brother yells 'YOU WANT US TO HAVE NO FUN EVER!' What did he just do?
answer: Straw man — He twisted her words into something bigger and sillier than she said.
choices: Straw man — He twisted her words into something bigger and sillier than she said.
He read her mind perfectly and got the real meaning of her plan in normal use.
He told the truth — saving any money means no fun is ever allowed in normal use.
He was kind and helpful and showed her what saving really means in normal use.
context: This dodge is called a strawman. You make the other person's idea sound silly, then knock down the silly version instead of the real one.

question: A kid says 'Maybe we should have less candy at lunch.' Another kid yells 'YOU WANT TO BAN ALL CANDY FOREVER!' What is wrong?
answer: The second kid made a small idea ('less') into a giant one ('ban all').
choices: The second kid made a small idea ('less') into a giant one ('ban all').
Nothing — that is exactly what the first kid said in her clear words.
Everything — but only because no candy is the right answer in school.
Nothing — kids are not allowed to talk about candy at any meal today.
context: Twisting a small idea into a giant scary one is a way to knock down something nobody actually said. Listen to the real idea first.

question: Every time Asher wears his red socks, his team wins. He says 'My red socks make us win!' What is the problem?
answer: Two things happening together does not mean one of them caused the other.
choices: Two things happening together does not mean one of them caused the other.
He is right — socks are the strongest thing in any soccer game ever.
He should also wear a red hat to double the power of the win effect.
He is wrong because his socks are blue, not red, in the first place.
context: Just because two things happen near each other does not mean one caused the other. The wins probably came from playing well.

question: Mia ate cereal, then aced her test. She says 'Cereal makes you smart!' What is wrong with her reason?
answer: One breakfast on one day does not prove cereal made her smart.
choices: One breakfast on one day does not prove cereal made her smart.
She is right — cereal is the smartest food and makes kids get an A.
She is wrong because cereal makes kids dumb, not smart, in the morning.
She is right but only because she ate cereal with extra sugar in it.
context: Two things happening one after the other does not prove one caused the other. A test score depends on many things, not just breakfast.

question: Sam says 'This book is the best because it is the best.' Why is this NOT a real reason?
answer: He used the thing he was supposed to prove as his own reason for it.
choices: He used the thing he was supposed to prove as his own reason for it.
He is right because saying it twice makes a thing twice as true now.
He is wrong because the book is the worst, not the best, on the shelf.
He is right because all best things have to be the best to start with.
context: Saying 'X is true because X is true' goes in a circle. A real reason would step OUT of the claim and bring in something else.

question: Deep thinkers — sometimes called thinkers about thinking — ask big questions: what is real? what is fair? what is true? What kind of thing IS this kind of asking?
answer: Stepping back from a day to ask why we live the way we do.
choices: Stepping back from a day to ask why we live the way we do.
Looking up answers in a book that has been written long ago by people.
Memorizing a list of right and wrong answers as fast as you can do.
Watching what other people say and copying them so you fit in better.
context: Deep thinkers do not just want facts — they want to step back and ask why we live the way we do, and what we should care about.

question: Why do deep thinkers keep asking big questions, even when they can't always reach a final answer?
answer: The asking itself helps you live in a smarter and more thoughtful way.
choices: The asking itself helps you live in a smarter and more thoughtful way.
They are paid by the government to ask questions, even silly ones.
They want to win a prize for asking the most questions in a row.
They have nothing else to do all day and want to look very busy.
context: An answer can be useful. But thinking about a hard question can change HOW you look at the world, even when you never reach the end.

question: Mia says 'I just KNOW broccoli is the worst!' Her dad asks her WHY. What is her dad really asking for?
answer: A reason — the thinking behind her view, not just the view by itself.
choices: A reason — the thinking behind her view, not just the view by itself.
He wants her to shout louder so he can really hear her words today.
He wants her to copy what her older brother thinks about broccoli now.
He wants her to change her view right away with no time to think.
context: An opinion is what you think. A reason is WHY you think it. Without a reason, an opinion is just a feeling. WITH a reason, you have something other people can think about with you.

question: Why do deep thinkers say a good question can be more useful than a quick answer?
answer: A good question keeps you open to new ideas. A quick answer can shut you down.
choices: A good question keeps you open to new ideas. A quick answer can shut you down.
A quick answer is illegal in school and only adults can give them out.
A quick answer is always wrong, no matter what the topic is about.
A good question is shorter than an answer and saves a lot of time.
context: Quick answers can settle you into one view too soon. A good question makes you stop and look — and sometimes find a better view.

question: Why do we call helping a hurt friend 'the right thing to do'?
answer: Because it cares for someone in need without harming anyone else.
choices: Because it cares for someone in need without harming anyone else.
Because helping a friend gets you a prize at the end of every day.
Because the adult in the room said helping was fine in this one case.
Because it happened to make you feel happy this week for any reason.
context: Calling something 'right' usually means it took care of people and treated them with respect. It is more than 'I got praised for it' or 'I felt good after.'

question: Why do we call stealing 'wrong,' even when nobody catches the thief?
answer: Because it hurts the person who lost the thing, whether they find out or not.
choices: Because it hurts the person who lost the thing, whether they find out or not.
Because the police always show up at last and arrest every thief alive.
Because the thief feels guilty later and his face will turn red on him.
Because grown-ups have decided that taking things makes their day grumpy.
context: Calling something 'wrong' usually means it hurt or cheated a real person without good cause. The harm is real even if no one is watching.

question: What is a value?
answer: Something you care about deeply, like kindness, honesty, or fairness.
choices: Something you care about deeply, like kindness, honesty, or fairness.
A number printed on a shirt tag that tells you how much it costs you.
A grade you get in school based on the answers you wrote down right.
A toy you keep in your closet because it is too special to play with now.
context: A value is what you treat as important. Different people have different values. Naming yours helps you live in a way that fits what you care about.

question: A school rule says 'Do not run inside.' Why is honesty NOT a rule in the same way?
answer: A rule tells you WHAT to do. Honesty is WHY you would do right with no one watching.
choices: A rule tells you WHAT to do. Honesty is WHY you would do right with no one watching.
Honesty is loud and rules are quiet, that is the only big difference for kids.
Honesty is for adults. Rules are for kids. Kids cannot really be honest yet.
Honesty and rules are the exact same thing said in two different voices today.
context: Rules can change, get bent, or run out. A deep value like honesty is INSIDE you — it can guide you even when no rule fits the moment you are in.

question: What is conscience?
answer: The quiet inside voice that says 'This feels right' or 'this feels wrong.'
choices: The quiet inside voice that says 'This feels right' or 'this feels wrong.'
A small tool used by doctors to listen to your heart in their office.
A list of rules taped to the wall of your school that everyone follows.
A test you take in fifth grade to see if you can grow up to be a kid.
context: Your conscience is that little voice you hear when nobody else is watching. People disagree about WHERE it comes from, but most agree it matters to listen.

question: Dad gives a small slice of pizza to the tiny baby and a bigger slice to the big sister. Is this 'fair'?
answer: Yes — sizes that fit each kid's appetite is one way of being fair.
choices: Yes — sizes that fit each kid's appetite is one way of being fair.
No — fair always means giving everyone the same size, no matter who.
No — the baby should get more so the big sister learns a lesson now.
Yes — but only if the big sister has had no lunch all the day so far.
context: Being fair is not always 'same for everyone.' Sometimes it means giving each person what fits what they need. Each case asks for thought.

question: Can two people disagree about what is right and both be a LITTLE right?
answer: Yes — many cases have more than one side, and both can hold some truth.
choices: Yes — many cases have more than one side, and both can hold some truth.
No — only one person can ever be right about any thing at any time.
Yes — but only on Tuesdays, because that is the day for being unsure.
No — once two kids disagree, they have to fight until one of them gives in.
context: Lots of real cases are not 'one right answer.' Two people can each see part of the truth. Talking is how we put the parts together.

question: What is a reason?
answer: Something that helps explain WHY you think the thing you said is true.
choices: Something that helps explain WHY you think the thing you said is true.
A loud noise you make when you want a person to stop talking to you.
A list of facts you write down to save for school the next day.
A way of making people scared of you so they will let you win an argument.
context: A reason is the work behind a claim. 'I think X' is just a thought. 'I think X because Y' is a real reason. The Y is what we can talk about.

question: Maya says she saw a bear behind the school. Her brother asks 'How do you know it was a bear?' What KIND of answer would help him believe her?
answer: Something she SAW or HEARD that points to a bear, like big paw prints by the door.
choices: Something she SAW or HEARD that points to a bear, like big paw prints by the door.
She just feels strongly that it was a real bear and not a big dog with brown fur.
Lots of kids said they saw one in the same place last spring on the playground.
Bears live in forests near schools, so it could have been a real bear out today.
context: Evidence is something you can SHOW. Footprints, a recording, a broken trash can � these are reasons OTHER people can check. Feelings, rumors, and what's possible are not the same.

question: Two things happen together. Does that mean one CAUSED the other?
answer: Not always — they could both be caused by a third thing, or just happen at once.
choices: Not always — they could both be caused by a third thing, or just happen at once.
Yes — anything that happens at the same time as another thing causes it.
Yes — but only if both things happen on the same day of the week.
No — and nothing ever causes anything else, that idea is made up.
context: Confusing 'happens with' and 'caused by' is one of the most common thinking mistakes. Roosters crow before sunrise — but they do not make the sun rise.

question: What is the difference between a FACT and an OPINION?
answer: A fact can be checked. An opinion is what someone thinks or feels about it.
choices: A fact can be checked. An opinion is what someone thinks or feels about it.
A fact is loud and an opinion is quiet. That is the only big difference.
A fact is on TV and an opinion is in a book. The TV is more correct.
A fact is for grown-ups and opinions are for kids who are still little.
context: 'Water freezes at 32 F' is a fact — you can check it. 'Winter is the best season' is an opinion — different people will feel differently. Both can be true, in different ways.

question: The moon is up there even when clouds cover it. We say the moon is REAL. What does that tell us about real things?
answer: Real things are there whether anyone is looking at them or not.
choices: Real things are there whether anyone is looking at them or not.
Only things kids can see are real, and grown-ups see different things.
Real things must cost money in a store and have a price tag on them now.
A thing is only real when every person in the world agrees it is there.
context: Calling a thing 'real' means it is there whether or not we see it. The moon is real even when clouds hide it. A dream you had last night is real in a much too — but a different way.

question: Can something be real even if you cannot see it?
answer: Yes — wind, love, and numbers are all real but cannot be seen with eyes.
choices: Yes — wind, love, and numbers are all real but cannot be seen with eyes.
No — only things you can see right now can really be called real ever.
Yes — but only ghosts, and nothing else at all, in any other way.
No — once a thing is hidden, it stops being real in every way at once.
context: Lots of real things cannot be seen. Wind moves leaves. A friend's love changes how she acts. Five plus five is ten even when no kid is doing math. 'Real' is bigger than 'can be seen.'

question: What is an IDEA?
answer: A thought inside your head that can be shared with other people.
choices: A thought inside your head that can be shared with other people.
A small bug that lives in your hair and gives you good thoughts at night.
A toy you can hold in your hand and play with on the floor by yourself.
A test you take in third grade to find out if you have any thoughts at all.
context: An idea is something you can think — and something you can pass to another person by talking, writing, or drawing. Ideas are not things you can touch, but they can still move the world.

question: Where do ideas LIVE?
answer: In minds — yours, mine, and the minds of people who share them with others.
choices: In minds — yours, mine, and the minds of people who share them with others.
In a special box at school that holds all the ideas safely each night.
In the sky, where they wait to be picked up by smart people on holidays.
In your shoes, which is why people get good ideas when they go for walks.
context: An idea has no body — but it lives wherever minds are thinking it. Once an idea is shared, it can keep living even after the person who first had it is gone.

question: What does it mean to KNOW something?
answer: To believe it AND have good reasons AND have it really be true.
choices: To believe it AND have good reasons AND have it really be true.
To feel very sure about it, even if no real reasons back it up at all.
To shout it loudly so the other kids in the room stop talking back.
To learn it once in school and then forget it for the rest of your life.
context: Knowing is more than just guessing right. Most thinkers say you need to believe it, have good reasons, AND have it really be true. All three parts matter.

question: What is the difference between BELIEVING and KNOWING?
answer: You can believe a thing without checking it. To know, you also need real reasons.
choices: You can believe a thing without checking it. To know, you also need real reasons.
Believing is in the morning and knowing is in the afternoon, each day.
Believing is for kids and knowing is for adults who have stopped guessing.
Believing is louder than knowing — that is the only difference between them.
context: We believe lots of things without proof. Some of those turn out true; some don't. To know, you need to back up your belief with reasons that hold up.

question: How can you tell if something is true?
answer: By checking the reasons, looking at evidence, and listening to people who disagree.
choices: By checking the reasons, looking at evidence, and listening to people who disagree.
By asking how it makes you feel and going with the warmest answer right away.
By picking the answer that the most popular kid in your class believes.
By saying the answer out loud three times until it starts to sound right.
context: Truth-checking takes work. You look at evidence, ask if the reasons fit together, and try hard to listen to people who see it the other way. That is how you weed out mistakes.

question: Two smart kids see the same thing happen. Later, they remember it in different ways. Why might that be?
answer: Each kid noticed different parts, and memory fills in the rest from what they expected.
choices: Each kid noticed different parts, and memory fills in the rest from what they expected.
One of the kids is lying on purpose and the other kid is telling the truth.
The thing did not really happen and both kids are just making it up now.
Smart kids always remember things exactly the same way as each other.
context: We do not record events like cameras. We notice what stands out to US, and our minds fill in gaps later. Two honest people can remember the same thing very differently.

question: What is beauty?
answer: A kind of feeling, when something pleases you in how it looks, sounds, or feels.
choices: A kind of feeling, when something pleases you in how it looks, sounds, or feels.
A score given by a judge to decide which thing wins a contest today.
A test you take in school to find out if you are pretty or not at all.
A rule that says only one kind of face or shape can ever be called pretty.
context: Beauty is one of those words that is hard to pin down. People for thousands of years have asked: is it in the thing, or in how I feel? Both, probably.

question: Is something beautiful just because MOST people say it is?
answer: Not always — crowds can miss beauty, and small details can be lovely too.
choices: Not always — crowds can miss beauty, and small details can be lovely too.
Yes — once enough kids say a thing is pretty, the thing is pretty for real.
Yes — a vote by the whole class is the right way to decide every time.
No — beauty does not exist at all, it is only a word adults made up.
context: Crowds can be right about beauty. They can also miss it. A song many people skipped once becomes a favorite ten years later. Tastes shift, even on what looks lovely.

question: Can a thing be ugly AND still be valuable?
answer: Yes — a beat-up old book can hold a story that changes your life forever.
choices: Yes — a beat-up old book can hold a story that changes your life forever.
No — once a thing is ugly, it has no use to any person ever again.
Yes — but only if it used to be pretty before it got broken or torn.
No — only pretty things can be useful, that is the rule of life today.
context: Pretty and valuable are not the same. A scarred-up pan in a kitchen cooks great food. An old book full of notes can teach you more than a fresh, untouched one.

question: What is fairness?
answer: Treating people in a way that fits what they did and what they need.
choices: Treating people in a way that fits what they did and what they need.
Letting the biggest kid get the most of everything, every single time.
Picking a winner before the game starts to save everyone some time today.
Giving the kid who whines the loudest whatever he asks his mom for that day.
context: Fairness is one of the oldest big ideas. It is not just 'same for everyone' — it is treating people in a way that fits what is going on.

question: What is a RULE?
answer: A clear statement of what people in a group are supposed to do or not do.
choices: A clear statement of what people in a group are supposed to do or not do.
A loud noise an adult makes when a kid is doing the wrong thing at all.
A toy passed around in class to remind kids to stop talking right away.
A test you take at the end of fifth grade to see if you have grown up.
