question: Survivorship bias: 'Successful CEOs all wake up at 5am, so waking early causes success.' What dataset is missing from the inference?
answer: Base rate neglect — all the people who woke at 5am and did NOT become successful CEOs -- the failures.
choices: Base rate neglect — all the people who woke at 5am and did NOT become successful CEOs -- the failures.
Data on what time the CEOs went to bed; you need both ends of the day to compare in normal use.
Data on whether the CEOs work harder than others; the wake time is a proxy variable in normal use.
Data on CEO demographics; without controls for age and sex the claim is unfounded in normal use.
context: Sampling on the dependent variable hides the base rate. To test 'early waking causes success,' you need to look at early wakers in general -- not only those who succeeded.

question: Tu quoque often has TWO valid uses and ONE fallacious. Naming the valid uses tightens criticism. What ARE they?
answer: Tu quoque — Exposing hypocrisy as character evidence, and exposing inconsistent commitments in argument.
choices: Tu quoque — Exposing hypocrisy as character evidence, and exposing inconsistent commitments in argument.
Replying with anger, and rebuilding lost trust between the two debaters in real time.
Showing the opponent reading from a script, and quoting his unflattering past actions.
Returning the favor in kind, and ensuring no debater enjoys an unfair speaking advantage.
context: Tu quoque becomes fallacious when used to AVOID the original point. It is legitimate when (1) the inconsistency is itself the point, or (2) character is the topic.

question: The 'motte and bailey' tactic: defend an indefensible claim (bailey) by retreating to a safer one (motte). Why is naming it useful in arguments?
answer: Naming the move forces an opponent to pick one ground and stay there.
choices: Naming the move forces an opponent to pick one ground and stay there.
Naming any fallacy in a debate wins on style; the opponent cannot recover politely.
Naming it is harmful because it sounds academic and confuses listeners on each side.
Naming it lets you push the bailey claim as the correct view of the whole disagreement.
context: Coined by Nicholas Shackel. Activists, politicians, and intellectuals deploy it constantly. Insisting on which thesis is actually under debate is the cleanest counter-move.

question: Strawson's 'reactive attitudes' -- resentment, gratitude, anger -- offer a way past the free-will debate. What did he argue these attitudes show?
answer: Holding people responsible is a fact of practice; abandoning it on theoretical grounds is impossible.
choices: Holding people responsible is a fact of practice; abandoning it on theoretical grounds is impossible.
Reactive attitudes are unreliable and should be replaced with a calmer attitude toward all people.
Reactive attitudes are evidence against determinism -- they imply we already know we are free.
Reactive attitudes only matter for personal life, not for any decisions about public policy.
context: Strawson's 'Freedom and Resentment' (1962) sidesteps the metaphysics. The community of responsibility-attributors is the very fabric of human life; theory can't really dissolve it.

question: Bayesian epistemology models belief as degrees of credence updated by evidence. What is the role of priors in this framework?
answer: They encode the agent's belief state before new evidence arrives -- the starting point for updating.
choices: They encode the agent's belief state before new evidence arrives -- the starting point for updating.
They constrain what evidence the agent is allowed to gather during the testing phase.
They give the agent's beliefs about which experiments to fund and which to reject going forward.
They specify the conclusion the agent intends to reach before any evidence has been examined.
context: Bayes's theorem updates priors with new evidence via likelihoods. Priors matter -- two agents with different priors confronted by the same evidence may end up with different posteriors. Disciplined disagreement is possible.

question: Closure principles in epistemology say: if you know P, and know P entails Q, then you know Q. Why is this contested by some epistemologists?
answer: Applied, closure seems to give you knowledge that 'I am not a brain in a vat' -- which feels wrong.
choices: Applied, closure seems to give you knowledge that 'I am not a brain in a vat' -- which feels wrong.
Closure makes knowledge gain too easy; you could derive all of math from any single fact.
Closure ignores the social character of knowledge and treats it as a private inference activity.
Closure conflicts with Bayesian updating because credences are not closed under deduction.
context: From 'I have hands' and 'having hands entails not being a handless brain in a vat,' closure gives 'I know I am not a handless brain in a vat.' Some reject closure to block this; others accept it and accept the consequence.

question: The free will defense (Plantinga) addresses the logical problem of evil. What is the structural claim?
answer: It is possible that any world with morally significant freedom contains some moral evil too.
choices: It is possible that any world with morally significant freedom contains some moral evil too.
Free will is more valuable than the absence of any evil and so God prefers the trade-off here.
Most evil comes from human choices and so God can be excused for not stopping each one of them.
God could prevent some evils but not all; the doctrine of omnipotence has to be qualified.
context: Plantinga's response targets the LOGICAL problem (Mackie). It needn't be plausible -- just possible. If even one possible world with free creatures necessarily contains evil, the contradiction dissolves.

question: Rowe and Draper's 'evidential' problem of evil grants that God and evil are logically possible. They ask: does the AMOUNT of seemingly pointless evil make theism unlikely?
answer: Rowe argued some evils seem pointless even after every theistic explanation has been considered.
choices: Rowe argued some evils seem pointless even after every theistic explanation has been considered.
Rowe argued there is no evil at all in the world; what people call evil is just inconvenience.
Rowe argued every evil has a known good purpose; the perplexity is only in our limited view.
Rowe argued God is responsible for every evil directly; the doctrine of providence ensures it.
context: Rowe's 'fawn in the forest fire' -- a slow agonizing death no one sees. Theists reply with skeptical theism (we can't track God's reasons). The debate is now over WHETHER we can read 'no apparent point' as evidence.

question: Maya says, 'All my friends have phones, so I should get one too.' What is wrong with that as the WHOLE reason?
choices: Bandwagon — What other people have doesn't show what is best for HER.
The friends have probably stolen their phones from each other.
Maya is simply not old enough to ever own such a device.
Phones are evil objects that destroy the souls of all kids.
answer: Bandwagon — What other people have doesn't show what is best for HER.
context: This is the bandwagon move — assuming popularity proves a thing is right. The truth depends on Maya's situation, not the crowd's. Also called 'appeal to popularity.'

question: A boy says, 'Everyone is making fun of the new kid, so it must be okay.' Where is his thinking off?
choices: Bandwagon — Crowds can be wrong — being cruel is cruel even when many do it.
The new kid actually deserves the teasing because of his shoes.
Group rules always work better than individual decisions and morals.
Making fun is fine as long as the teacher isn't in the room watching.
answer: Bandwagon — Crowds can be wrong — being cruel is cruel even when many do it.
context: Bandwagon fallacy. 'Many people do X' is not evidence X is right. The size of the crowd doesn't change the action.

question: Sara hears, 'This song sold a million copies, so it must be good.' What is sneaky about that claim?
choices: Sales count how many bought it, not whether it is actually good.
A million is actually a small number for popular music sales.
Songs never sell — most streaming today is free for everyone.
Sara should not listen to popular music made by any artist.
answer: Sales count how many bought it, not whether it is actually good.
context: Popularity is not quality. Many things sell well because of marketing or trends, not because they are excellent.

question: A kid says, 'Lots of kids cheat on this teacher's tests, so cheating is fine.' What is wrong with the reasoning?
choices: Bandwagon — What others do does not change whether YOUR action is right.
The teacher made the tests too hard, so cheating is justified.
Cheating is fine because the kid won't get caught this time.
Most kids actually do not cheat — the kid is exaggerating numbers.
answer: Bandwagon — What others do does not change whether YOUR action is right.
context: Bandwagon defense. Ethics is about your own act, not the crowd's. The number of people doing wrong does not make it right.

question: Aiden argues, 'My YouTuber has 5 million followers, so he must be telling the truth.' Where is the flaw?
choices: Followers measure popularity, not whether the words are true.
Five million followers is too small to count as proof of trust.
YouTubers are paid for views, so they always say false things.
Aiden should follow only YouTubers with ten million or more.
answer: Followers measure popularity, not whether the words are true.
context: Popularity does not equal truth. A creator can be widely followed AND wrong about the facts at the same time.

question: 'Everyone is wearing baggy jeans this year, so they must be the best style.' What is wrong with that as a reason?
choices: Bandwagon — Trends change — what is popular today is not always best.
Baggy jeans are objectively the worst clothing item invented.
Style is decided by famous fashion designers in big cities only.
The speaker should wear baggy jeans every day until next year.
answer: Bandwagon — Trends change — what is popular today is not always best.
context: Bandwagon plus a side helping of trend-following. What is fashionable now will look silly later — that fact alone shows popularity is not quality.

question: 'My whole class is going to the dance, so my parents should let me go.' What is the WEAKEST part of that argument?
choices: Bandwagon — the class going does not show the dance is right for ME.
The kid's class is actually too small to count as a real group.
Parents should let kids go wherever the school says is allowed.
Dances are universally good for every kid in every grade level.
answer: Bandwagon — the class going does not show the dance is right for ME.
context: Bandwagon again. The crowd's plans do not change YOUR family's reasons. The argument should focus on the dance itself, not on who else is going.

question: Pia says, 'Half the school plays this game, so it must be safe.' What is she missing?
choices: Bandwagon — Lots of people doing a thing does not prove the thing is safe.
Pia is mistaken — only a third of the school actually plays it.
The game has been tested by professional safety inspectors yearly.
Pia is too young and small to know what counts as safe for kids.
answer: Bandwagon — Lots of people doing a thing does not prove the thing is safe.
context: Bandwagon meets safety claims. Many people can do something risky without realizing it. Popularity gives no real evidence about danger.

question: A girl says, 'It must be a real story — millions of people are sharing it!' What does that miss?
choices: Stories can spread because they're exciting, not because they're true.
Millions of people would never share a story if it was untrue.
Sharing means each person has verified all facts independently.
Only stories with proof get shared more than a million total times.
answer: Stories can spread because they're exciting, not because they're true.
context: False stories often spread FASTER than true ones because they're shocking. Popularity online is not evidence at all.

question: 'Nobody on the team thinks it's a foul, so it isn't one.' What is the trouble with that?
choices: Bandwagon — the team agreeing does not change what actually happened on the play.
The referee should let the team decide all fouls by majority vote in every case that comes up.
Teams know the rules better than the people in striped uniforms in every case that comes up.
Fouls are made up by referees to slow down good winning teams in every case that comes up.
answer: Bandwagon — the team agreeing does not change what actually happened on the play.
context: Bandwagon over evidence. Group agreement is comforting but it doesn't replace looking at what actually happened.

question: Dad tells Lily not to leave dishes in the sink. Lily replies, 'YOU left dishes there yesterday!' What is wrong with her reply?
choices: Tu quoque — Even if Dad did it, that doesn't make HER dishes okay to leave.
Dad is a complete hypocrite, so nothing he says counts as fair.
Lily is allowed to break the rule whenever she sees Dad break it.
Yesterday's dishes are way worse than today's dishes ever could be.
answer: Tu quoque — Even if Dad did it, that doesn't make HER dishes okay to leave.
context: This is 'tu quoque' — the 'you too' move. It changes the subject. The original question (should Lily leave dishes?) doesn't depend on what Dad did.

question: Marco breaks a vase and says, 'My brother broke one last week!' Why is this NOT a defense?
choices: What his brother did doesn't change that Marco broke the vase NOW.
His brother should be punished first before anyone looks at Marco.
Two broken vases proves the family has cheap and breakable items.
Marco's brother is the one truly responsible for both of the vases.
answer: What his brother did doesn't change that Marco broke the vase NOW.
context: 'You-too' defense. Pointing at someone else's mistake doesn't undo yours. The question is still: what should Marco do about THIS vase?

question: When told not to interrupt, Beth says, 'But Sam interrupts all the time!' What is the flaw?
choices: Tu quoque — Sam's behavior doesn't decide whether BETH should interrupt.
Sam's interrupting is much worse than Beth's interrupting today.
Adults should always punish Sam first before they punish Beth.
Interrupting is fine if there is at least one other person doing it.
answer: Tu quoque — Sam's behavior doesn't decide whether BETH should interrupt.
context: Tu quoque. The right question is about Beth's own action. Sam can be wrong AND Beth can also be wrong — two separate issues.

question: A coach tells Theo to stop showing off. Theo replies, 'But COACH yells all game!' Why isn't that an answer?
choices: Tu quoque — pointing at the coach doesn't address whether THEO is showing off.
The coach should stop yelling first before correcting any player.
Showing off is allowed for any player whose coach also makes noise.
Coaches are supposed to set the example, so Theo wins this argument.
answer: Tu quoque — pointing at the coach doesn't address whether THEO is showing off.
context: Tu quoque dodges the question by accusing the accuser. It's a popular move because it FEELS like a defense — but it doesn't actually answer.

question: When caught lying, Reggie says, 'Adults lie too!' How is that NOT a good defense?
choices: Tu quoque — Whether others lie has nothing to do with whether HE lied.
Adults lying is much worse, so kid lies should be ignored entirely.
Kids are always allowed to copy the bad habits they see in adults.
Reggie is too young to understand the harm that his lying causes.
answer: Tu quoque — Whether others lie has nothing to do with whether HE lied.
context: Tu quoque. The question on the table is Reggie's lie, right now. Other people's lies are separate questions, even if also worth examining.

question: Jamie says we should eat less candy because sugar hurts teeth. Mike replies, 'Jamie is bad at math!' What's wrong with Mike's reply?
choices: Ad hominem — Mike attacks Jamie, not the argument about sugar and teeth.
Jamie being bad at math means her claim about sugar must be wrong.
Only kids who are great at math are allowed to talk about teeth.
Mike should have attacked Jamie's reading score instead of math.
answer: Ad hominem — Mike attacks Jamie, not the argument about sugar and teeth.
context: This is 'ad hominem' — Latin for 'to the person.' Attacking the person doesn't disprove their argument.

question: Mia argues recess should be longer. Tom replies, 'You can't trust Mia — she wears weird socks.' What's wrong?
choices: Ad hominem — Tom attacks Mia's clothes, not her actual argument.
Mia's weird socks prove her recess ideas are silly in normal use.
Only normal-clothed kids should propose new rules in normal use.
Tom should have insulted her hair instead of socks in normal use.
answer: Ad hominem — Tom attacks Mia's clothes, not her actual argument.
context: Ad hominem. Mia's socks have nothing to do with whether recess should be longer. Tom dodged the real question.

question: A kid says, 'My teacher's homework idea is dumb because she's old.' What is the flaw?
choices: Ad hominem — How old the teacher is doesn't tell us if the idea is good or bad.
Old teachers can never have good or useful ideas about homework in normal use.
Young teachers always have the better ideas because of newness in normal use.
The kid should attack the teacher's clothes too for completeness in normal use.
answer: Ad hominem — How old the teacher is doesn't tell us if the idea is good or bad.
context: Ad hominem aimed at age. The idea has to be checked on its OWN merits. Age is irrelevant to whether the homework plan works.

question: Sam says his game plan is fair. Lucas yells, 'You always wear that ugly hat — your plan is dumb!' What is wrong?
choices: Ad hominem — Lucas talked about Sam's hat, not whether the game plan is fair.
Sam's hat is so distractingly ugly that it makes everything else bad.
Plans made by hat wearers are typically less fair than other plans.
Lucas should have insulted Sam's shoes, which are even uglier.
answer: Ad hominem — Lucas talked about Sam's hat, not whether the game plan is fair.
context: Ad hominem. Lucas needed to attack the PLAN — show what's unfair about it. Attacking the hat dodges the real argument.

question: Lily says screens late at night make sleep worse. Her brother says, 'You don't even have a phone, so you can't talk!' What is the flaw?
choices: Ad hominem — Whether Lily has a phone doesn't change if her CLAIM is true.
People without phones cannot have opinions about phones, ever.
Lily should buy a phone first and then form an opinion about them.
Her brother is right because he is older and uses more screens.
answer: Ad hominem — Whether Lily has a phone doesn't change if her CLAIM is true.
context: Ad hominem in disguise — attacking Lily's standing rather than her argument. Even people without phones can be right about phones.

question: Ben proposes a kinder cafeteria rule. A classmate replies, 'But you got a C in Math!' Why is this a poor response?
choices: Ad hominem — his math grade has nothing to do with whether the rule would be kinder.
Only students with A grades are allowed to propose any new rules in every case that comes up.
Math grades are the official measure of who deserves to be heard in every case that comes up.
Ben should have proposed a math rule instead of a cafeteria one in every case that comes up.
answer: Ad hominem — his math grade has nothing to do with whether the rule would be kinder.
context: Ad hominem aimed at school performance. The classmate didn't address the rule itself. Math grades don't change whether a rule is fair.

question: Sophie says we should walk more for our health. A boy laughs, 'You're not even fast!' What is wrong with his response?
choices: Ad hominem — his joke is about Sophie, not about whether walking is healthy.
Slow people give bad health advice that should never be trusted.
Only fast runners are allowed to speak about exercise of any kind.
Walking is only healthy for people who can also run very fast.
answer: Ad hominem — his joke is about Sophie, not about whether walking is healthy.
context: Ad hominem. The health claim is separate from how fast Sophie can move. Walking can be good for everyone regardless of any single person's speed.

question: Ravi argues the science fair should be longer. Another kid sneers, 'You smell like fish.' Why doesn't this answer Ravi?
choices: Ad hominem — How Ravi smells has nothing to do with the fair's length.
Smelly kids are not allowed to suggest changes to school events.
The science fair should be shorter to keep smelly kids away faster.
Ravi should bathe before being allowed to propose any school changes.
answer: Ad hominem — How Ravi smells has nothing to do with the fair's length.
context: Crude ad hominem. The mockery dodges the actual proposal. To beat Ravi's argument, the kid would need to say WHY the fair is fine at its current length.

question: A kid says, 'Either you love my idea or you hate me.' Why is this UNFAIR?
choices: False dilemma — most people can disagree with an idea AND still like the person.
Loving the idea is the only way to show you care about a friend in normal use.
Hating someone is the natural result of disliking their ideas in normal use.
Ideas and people are exactly the same thing, so you must agree in normal use.
answer: False dilemma — most people can disagree with an idea AND still like the person.
context: False dilemma — pretending only two choices exist when there are more. Real life has lots of in-between options.

question: Mom says, 'Eat your spinach or you don't love me.' What kind of trap is in this question?
choices: False dilemma — It pretends only two choices exist — eat or not love mom.
Spinach is the only proper food for kids to eat at dinner time.
Loving mom always requires eating exactly what she serves you.
Refusing spinach is the same thing as openly hating your parents.
answer: False dilemma — It pretends only two choices exist — eat or not love mom.
context: False dilemma. The kid can love mom AND not love spinach. The question forces a false either-or.

question: Dad says, 'You're either the best in class or you're a loser.' What's the trick in that?
choices: False dilemma — most kids are neither the best NOR losers — there is a wide middle.
Being second-best counts as losing in any classroom comparison in every case that comes up.
Class rankings are the only way to measure a kid's true value in every case that comes up.
Losers are kids who do not try hard enough to be the very best in every case that comes up.
answer: False dilemma — most kids are neither the best NOR losers — there is a wide middle.
context: False dilemma plus a side of harsh judgment. Most of life has more than two boxes. Pretending otherwise is a trap.

question: A kid says, 'You either play my game or you're not my friend.' What's wrong with the choice?
choices: False dilemma — Friends often want different games and stay friends.
Refusing one game always ends a real friendship in every case that comes up.
Friendship requires matching every single activity in every case that comes up.
Game-pickers always decide who counts as friends in every case that comes up.
answer: False dilemma — Friends often want different games and stay friends.
context: False dilemma. The two choices given aren't the only options. A real friend can decline a game AND still be a friend.

question: A speaker says, 'You're either with us or you're against us.' Why might this be unfair?
choices: Many people are in between — agreeing on some things, not others.
Everyone must pick a complete side because no middle ground exists.
Disagreement on any single issue means total opposition forever.
Speakers always know which side is right, so listeners should obey.
answer: Many people are in between — agreeing on some things, not others.
context: Forced binary. Most real disagreements have lots of degrees. Pretending there are only two sides is a way to bully people into choosing.

question: Coach yells, 'Either you win this game or you're worthless!' What is the false choice?
choices: False dilemma — Worth isn't decided by winning ONE game.
Losers never have any worth in life in every case that comes up.
Winning is the only measure of value in every case that comes up.
Coaches always know who is worthless in every case that comes up.
answer: False dilemma — Worth isn't decided by winning ONE game.
context: False dilemma about identity. There are many ways to be valuable that don't depend on the score of a single game.

question: Mom says, 'If we let the dog on the couch, soon he'll sleep in our beds, then eat off our plates, then run the house!' What is wrong?
choices: Slippery slope — each big step needs its OWN reason — not just 'one led to the other.'
Dogs always take over houses once you let them on the couch in every case that comes up.
The couch is a sacred space that no animal should ever touch in every case that comes up.
Letting a dog up is the first step in a totally unstoppable chain in every case that comes up.
answer: Slippery slope — each big step needs its OWN reason — not just 'one led to the other.'
context: Slippery slope. The first step (couch) doesn't FORCE the last step (house). Without showing the connection, it's just scary guessing.

question: Dad says, 'If I let you stay up late tonight, soon you'll be up till dawn every night!' What is the flaw?
choices: Slippery slope — One late night doesn't make every night late — each night is its own choice.
Late nights snowball into total all-night habits without exception in every case that comes up.
Kids who stay up once will lose the ability to sleep early forever in every case that comes up.
Sleep schedules are like dominoes — push one and they all fall in every case that comes up.
answer: Slippery slope — One late night doesn't make every night late — each night is its own choice.
context: Slippery slope. The argument skips from tonight to 'every night' without showing why one must lead to the other.

question: A coach says, 'If we let players take breaks, soon nobody will train at all!' What's missing?
choices: Slippery slope — He skipped showing why one break makes everyone stop training.
Allowing any break is the first step toward total team laziness.
Players who rest once will permanently lose all desire to practice.
Breaks during practice always lead to teams quitting their sport.
answer: Slippery slope — He skipped showing why one break makes everyone stop training.
context: Slippery slope. Reasonable breaks and no-training are NOT the same thing. The middle ground exists.

question: A teacher warns: 'If I let one kid skip homework, soon NOBODY will turn it in!' What is wrong with this?
choices: Slippery slope — One kid's situation doesn't force everyone else's behavior to change.
Kids always copy any rule break they see another student get away with.
Allowing one exception to homework rules destroys the whole class system.
Teachers should never adjust homework rules for any individual student.
answer: Slippery slope — One kid's situation doesn't force everyone else's behavior to change.
context: Slippery slope. A single exception doesn't trigger a flood — unless someone shows EVIDENCE for that link, the prediction is just fear.

question: An older kid says, 'If you say no to this small thing, you'll be saying no to everything fun!' What is wrong?
choices: Slippery slope — One 'no' doesn't decide every future 'no' — each choice stands alone.
Saying no even once permanently makes a kid into a no-fun person in every case that comes up.
Refusing one small request leads to refusing every fun thing in life in every case that comes up.
Older kids always know the consequences of small refusals best in every case that comes up.
answer: Slippery slope — One 'no' doesn't decide every future 'no' — each choice stands alone.
context: Slippery slope used to pressure someone. The 'one no leads to all nos' chain isn't supported. It's a guilt trick.

question: A speaker says, 'If kids get phones in 6th grade, soon they'll get phones in kindergarten!' What's the gap?
choices: Slippery slope — 6th-grade decisions don't automatically apply to kindergartners.
Phone-giving spreads down through the grades like a contagious cold.
Once any kid gets a phone, every younger kid will demand one too.
Parents have no ability to stop the slide once 6th graders have phones.
answer: Slippery slope — 6th-grade decisions don't automatically apply to kindergartners.
context: Slippery slope without the slope. The argument assumes one rule will keep sliding to younger ages — but each age can be its own decision.

question: 'If we shorten one test by 10 minutes, soon kids will have NO TESTS at all!' How is this off?
choices: Slippery slope — each rule change is its own decision — they don't keep happening on their own.
Shortening any test once will lead to all tests disappearing this year in every case that comes up.
Time-related rule changes are impossible to control once they start in every case that comes up.
Teachers always cave to test pressure and remove more time every year in every case that comes up.
answer: Slippery slope — each rule change is its own decision — they don't keep happening on their own.
context: Slippery slope. Without a real mechanism linking 'shorter test' to 'no tests,' the argument is just scary speculation.

question: Mom warns: 'If you skip one piano practice, soon you'll quit piano entirely.' Why is this NOT a sure thing?
choices: Slippery slope — Skipping once doesn't mean quitting — most kids skip and come back.
All quitters in the world started with skipping just one practice in normal use.
Piano teachers consider one skipped practice a clear sign of giving up in normal use.
Practice habits are so fragile that one miss destroys all future work in normal use.
answer: Slippery slope — Skipping once doesn't mean quitting — most kids skip and come back.
context: Slippery slope plus a false certainty. The 'one skip → quit' line is a fear, not a proven path. Real practice has bad days mixed with good ones.

question: Tim says, 'My grandpa smoked for 50 years and lived to 90. So smoking can't be bad.' What's the trouble?
choices: Hasty generalization — One person doesn't show what's true for everyone.
Grandfathers prove the truth about cigarettes in every case that comes up.
Smoking is fine because Tim's grandpa lived long in every case that comes up.
His grandpa must have used the safer tobacco in every case that comes up.
answer: Hasty generalization — One person doesn't show what's true for everyone.
context: Hasty generalization — drawing a big rule from one case. Grandpa's life is one data point. Studies of millions of smokers show different overall odds.

question: After one bad pizza, Kim says, 'I'm never eating pizza again — it's all gross!' Where is her reasoning off?
choices: Hasty generalization — One bad pizza doesn't tell her about every pizza.
Pizza is gross — Kim has finally seen the truth in every case that comes up.
All pizzas come from one giant factory in town in every case that comes up.
Bad first tries should always be trusted forever in every case that comes up.
answer: Hasty generalization — One bad pizza doesn't tell her about every pizza.
context: Hasty generalization. One sample isn't enough to judge a whole category. Other pizzas might be wonderful — Kim's experience can't predict that.

question: A boy says, 'I met two rude tourists, so tourists are all rude.' Why isn't this fair?
choices: Hasty generalization — Two people can't speak for millions of others.
Two rude tourists prove a clear group pattern in every case that comes up.
Tourists are nearly all rude across the world in every case that comes up.
Polite tourists are too rare to ever count here in every case that comes up.
answer: Hasty generalization — Two people can't speak for millions of others.
context: Hasty generalization across a huge group. Even ten bad experiences don't tell you about the millions you haven't met.

question: A girl says, 'My uncle is bald. My dad is bald. So all men go bald.' What is the trouble?
choices: Hasty generalization — Two relatives isn't enough to say something about ALL men.
Family baldness is the perfect test of what happens to every man.
All men go bald eventually — her family is just catching it earlier.
Her dad and uncle are the average examples for the entire male population.
answer: Hasty generalization — Two relatives isn't enough to say something about ALL men.
context: Hasty generalization from family. Genes vary widely. Looking at two cases (especially related ones) won't tell you about everyone.

question: After one bad game, a coach says, 'This team can't play — they're hopeless.' What's missing?
choices: Hasty generalization — One game isn't enough to judge a whole season's potential.
Bad games always perfectly predict the rest of a sports season in normal use.
Hopeless teams give themselves away in their very first weak game in normal use.
Coaches are paid to make quick judgments after one performance only in normal use.
answer: Hasty generalization — One game isn't enough to judge a whole season's potential.
context: Hasty generalization in sports. One performance — good or bad — doesn't tell you what the team can do across many games.

question: 'I tried one science book and it was boring, so science books are all boring.' What's the flaw?
choices: Hasty generalization — Trying one book can't tell you about every book on a subject.
Science books are nearly all boring — one is plenty to prove this in normal use.
Books on the same topic always share the same level of fun or boring in normal use.
Boring first samples always represent the entire category accurately in normal use.
answer: Hasty generalization — Trying one book can't tell you about every book on a subject.
context: Hasty generalization. Books vary hugely. To judge a whole topic, you'd need to read several, especially the well-loved ones.

question: 'My one friend who plays violin practices a lot, so all violin players must be obsessed.' What is the gap?
choices: Hasty generalization — One friend doesn't speak for everyone who picks up the instrument.
Violin players are obsessive — the friend is showing the typical case in normal use.
Practicing a lot is the defining trait of every single violin student in normal use.
His one friend is the standard example of all string instrument players in normal use.
answer: Hasty generalization — One friend doesn't speak for everyone who picks up the instrument.
context: Hasty generalization from one person. Music students vary — some practice hours, some just enough. One friend's habits don't define the group.

question: 'It snowed twice this week, so winter must be the snowiest ever!' What's the trouble?
choices: Hasty generalization — Two snowfalls in a week can't show what a whole season will do.
Weather patterns within one week predict the entire winter ahead in every case that comes up.
The earliest snow each year always tells us the season's total amount in every case that comes up.
Snowy weeks always continue snowing through the rest of the season in every case that comes up.
answer: Hasty generalization — Two snowfalls in a week can't show what a whole season will do.
context: Hasty generalization in weather. Short patterns don't predict seasons. Real climate data looks at many months across many years.

question: 'You HAVE to give me a phone — if you don't, I'll cry for a week!' Why isn't this a real reason?
choices: Appeal to emotion — Tears are a feeling — they don't show the phone is the right choice.
Crying for a long time is the best argument any kid can make in every case that comes up.
Parents are required to give in to any threat involving prolonged tears in every case that comes up.
Tears prove that the thing being asked for is genuinely needed now in every case that comes up.
answer: Appeal to emotion — Tears are a feeling — they don't show the phone is the right choice.
context: Appeal to emotion. Strong feelings are real, but they don't replace reasons. The phone question has to be answered by looking at facts, not tears.

question: A speaker says, 'If you don't agree with me, this poor puppy will be sad.' Why is this trick UNFAIR?
choices: Appeal to emotion — Puppy sadness doesn't make a bad argument good.
Puppies suffer harm whenever people disagree in every case that comes up.
Disagreement should cause pain to nearby pets in every case that comes up.
Speakers can use pets to win any kind of argument in every case that comes up.
answer: Appeal to emotion — Puppy sadness doesn't make a bad argument good.
context: Appeal to emotion using sympathy. The puppy is being used to push you past your real thinking. A bad argument stays bad even when wrapped in cuteness.

question: 'You should buy this game — imagine how SAD you'll be missing out!' What's the trick?
choices: It uses sadness to push you, not facts about whether the game is good.
Missing out is the worst possible feeling and must always be avoided.
Games are proven to prevent sadness in every kid who buys them.
Sales pitches that promise sadness are the most honest type of ad.
answer: It uses sadness to push you, not facts about whether the game is good.
context: Appeal to fear-of-missing-out. The pitch never tells you why the game is GOOD — only that not having it would feel bad. Two different things.

question: Mom says, 'If you don't visit Grandma, she'll be heartbroken.' How could this be misleading?
choices: Guilt is a feeling — it shouldn't be the ONLY reason to do a thing.
Grandmothers control all family decisions through their broken hearts.
Visits are required whenever any grandparent might feel disappointed.
Heartbreak is the only valid measure of when family visits should happen.
answer: Guilt is a feeling — it shouldn't be the ONLY reason to do a thing.
context: Appeal to guilt. The visit might be a good idea, but the REASON to visit should be about real connection, not pure pressure.

question: 'Vote for my idea or you'll be lonely at lunch!' What's the trick?
choices: It threatens a feeling instead of giving a reason the idea is good.
Loneliness during lunch is the strongest possible argument anywhere.
Lunch tables decide which ideas in school are valid and which are not.
Threatening other kids is the most reliable way to win a class vote.
answer: It threatens a feeling instead of giving a reason the idea is good.
context: Appeal to fear. The argument never says WHY the idea is good — it just threatens an unpleasant feeling if you don't agree.

question: An ad says, 'You'll feel SO HAPPY if you buy this!' Why might this not prove the thing is good?
choices: Appeal to emotion — Promising happiness doesn't make the product actually work or be worth it.
Ads are required by law to only promise feelings that the product gives in every case that comes up.
Happiness is the same thing as the actual value of any product sold in every case that comes up.
Buyers always feel exactly the way the ads predict they will feel afterward in every case that comes up.
answer: Appeal to emotion — Promising happiness doesn't make the product actually work or be worth it.
context: Appeal to emotion in ads. Most ads promise feelings rather than describe what the thing actually does. Real evaluation has to look past the feelings.

question: Sam promised to help Tom rake leaves. A friend invites Sam to a movie. Sam goes to the movie. What's the moral wrong?
choices: Breaking a promise treats the other person's trust as worthless.
Movies are always more important than helping with yard chores.
Promises only count if the other person reminds you of them.
Tom should have raked his leaves earlier so Sam wouldn't be needed.
answer: Breaking a promise treats the other person's trust as worthless.
context: Promises are commitments. When you make one and then drop it, you tell the other person their trust didn't matter to you — that's the real cost.

question: A kid breaks a window playing ball. He says, 'I'll just say a stranger did it.' Why is this wrong even if no one finds out?
choices: A lie hides what really happened — others deserve the truth.
Lies that are not discovered cause no harm to anyone involved.
Strangers in a neighborhood should take blame for any broken windows.
Windows are not valuable enough to justify telling the truth about them.
answer: A lie hides what really happened — others deserve the truth.
context: Lies harm even when undiscovered. They build a false picture of the world for the people you lied to. The harm is real even if the lie is never exposed.

question: Two friends find a wallet full of cash. One says, 'No one saw — let's keep it!' What kind of question is this?
choices: An ethical one — about right and wrong even when nobody is watching.
A finder's question, which is decided by old playground keeping rules.
A math question about how much each friend should get from the wallet.
A simple question about how fast they can leave before being seen.
answer: An ethical one — about right and wrong even when nobody is watching.
context: Ethics is what you do when nobody's watching. The wallet's owner is still real, still lost it, still wants it back — whether or not they can see you.

question: Mia says, 'Everyone lies sometimes, so MY lie isn't a big deal.' What's wrong with that?
choices: Common doesn't equal okay — many people lie AND lying still hurts people.
Lies are completely normal and so they cause no harm to anyone ever.
Mia's lie matters less because she rarely tells lies during the week.
Other people's lies set the rules for whether Mia's lying counts as bad.
answer: Common doesn't equal okay — many people lie AND lying still hurts people.
context: Mixing 'what's common' with 'what's right.' A behavior can be widespread AND wrong at the same time. Ethics asks about the act, not the frequency.

question: A kid is told, 'You can have ONE cookie before dinner.' She takes three. She says, 'I just took an extra TWO.' What is the trouble?
choices: She broke the rule — describing it as 'extra' doesn't change what she did.
Two cookies extra is fine because the kid called it a small addition.
Rules about cookies do not count when there are more than one available.
Dinner is overrated, so taking cookies before it should be totally allowed.
answer: She broke the rule — describing it as 'extra' doesn't change what she did.
context: Renaming a rule break doesn't undo it. The action is the same regardless of how you phrase it. Honest reasoning requires honest labeling.

question: A kid says, 'Most people would lie to get out of trouble, so it's fine for me to lie.' What is the flaw?
choices: What's common doesn't decide what's right.
Most people lying makes lying morally fine.
Lying to escape trouble is universally allowed.
Common acts are the most ethical kind of acts.
answer: What's common doesn't decide what's right.
context: Mixing common with right. Many people doing a thing tells us about HABITS, not about whether the thing is good or harmful.

question: 'Most kids think homework is pointless, so homework MUST be pointless.' Where is the gap?
choices: Appeal to popularity — Lots of kids agreeing doesn't show the homework is actually useless.
Kid opinions are the most reliable way to measure schoolwork value in every case that comes up.
Homework is genuinely pointless and most kids are correctly noticing it in every case that comes up.
Teachers should always trust majority kid opinions about homework worth in every case that comes up.
answer: Appeal to popularity — Lots of kids agreeing doesn't show the homework is actually useless.
context: Appeal to popularity. Whether homework helps learning is a question about results, not about how many kids dislike it.

question: A coach says, 'All the best players use this drink, so it must make you better.' What's missing?
choices: Lots of players using the drink doesn't show the drink is what makes them good.
Top athletes always know exactly which sports drink truly boosts performance.
Drinks chosen by champions are guaranteed to make any user a champion too.
Coaches always recommend drinks that have been scientifically proven to work.
answer: Lots of players using the drink doesn't show the drink is what makes them good.
context: Mixing popularity with cause. The best players got good through long practice. The drink they happen to use isn't the reason.

question: 'Five out of six adults agree that this cereal is healthiest.' How might this not prove the cereal IS healthiest?
choices: An opinion poll measures what people think, not what's true.
Most adults studied nutrition deeply and can name the healthiest cereal.
Five out of six adults is a flawless sample for testing health claims.
Health is whatever most adults agree to call healthy in any given year.
answer: An opinion poll measures what people think, not what's true.
context: Popularity is not nutrition. To know if a cereal is healthy, you check what's in it — not the opinion poll.

question: A kid is caught pushing in line. He says, 'What about LAST week when SOMEONE ELSE pushed?' Why doesn't this answer the question?
choices: Whataboutism — It changes the subject — last week's pushing doesn't excuse today's.
Last week's pusher should be punished first before anyone else is in normal use.
Lines are unfair places, so pushing is always justified for any kid in normal use.
Whoever pushed first should bear the full blame for all future pushing in normal use.
answer: Whataboutism — It changes the subject — last week's pushing doesn't excuse today's.
context: Whataboutism — answering a question by pointing at someone else's behavior. It's a way to dodge without admitting wrong.

question: When told he interrupted, Mike says, 'But what about that time YOU interrupted ME in 3rd grade?' Why is this off?
choices: Whataboutism — an old event doesn't change what just happened now.
Third-grade events excuse all later interruptions in every case that comes up.
All interrupting throughout life counts the same in every case that comes up.
Remembering old wrongs counts as solving them now in every case that comes up.
answer: Whataboutism — an old event doesn't change what just happened now.
context: Whataboutism reaching far back. Even if the old event was real and bad, it doesn't excuse the new one. Each moment is its own.

question: 'YOU never share, so I don't have to either!' Why doesn't this work as an excuse?
choices: If someone else is wrong, that's a separate issue — it doesn't make YOUR refusal right.
Sharing must always be mutual or it does not count as real sharing.
Two wrong refusals to share will somehow balance out into one fair situation.
Refusing to share is fine whenever another kid has refused to share earlier.
answer: If someone else is wrong, that's a separate issue — it doesn't make YOUR refusal right.
context: Whataboutism. Their not-sharing and YOUR not-sharing are TWO problems, not a cancellation. Solving one doesn't address the other.

question: Theo says, 'I WANT it to be true that this candy is healthy — so it IS healthy.' What's wrong?
choices: Wishful thinking — Wanting a thing to be true doesn't change whether it actually IS.
Strong wishing has been shown to change candy nutrition in many studies.
Candy becomes healthy whenever a kid wants it to be a healthier food.
Wishing makes things real in any case where the wisher believes strongly.
answer: Wishful thinking — Wanting a thing to be true doesn't change whether it actually IS.
context: Wishful thinking. Reality doesn't bend to our wishes. Candy stays candy whether we want it to be healthy or not.

question: A boy hopes it won't rain tomorrow. He says, 'I'm SURE it won't rain.' How is his certainty off?
choices: Wishful thinking — Hoping for no rain doesn't predict the actual weather.
Strong certainty can change weather patterns directly in every case that comes up.
Hope is the most reliable forecasting tool around in every case that comes up.
Boys can confidently predict weather from their wishes in every case that comes up.
answer: Wishful thinking — Hoping for no rain doesn't predict the actual weather.
context: Wishful thinking about the future. The weather happens for its own reasons — our hopes are not one of them.

question: Lila says, 'I really want to be picked first, so I will be picked first.' What is missing?
choices: Wishful thinking — Wanting it doesn't give a reason it will actually happen.
Strong wishing always brings the result the wisher wants in every case that comes up.
Picking order is decided by the kid who hopes the hardest in every case that comes up.
Being picked first is owed to whoever wants it the most in every case that comes up.
answer: Wishful thinking — Wanting it doesn't give a reason it will actually happen.
context: Wishful thinking about an outcome. Real reasons for being picked first (skill, the picker's preferences, luck) are separate from our wish.

question: A kid says, 'I don't WANT the test to be hard, so it must be easy.' What is the flaw?
choices: Wishful thinking — Wanting one thing doesn't decide what the test will actually be like.
Tests are required to match the difficulty level the students hope for in normal use.
Easy tests appear whenever a kid genuinely does not want a hard one in normal use.
Hard is unfair, so any test a kid dislikes will always turn out easy in normal use.
answer: Wishful thinking — Wanting one thing doesn't decide what the test will actually be like.
context: Wishful thinking about facts. The test is what it is, regardless of our wishes. Better to study than to hope.

question: In a class debate about recycling rules, Mia presents data on lunch trays. Sam replies, 'Mia got a C in science last term, so ignore her.' Where does Sam go wrong?
choices: Ad hominem — Sam attacks Mia's record instead of dealing with the actual data she presented.
Mia's grades prove she cannot speak about the cafeteria rules at any school in normal use.
Sam should have brought his own data on tray usage before any debate began in normal use.
Mia's data is wrong because the lunchroom workers refuse to count the trays in normal use.
answer: Ad hominem — Sam attacks Mia's record instead of dealing with the actual data she presented.
context: Classic ad hominem — attack the person, not the argument. Aristotle was the first to catalog this move. A bad grade in science last term does not erase whether the recycling data is right.

question: On a group chat, Lia posts a careful argument about the team captain vote. Devon types: 'Lol you are always so dramatic.' What did Devon avoid?
choices: Ad hominem — Devon dodged the argument by labeling Lia rather than answering what she said.
Devon should have used voice chat to actually present a counter-claim to her.
Devon is right that drama queens cannot be trusted to make team rules at all.
Devon needed more group chat reactions before he could fairly respond to Lia.
answer: Ad hominem — Devon dodged the argument by labeling Lia rather than answering what she said.
context: Calling someone 'dramatic' or 'angry' to skip what they wrote is a tone-policing version of ad hominem. The label can be true and the argument still stand.

question: Coach posts a new lineup. A teammate complains: 'The new kid plays first because Coach hates the rest of us.' What is wrong with framing it that way?
choices: Ad hominem — attacking Coach's motives skips the question of whether the new kid is actually faster.
The new kid should never start ahead of teammates who have been on the squad longer.
The teammate should ask Coach in private rather than complain to the rest of the team.
Coaches always hate the bench players, so the complaint is correct about him truly.
answer: Ad hominem — attacking Coach's motives skips the question of whether the new kid is actually faster.
context: Ad hominem with a motive twist — guessing Coach 'hates us' instead of asking if the lineup tracks performance. Real arguments work even when motives are mixed.

question: In a school council meeting, Jordan suggests a longer lunch period. Riley responds: 'Jordan is only saying that because his locker is far from the cafeteria.' What slips by here?
choices: Ad hominem — Whether a longer lunch would actually help students who eat slowly or stand in long lines.
Whether Jordan's locker is really far from the cafeteria or only feels that way to him.
Whether Riley should run for office against Jordan in the next student election cycle.
Whether the council has the power to extend lunch over the principal's loud objections.
answer: Ad hominem — Whether a longer lunch would actually help students who eat slowly or stand in long lines.
context: Even if Jordan benefits, the proposal can still be good for others. Pointing at his motive does not refute the idea. This 'genetic' style of ad hominem is very common.

question: A video creator argues a popular app is unsafe for kids. A commenter writes: 'You only have 200 followers, sit down.' What did the commenter miss?
choices: Ad hominem — Whether the warnings about the app are correct, which is what the creator was really claiming.
Whether the small creator should grow her channel first before posting safety claims online.
Whether 200 followers is actually small compared to the typical channel about apps for kids.
Whether the popular app has paid the bigger creators to keep quiet about all the safety bugs.
answer: Ad hominem — Whether the warnings about the app are correct, which is what the creator was really claiming.
context: Follower count is not evidence of being wrong. This is ad hominem by credential — dismissing someone for low status rather than checking the claim itself.

question: At a fundraiser meeting, Becca proposes a bake sale. Tom says: 'Becca dropped the cookies last year, so we should reject her plan.' Where is the slip?
choices: Ad hominem — One past mistake does not show this year's bake sale plan is itself a bad idea today.
Becca should not be allowed near baked goods after dropping the cookies last year again.
Tom is right that anyone who has dropped food once cannot run a fundraiser for the club.
The bake sale will fail because dropping cookies always happens to the same person twice.
answer: Ad hominem — One past mistake does not show this year's bake sale plan is itself a bad idea today.
context: Ad hominem by past blunder — using an old slip to dismiss a current proposal. Even people who have failed before can have good new ideas worth hearing.

question: A new student suggests a study schedule for finals. An older student says: 'You just moved here, so your idea does not count.' What is missing from this response?
choices: Ad hominem — Any reason WHY being new makes the schedule wrong instead of just an attack on the speaker.
Any chance for the new kid to defend his time being short at this school over the past month.
Any teacher to step in and rule on whether new students may post schedules during finals week.
Any backup plan for finals studying in case the new student's schedule is rejected as foreign.
answer: Ad hominem — Any reason WHY being new makes the schedule wrong instead of just an attack on the speaker.
context: 'You are new' is identity-attacking ad hominem. The student's status does not test whether the schedule works. Logic is logic regardless of who proposes it.

question: A student raises a real safety problem with the gym mats. The principal responds, 'You have been in trouble before, so your complaint is invalid.' Where is the flaw?
choices: Ad hominem — the mats are either unsafe or not — past trouble does not change the physical risk on them.
Students who get in trouble lose the right to complain about safety issues at their schools.
The principal should suspend the student again for raising a complaint about the gym mats.
The mats might be safe because a student in trouble can never spot a real safety risk truly.
answer: Ad hominem — the mats are either unsafe or not — past trouble does not change the physical risk on them.
context: Ad hominem by irrelevant history. A person's record does not change physical facts. Evaluate the claim, then separately decide what to do about the speaker.

question: Online, Ari argues that a new game's lootboxes are unfair. A reply says: 'Ari is just bad at the game.' What did the reply skip?
choices: Ad hominem — Whether the lootboxes really are unfair — which works the same for skilled and unskilled players.
Whether Ari is actually bad at the game or only bad at the parts other players enjoy the most.
Whether Ari should improve his skill before he is allowed to post critiques of the loot system.
Whether the game company has paid reviewers to call lootboxes fair on the most popular sites.
answer: Ad hominem — Whether the lootboxes really are unfair — which works the same for skilled and unskilled players.
context: Skill at a game does not change whether the rules are fair. Ad hominem via competence — dismiss the critic as bad, ignore whether the critique lands. The point is fairness, not skill.

question: A class is voting on a project topic. After Emma's pitch, Jake says: 'Emma's family is weird, so her topic is bad.' What does the class need to do instead?
choices: Ad hominem — Judge Emma's pitch on the topic itself, not on facts about her family at home.
Vote against Emma because the class should not pick topics from weird families.
Ask Jake to explain WHICH parts of Emma's family are weird before voting begins.
Skip the vote and just have the teacher pick the project topic for the whole class.
answer: Ad hominem — Judge Emma's pitch on the topic itself, not on facts about her family at home.
context: Ad hominem by family / association. Who Emma's people are has no bearing on the project pitch. Strip the personal frame and judge only the proposal.

question: Lin says, 'I think the team should warm up for ten more minutes.' A teammate replies, 'So you want practice to last all night??' What did the teammate do?
choices: Straw man — Stretched 'ten more minutes' into 'all night' so it would be much easier to argue against.
Asked a fair clarifying question about how long the team should be expected to stay tonight.
Pointed out that ten extra minutes will, in practice, always slide into a full hour every day.
Reminded Lin that some teammates have to leave on time for jobs after the practice is done.
answer: Straw man — Stretched 'ten more minutes' into 'all night' so it would be much easier to argue against.
context: Straw man — replace the real position with a giant, easy-to-attack fake. Always ask: did the person actually say THAT? Aristotle warned about this in the Topics.

question: A student council asks for one quiet hour in the library. The school newspaper writes: 'Council demands SILENCE in the whole school.' What did the paper do wrong?
choices: Straw man — Blew up 'one quiet hour in one room' into 'silence everywhere' to make it easy to attack.
Picked a different policy entirely instead of writing about what the council actually asked.
Pointed out, correctly, that one hour of quiet always grows into a full day of silence next.
Forgot to interview the council president before publishing the editorial about the policy.
answer: Straw man — Blew up 'one quiet hour in one room' into 'silence everywhere' to make it easy to attack.
context: Straw man by exaggeration — stretch the scope until the position sounds absurd. Then attack the absurd version, not the real one. Check the actual proposal.

question: Sam suggests the team try a new drill. Coach says: 'So you think our old drills are completely useless?' What is wrong with how Coach framed it?
choices: Straw man — Sam said 'Try a new one' — not 'throw out the old ones,' which is what Coach made it sound like.
Sam was clearly attacking the team's history and the entire system that the coach designed.
Coach is right because adding a new drill always proves that the older drills have been useless.
Sam should not have brought up new drills at practice without first telling Coach in private.
answer: Straw man — Sam said 'Try a new one' — not 'throw out the old ones,' which is what Coach made it sound like.
context: Straw man — Coach replaced 'add' with 'replace.' Adding does not require trashing what works. Quote the actual proposal and answer that.

question: Priya posts: 'We should allow phones during breaks.' Dre comments: 'So you want kids on phones the WHOLE school day?' How did Dre twist it?
choices: Straw man — He replaced 'breaks only' with 'the whole school day' to make Priya's idea sound much wider.
He raised an important point — breaks always grow until they take up the entire class time too.
He correctly noticed that phones during breaks would lead to phones during quiet test sessions.
He waited too long to reply, so by the time he commented the other kids had already moved on.
answer: Straw man — He replaced 'breaks only' with 'the whole school day' to make Priya's idea sound much wider.
context: Straw man via scope-creep. 'Some' becomes 'all,' 'breaks' becomes 'all day.' This makes Priya's idea easier to mock but no longer her actual idea.

question: A teacher proposes one optional club for chess. A parent emails: 'So you want to force kids into chess and replace gym?' What did the parent change?
choices: Straw man — Turned 'one optional club' into 'force all kids and remove gym,' a much bigger and scarier claim.
Pointed out the very real risk that adding one chess club always squeezes out the gym budget.
Asked good questions about which grade levels would actually be involved in the chess program.
Suggested a compromise where chess clubs could meet during one of the after-school time slots.
answer: Straw man — Turned 'one optional club' into 'force all kids and remove gym,' a much bigger and scarier claim.
context: Straw man — optional became forced, one club became all clubs, and chess somehow ate gym class. Each shift was needed to make the proposal attackable.

question: Eli says: 'I like both reading and video games.' A classmate responds: 'Oh, so you think books are stupid?' What is the obvious twist?
choices: Straw man — Eli said he LIKES both — the classmate flipped that into hating books, the opposite stance.
Eli does dislike books, since anyone who plays video games cannot really enjoy reading them too.
The classmate is right that mentioning video games at all proves you secretly hate hard reading.
Eli should not have brought up video games in a room full of kids who love their library hours.
answer: Straw man — Eli said he LIKES both — the classmate flipped that into hating books, the opposite stance.
context: Straw man by reversal — claim someone holds the opposite of what they actually said. The give-away: paraphrase what the person said back to them and see if they nod.

question: A student paper asks for more healthy snacks in vending machines. A reply says: 'So they want to BAN candy from school?' What did the reply do wrong?
choices: Straw man — Stretched 'add healthy snacks' into 'ban candy' — a far harsher position the paper never took.
Pointed out, correctly, that adding healthy snacks always means cutting candy from the machines.
Asked a useful clarifying question about whether the paper meant only nuts or also dried fruits.
Stayed on topic but happened to use stronger language than the original editorial board did.
answer: Straw man — Stretched 'add healthy snacks' into 'ban candy' — a far harsher position the paper never took.
context: Straw man — replace 'add option A' with 'ban option B.' Adding does not require banning. The give-away is the leap from 'more X' to 'no Y.'

question: On a group chat, Mara says she wants one tournament rule changed. Jay replies: 'So you want to throw out the whole rulebook??' What slip did Jay make?
choices: Straw man — One rule is not the whole book — Jay turned a small change into a total rewrite of the system.
Mara never picked WHICH rule she wanted changed, so Jay assumed she meant every rule at once.
Jay correctly noted that any rule change tends to cascade until the whole rulebook is rewritten.
Mara was using the wrong group chat to bring up tournament rules, which Jay was right to flag.
answer: Straw man — One rule is not the whole book — Jay turned a small change into a total rewrite of the system.
context: Straw man via inflation — one becomes all, a tweak becomes a teardown. Quoting the actual proposal is the cure: 'You said change rule 7. That is what I will answer.'

question: Ana asks for more time for art on Fridays. Her brother says: 'So you want to skip math and science FOREVER?' What did the brother twist?
choices: Straw man — Ana said 'More art on Fridays,' not 'cut all math and science' — those are very different requests.
Ana made a vague case, since 'more art time' could mean trading off any of the other class slots.
The brother is right that adding art always means removing some math, even if it is not stated.
The brother used capital letters, which is not how kids should make their point in a calm debate.
answer: Straw man — Ana said 'More art on Fridays,' not 'cut all math and science' — those are very different requests.
context: Straw man via 'forever' and 'all subjects.' Replace targeted with total, sometimes with forever. The fix: paraphrase the actual claim before answering it.

question: Beth says: 'Maybe our school could try a half-day on the last Friday of the month.' Carlos answers: 'So you want NO school at all?' What is the problem?
choices: Straw man — He swapped one half-day a month for 'no school ever,' a vastly larger and easier-to-mock claim.
He noticed, correctly, that any reduction in school time always slides into the end of school.
He simply repeated her position more clearly so that everyone in the room could understand her.
He used punctuation that was too strong for a topic about how often the school should be open.
answer: Straw man — He swapped one half-day a month for 'no school ever,' a vastly larger and easier-to-mock claim.
context: Straw man — one half-day a month is far from 'no school.' The leap from a modest tweak to total abolition is the calling-card of this fallacy.

question: A friend says, 'Either you stand up for me in the group chat, or you are not really my friend.' What is wrong with how he framed it?
choices: False dilemma — He left out lots of options — like talking with him later or asking what really happened first.
He is right — true friends always defend each other publicly, no matter the actual situation.
He should have texted privately rather than calling out the issue inside the group chat itself.
He needs to find better friends than people who hesitate to defend him on the group chats.
answer: False dilemma — He left out lots of options — like talking with him later or asking what really happened first.
context: False dilemma — pretend only two choices exist. Real friendships have many in-between moves: ask, listen, defer judgment. Two-option framing is almost always a trick.

question: Mom says, 'Either you finish ALL your chores or you get ZERO screen time this week.' Why might this framing be unfair?
choices: It pretends only the two extremes exist — partial chores might earn partial screen time fairly.
It is the only honest way to make sure kids actually finish the household chores each week.
Chores are nobody's choice in the family, so the rule should match what the parent decides.
All-or-nothing rules are the only way for a family to be respected and run smoothly each week.
answer: It pretends only the two extremes exist — partial chores might earn partial screen time fairly.
context: Black-and-white fallacy. Most real choices are sliders, not switches. The trick is to notice when someone hides the middle on purpose to push you to one side.

question: At tryouts, Coach announces, 'You are either ALL-IN on this team, or you should quit today.' What option got hidden in his framing?
choices: False dilemma — Trying hard while also playing other sports — being committed does not need to be 100% of life.
Just quitting today is the correct call since real teams require all of your attention and time.
Saying 'all-in' is the only way a young athlete will ever reach a serious competitive level later.
Coaches who use all-or-nothing language are the kind of coaches who win the most championships.
answer: False dilemma — Trying hard while also playing other sports — being committed does not need to be 100% of life.
context: False dilemma — 'all-in or out' erases the realistic middle of being committed and also balanced. Watch for this in coaches, advertisers, and arguments online.

question: A class president candidate says, 'Vote for me, or get stuck with terrible school lunches forever.' What is sneaky about that?
choices: False dilemma — Other candidates might also fix lunch — and the current candidate might also fail at the job.
Voters should pick on lunches alone, since no other issue at school is anywhere near as important.
The candidate is the only person on the ballot who has even considered changing the lunch menu.
Promising to fix lunches is the strongest possible reason to vote for any student candidate now.
answer: False dilemma — Other candidates might also fix lunch — and the current candidate might also fail at the job.
context: False dilemma — the candidate frames the choice as 'me OR doom' when more options exist. Politicians (and student politicians) lean on this trick a lot.

question: Dad says, 'Either I trust you with the new phone or I have to track every single thing you do.' What middle option did he miss?
choices: False dilemma — some trust now plus regular check-ins later — trust can be partial and can also grow over time.
Dad is correct because phones can only be used by kids who get either total trust or total tracking.
Kids should not have phones at all if their parents are unable to track every single action online.
Total tracking is the safer choice for any parent who is going to give their kid a phone right now.
answer: False dilemma — some trust now plus regular check-ins later — trust can be partial and can also grow over time.
context: False dilemma — total trust vs. total surveillance. Real parenting and real friendships live in the in-between. Notice the missing middle.

question: A teammate insists, 'Either we run this play exactly OR we should not bother playing.' What option got buried by this framing?
choices: False dilemma — Run a similar play, adjust as the game goes, and learn together — sport is not all-or-nothing.
Quit the team if you cannot run this exact play, since that is what every real teammate would do.
Wait for the coach to call a fully different play before any of the team makes a single move.
Run the play exactly even if it is wrong, because picking another option just shows weakness now.
answer: False dilemma — Run a similar play, adjust as the game goes, and learn together — sport is not all-or-nothing.
context: False dilemma. Sports, like most things, have many shadings: improvise, adapt, learn. The 'this exact way or nothing' move is a clue someone wants to shut down options.

question: An online ad says: 'BUY now or be the only kid without the toy.' What is the false choice?
choices: False dilemma — Many kids will not buy it, and skipping a toy is not 'being the only one' without anything fun.
Buying now is the smartest move since being last to own the toy will obviously feel terrible later.
The ad is right that anyone who skips this purchase will end up regretting it through the school year.
Toys are the only way for kids to fit in, so the ad's logic about buying soon is basically correct.
answer: False dilemma — Many kids will not buy it, and skipping a toy is not 'being the only one' without anything fun.
context: False dilemma plus fear-of-missing-out. Ads love this combo: 'Buy or be alone.' In real life, the third option — 'not buy, still fine' — is the most common one.

question: A parent says, 'If I let you stay up until 10 once, soon you'll be up at midnight, then dawn, then failing every class.' Why is that not solid reasoning?
choices: Slippery slope — each step in the chain needs its own evidence — staying up once does not force the rest at all.
It is correct because any small change in bedtime always escalates into a full disaster by week end.
The parent should ban any change to bedtime forever to be safe about how the situation will unfold.
Going to bed at 10 is so risky that the chain to midnight and failure can be skipped over entirely.
answer: Slippery slope — each step in the chain needs its own evidence — staying up once does not force the rest at all.
context: Slippery slope — one small step is treated as guaranteed to cascade. Each arrow in the chain has to be shown, not assumed. Often the cascade just does not happen.

question: A teammate warns, 'If Coach lets the new kid start one game, soon she will start every game, then we will all sit on the bench forever.' What is the flaw?
choices: Slippery slope — There is no real link from 'one game' to 'forever' — many in-between outcomes are also possible.
There is no other way for benching to happen, so the teammate's prediction is basically perfect.
Coaches always replace the entire starting roster after letting just one new player into the lineup.
Any new starter automatically locks in for the season unless the rest of the team boycotts a game.
answer: Slippery slope — There is no real link from 'one game' to 'forever' — many in-between outcomes are also possible.
context: Slippery slope — predict disaster from one harmless step with no proof of each link. Lots of one-game starts never become permanent. Ask: WHY would each step follow?

question: A parent argues, 'If you have a small piece of cake today, soon you'll eat cake daily, then candy daily, then never eat vegetables.' Where is the trouble?
choices: Slippery slope — each step is just claimed, not shown — kids eat cake all the time without giving up vegetables.
The parent is right because one piece of cake biologically rewires kids into hating vegetables fast.
The kid should not eat any cake until they prove they can avoid the full chain of bad future choices.
Vegetables and cake cannot share a kid's diet — once cake enters, the vegetables always disappear.
answer: Slippery slope — each step is just claimed, not shown — kids eat cake all the time without giving up vegetables.
context: Slippery slope. Each link is asserted but unproven. Many people eat occasional cake AND vegetables their whole lives. The chain skips reality.

question: A teacher argues, 'If I allow notes on this quiz, then on tests, then on finals, then no one will ever study.' What did the teacher skip?
choices: Slippery slope — Showing WHY allowing notes on one quiz must lead to all that — most quizzes do not snowball like this.
Asking the class first — students might admit they were going to stop studying anyway this year in normal use.
Pointing out that any teacher who lets one quiz be open-note has obviously already given up in normal use in normal use.
Studying is not the kind of habit a student can choose to keep when even one note is allowed in normal use.
answer: Slippery slope — Showing WHY allowing notes on one quiz must lead to all that — most quizzes do not snowball like this.
context: Slippery slope — chain a small allowance to a big disaster with no proof of each step. Most schools allow notes on some assessments and not others without collapse.

question: An older sibling says, 'If you watch one episode tonight, you'll binge the whole season, then a new show, then never sleep again.' What is missing?
choices: Slippery slope — Evidence that watching ONE episode forces every next step — most people stop after one episode just fine.
Permission from the parent for either of the kids to choose any episode of any show on the screen in normal use.
A way to know which season the younger sibling is talking about starting on the screen tonight in normal use.
Proof that binging is automatic; if a kid does not binge once, they may never figure out how to do it in normal use.
answer: Slippery slope — Evidence that watching ONE episode forces every next step — most people stop after one episode just fine.
context: Slippery slope built on hidden assumptions: 'One episode means binge.' Some viewers do binge — but the warning treats the bad path as forced, not chosen.

question: A coach says: 'If you wear that bracelet at practice ONCE, soon the whole team will, then we will all forget our skills, then we lose state.' The coach MAY have a real concern about discipline — but his argument has a specific flaw. What is it?
choices: Slippery slope — the bracelet-to-state-loss chain is unjustified. A direct case for discipline would need to be made separately.
The coach is wrong about everything because uniforms have nothing to do with discipline or any sports outcomes.
The coach is fully correct because one rule break always cascades through a team in any sport across any season.
Skills disappear in the presence of jewelry, so the chain the coach described is in fact entirely accurate.
answer: Slippery slope — the bracelet-to-state-loss chain is unjustified. A direct case for discipline would need to be made separately.
context: Slippery slope — a chain of unsupported steps. The coach may have a legitimate concern about discipline; spotting a fallacy in his argument doesn't prove him wrong about discipline itself. It just means the argument he made doesn't establish it. This nuance — the 'fallacy fallacy' — is critical: a bad argument for X doesn't show X is false.

question: An adult argues, 'If we let kids vote on lunch menu items, soon they will vote on the school budget, then run the whole school.' Why is that shaky?
choices: Slippery slope — There are real limits on what kids can vote on — the chain skips every rule between menu and budget.
It is correct because giving kids any vote anywhere always leads to them taking over every decision.
The adult should ban menu voting because there is no way to keep a list of which topics kids may vote on.
Budgets and lunch menus are the same kind of choice, so it is fair to assume the kids would vote both.
answer: Slippery slope — There are real limits on what kids can vote on — the chain skips every rule between menu and budget.
context: Slippery slope — the chain ignores that real systems have stop points, rules, and reviews. Each link in the chain needs reasons, not just dread.

question: On a group chat, someone warns, 'If we add ONE meme channel, soon the chat will be only memes, then no one will plan anything ever again.' What is the slip?
choices: Slippery slope — Adding one channel does not force the others to die — most chats stay mixed even after a meme room opens.
It is correct because a meme channel in a group chat instantly kills the rest of the topics in the chat.
Meme channels and planning channels cannot exist together in one group chat under any conditions ever.
The warning is right and the only safe move is to refuse to ever create a new channel of any kind today.
answer: Slippery slope — Adding one channel does not force the others to die — most chats stay mixed even after a meme room opens.
context: Slippery slope. 'One small addition kills everything' is rarely true in social systems. Watch for forecasts with no mechanism — that is the give-away.

question: A classmate insists, 'EVERYONE in 6th grade is going to the late movie, so my parents should let me go too.' What is wrong with this as the whole reason?
choices: Bandwagon — What other kids are allowed to do does not show what is right for THIS kid in THIS family.
