Sixth graders cannot be wrong as a group, so the classmate is being treated unfairly by his parents.
Parents who say no to movies should be reported to the school for not being like other parents.
Late movies are clearly the best choice for everyone — saying no is just being stuck in old ways now.
answer: Bandwagon — What other kids are allowed to do does not show what is right for THIS kid in THIS family.
context: Bandwagon — 'everyone is doing it' is the oldest peer-pressure move. The crowd's choice does not prove anything about this kid, this family, or this movie.

question: Online, a creator says, 'This video has TEN MILLION likes, so its tips are obviously correct.' Where is the slip in that line of thinking?
choices: Bandwagon — Likes count who clicked a button, not whether the tips actually work when a person tries them out.
Ten million likes is a small number on the internet, so the proof from likes is too weak to use.
Likes are clearly the best test of truth, since they are easier to count than evidence or studies.
The creator should have asked for more likes before claiming the tips were correct in the first place.
answer: Bandwagon — Likes count who clicked a button, not whether the tips actually work when a person tries them out.
context: Bandwagon / appeal to popularity — many likes do not prove the tips work. Lots of viewers can be wrong, especially when 'liking' takes one second of attention.

question: On a class trip, a kid says, 'Everyone is sneaking soda into the lunchroom, so it must be allowed.' Where is the move wrong?
choices: Bandwagon — What other kids are doing does not change the school rule — rules and habits are very different things.
Sneaking is the same as allowing, because if no one is stopping the kids the rule must be already gone.
The rule should obviously be changed since the kids have already voted by sneaking in their own sodas.
Sodas in a lunchroom are too small a thing to count as a rule, so the kid's reasoning is just fine.
answer: Bandwagon — What other kids are doing does not change the school rule — rules and habits are very different things.
context: Bandwagon defense. 'Lots of people break rule X, so X is fake' confuses popularity with permission. The rule stands until it is actually changed by people who can change it.

question: A friend says, 'All the popular kids in our grade have started using this slang, so we have to use it or look bad.' What did the friend assume?
choices: Bandwagon — that fitting in is the only goal — but plenty of kids stay themselves AND get respected just fine.
That the slang is wrong on its face, since real kids do not just copy whatever the popular kids do.
That the popular kids will be popular forever and so every slang they use will stay forever as well.
That refusing to use the slang will lead instantly to being kicked out of the entire 6th-grade year.
answer: Bandwagon — that fitting in is the only goal — but plenty of kids stay themselves AND get respected just fine.
context: Bandwagon plus peer pressure. The crowd's word is treated as the only safe word. Notice the hidden assumption that fitting in is the only thing that matters.

question: A student tried sushi once at the cafeteria, did not like it, and now says, 'All sushi is gross.' What is wrong with that move?
choices: Hasty generalization — ONE bad cafeteria sushi roll does not prove a whole world of sushi places and styles is all gross.
Sushi is too varied for anyone to make any kind of claim about whether it is gross or not at all in normal use.
Cafeterias are the only fair test of any food, so the student's claim about sushi is basically right in normal use.
Sushi is correctly judged to be gross once any single person has had even one bad roll of it ever in normal use.
answer: Hasty generalization — ONE bad cafeteria sushi roll does not prove a whole world of sushi places and styles is all gross.
context: Hasty generalization — leap from one sample to a sweeping claim. Real testing needs many samples across many settings. One bad roll proves one bad roll.

question: A boy says, 'My one friend who plays that game stays up too late, so EVERY kid who plays it stays up too late.' Where is the leap?
choices: Hasty generalization — ONE friend's habit does not show what the millions of other players do at bedtime each night.
Late nights are perfectly predicted by any single example, so the boy is fully right about all players.
The friend who stays up late is the only kid whose sleep matters, so the whole claim is basically true.
All gamers in the world stay up too late once at least one of them has been spotted doing it once.
answer: Hasty generalization — ONE friend's habit does not show what the millions of other players do at bedtime each night.
context: Hasty generalization. One person's habit is not the species. Look at lots of cases before claiming the pattern holds across millions.

question: After meeting one rude kid from a different school, Ben says, 'Every kid at that school is rude.' What flaw is showing in his thinking?
choices: Hasty generalization — One kid does not stand in for a whole school — most schools have a mix of kids, polite and rude both.
The school must be a problem because one student from it was rude to Ben in one short moment today in normal use.
Ben should not visit that school again until every single student there proves themselves to be polite in normal use.
All schools share one mood, so the rude kid is correctly seen as a sample of all of them at his school in normal use.
answer: Hasty generalization — One kid does not stand in for a whole school — most schools have a mix of kids, polite and rude both.
context: Hasty generalization — judge a whole group by a single bad example. Almost any large group has mixes of behavior. A good cure: actively look for counter-examples.

question: Lila got one cold answer from the school office and now thinks 'The entire staff is mean.' What is wrong with that conclusion?
choices: Hasty generalization — One cold reply does not show that ALL the staff are mean — many people work in the office each day.
Cold answers are rare from school staff, so one is enough to prove that every staffer is being mean.
Lila is right because school offices are run by people who must all share one personality every day.
Schools are required to keep all the staff in one mood, so a cold answer proves the whole place is mean.
answer: Hasty generalization — One cold reply does not show that ALL the staff are mean — many people work in the office each day.
context: Hasty generalization. One bad interaction in one moment is not the whole staff. A bad day, a hard call, a misread tone — all could explain one cold answer.

question: A boy reads ONE bad book in a series and says, 'The whole series is terrible.' Where does his reasoning slip?
choices: Hasty generalization — Series swing a lot — one weak book in a long set does not show the rest are weak as well over time.
The author has to be terrible since one book in a series was bad, and that is enough proof to stop in normal use.
Series are built so that all books inside them must always be exactly the same level of quality also in normal use.
The boy should never read another book by the author until every single book in the series is good in normal use.
answer: Hasty generalization — Series swing a lot — one weak book in a long set does not show the rest are weak as well over time.
context: Hasty generalization. One sample tested = one data point. A great series can have a weak entry. The cure is to read another book before swearing off the series.

question: After a hard test, Mara says, 'I bombed it, so I am terrible at math.' What might she be missing in her thinking?
choices: Hasty generalization — One test on one topic on one day does not measure her math ability across every topic she has had.
One bombed test is the only test that should ever count, so the conclusion she is terrible is fine.
She is right because anybody who fails one math test obviously cannot pass any other math test later.
Math is judged only by recent tests, so the new score is the only fair way to talk about her ability.
answer: Hasty generalization — One test on one topic on one day does not measure her math ability across every topic she has had.
context: Hasty generalization about yourself. One test is a snapshot. Performance varies by topic, sleep, mood. Look at trends across many tests, not one slip.

question: Eric tried a new sport once, got hurt, and decided, 'This sport is dangerous for everyone.' Where is the leap?
choices: Hasty generalization — One injury to one person does not show the sport is dangerous for most others who play it often.
Eric is right because if one person gets hurt the sport is, by simple logic, hazardous for all others.
Sports are safe only if not even one player ever gets hurt, so Eric's conclusion is logically correct.
Sports are equally risky to everyone, so the injury to Eric proves it to be dangerous for them all too.
answer: Hasty generalization — One injury to one person does not show the sport is dangerous for most others who play it often.
context: Hasty generalization plus injury bias. One person's experience does not give us the rate of injuries across millions of players. Look up the data, not just the story.

question: Aisha watched ONE video about a snack being unhealthy and now says 'All snacks like that are unhealthy.' Where is the leap?
choices: Hasty generalization — ONE video about ONE snack does not prove every similar snack is also unhealthy in the same way at all.
The video must be right since it is on the internet and any single online claim is automatically true in normal use.
Aisha is right to drop the snack since one video is enough proof to ban any food from the household now in normal use.
All snacks are the same in any category, so Aisha is correct to lump them all into one group like that in normal use.
answer: Hasty generalization — ONE video about ONE snack does not prove every similar snack is also unhealthy in the same way at all.
context: Hasty generalization plus single-source trust. One video, one snack, one claim — none of that proves a category. Look for multiple sources covering multiple products.

question: A parent asks, 'Why is your homework not finished?' The kid replies, 'But my room is the cleanest it has ever been!' How did the kid dodge?
choices: Red herring — He swapped the question about homework for a different topic he can win on — his clean room.
He correctly pointed out that a clean room and a finished homework set always show up together.
He is right because rooms and homework are the same chore, so cleaning means the homework is done.
He should have stayed quiet, since speaking at all when caught is what makes parents stay angry now.
answer: Red herring — He swapped the question about homework for a different topic he can win on — his clean room.
context: Red herring — drag a shiny new topic across the trail to pull the questioner away. The right reply is: 'We can talk about your room AFTER you answer about the homework.'

question: In a class debate about uniforms, Sam responds, 'But the cafeteria food is also terrible!' How does this hurt the debate?
choices: Red herring — It pulls the talk off uniforms onto food, a separate issue that does not settle the uniform question.

It correctly notes that since one school thing is bad, fixing uniforms is now obviously not allowed.

answer: Red herring — It pulls the talk off uniforms onto food, a separate issue that does not settle the uniform question.
context: Red herring — change the subject to a topic where you feel stronger. The debate question stays open; only the audience's attention has moved. Push the topic back.

question: After a coach asks why a player skipped practice, the player says, 'But the lockers are filthy and no one cleans them.' How did the player avoid the question?
choices: Red herring — He changed the topic from his missing practice to something else — locker cleanliness in the gym halls.
He correctly raised a school-wide issue that has to be fixed before any practice can be properly held.

answer: Red herring — He changed the topic from his missing practice to something else — locker cleanliness in the gym halls.
context: Red herring. The locker complaint may be valid, but it is unrelated to why he skipped. Insist on answering one question before switching to another.

question: In a debate about phones in class, Pat says, 'Well, what about kids who skip school entirely? That is way worse!' What did Pat just do?
choices: Whataboutism — Shifted the discussion from phones in class to a different topic — skipping school — to escape the issue.
Made a great point because no debate about phones can be held without first solving the skipping problem.

answer: Whataboutism — Shifted the discussion from phones in class to a different topic — skipping school — to escape the issue.
context: Red herring with a 'whataboutism' flavor. Bring up something WORSE to make the current topic feel small. The current topic still deserves its answer first.

question: A teacher asks Ann about her late paper. Ann answers, 'But Jamal is always on his phone in class — why focus on me?' What is the dodge here?
choices: Red herring — Ann moved the topic from her own paper to a separate complaint about Jamal's habits in the classroom.
Ann correctly pointed out that no late paper can be discussed without first dealing with phones in class.

answer: Red herring — Ann moved the topic from her own paper to a separate complaint about Jamal's habits in the classroom.
context: Red herring plus 'but what about them?' Drag in someone else's problem to dilute your own. The two issues are independent — both might deserve attention, but separately.

question: A campaign poster asks, 'Why pick HER for class president?' The candidate replies, 'I once helped a stray cat — isn't that amazing?' Where is the trick?
choices: Red herring — She shifted from why she should LEAD to a separate good deed that does not answer the leadership claim.

answer: Red herring — She shifted from why she should LEAD to a separate good deed that does not answer the leadership claim.
context: Red herring — toss out a heartwarming story to dodge the substantive question. Listen for: 'Wait, that was nice, but it does not answer what was asked.'

question: An online ad says, 'This famous actor recommends this brand of math tutoring, so it must work.' What is shaky about that?
choices: Appeal to authority — Acting skill does not prove anything about how a math program works — those are very different subjects.

context: Appeal to authority done wrong — the 'expert' is famous in an unrelated field. A math program needs math people. Fame is not expertise. Ask: expert in WHAT?

question: A video says, 'This top chef thinks this new car is the safest on the road, so we should buy it.' Where is the problem?
choices: Cooking expertise does not transfer to crash safety — that comes from engineers, tests, and crash data.

context: Wrong-field authority. Famous chef + car safety = mismatch. Real authority requires real expertise IN the relevant area. Trust experts within their lane.

question: An ad uses an athlete to recommend a vitamin saying, 'Champions take it, so it must boost grades.' Where is the slip?
choices: Appeal to authority — Sport champions are not the right experts on whether vitamins help school grades — that takes a study.

answer: Appeal to authority — Sport champions are not the right experts on whether vitamins help school grades — that takes a study.
context: Appeal to authority — athletes know sports, not nutrition research. And vitamins boosting grades is a separate claim that needs studies, not endorsements.

question: A friend says, 'My favorite singer says this game is dangerous for kids, so we should all stop playing.' What is wrong with this as the whole reason?
choices: Appeal to authority — Singers do not have special training to judge game risks — that needs researchers and game designers.

answer: Appeal to authority — Singers do not have special training to judge game risks — that needs researchers and game designers.
context: Appeal to authority done wrong. Fame in one area does not give expertise in another. Real game-risk claims need real evidence — not just a celebrity endorsement.

question: Aiden defends a study habit by saying, 'My older cousin who never went to college says it is the BEST way.' What is shaky about this proof?
choices: Not going to college does not make someone a study expert — that takes a real record of success.

answer: Not going to college does not make someone a study expert — that takes a real record of success.
context: Misplaced authority. Being older or being a relative does not make someone an expert. Ask what TRACK RECORD backs the advice — not just who is giving it.

question: A friend says, 'This drink is healthy because all the ingredients are NATURAL.' Why is that not enough to prove it is good for you?
choices: Appeal to nature — Plenty of natural things are harmful — poison ivy and bad mushrooms are natural and still hurt people.

answer: Appeal to nature — Plenty of natural things are harmful — poison ivy and bad mushrooms are natural and still hurt people.
context: Appeal to nature — 'natural' gets treated as automatically good. Plenty of natural things are dangerous. Plenty of made things are safe. The label does not settle it.

question: A friend defends a habit by saying, 'Humans are built to do this — it is natural.' What is wrong with that as a full defense?
choices: Appeal to nature — 'Natural' is not the same as 'good' — humans are also built to fight and lie, which are not always wise.
Anything humans are built to do is right by default, so the friend's defense of the habit is correct in normal use.

context: Appeal to nature. Even our biology gives us drives that need shaping. 'Natural' is a starting fact, not a moral verdict. Ethics asks what we DO with the drive.

question: A trending post says, 'A million people shared this fact, so it must be true.' What does that argument leave out?
choices: Shares show how many liked the post, not whether anybody actually checked the underlying fact at all.
Anything reshared a million times is automatically researched by everyone who clicks the share button.

answer: Shares show how many liked the post, not whether anybody actually checked the underlying fact at all.
context: Popularity is not truth. False claims have gone viral for centuries. Many shares = many shares — they do not equal accuracy. Always check the source independently.

question: At lunch, kids agree that a certain rumor about a teacher is true 'because everyone is saying it.' Where is the slip?
choices: A rumor staying alive only means many mouths repeat it — not that anyone has checked the facts at all.
Lots of mouths saying a rumor is the strongest possible proof, so the kids at the lunch table are right.
Rumors are checked automatically at lunch tables, so the kids' belief in the rumor is fully supported.

answer: A rumor staying alive only means many mouths repeat it — not that anyone has checked the facts at all.
context: Popularity does not make a rumor true. A story can spread through hundreds of mouths without ever passing through a fact-check. Always ask: who actually witnessed this?

question: An ad reads, 'Most kids prefer this candy, so this is the BEST candy.' What is the slip in calling popular 'best'?
choices: Preferred and best are different — sugary, easy-to-find candy is bought a lot even when it is not 'best.'
Popularity is the only fair way to test quality, so the ad has chosen the best candy by perfect logic.

Most kids cannot be wrong about candy in any way, so the ad's reasoning about quality is correct here.
answer: Preferred and best are different — sugary, easy-to-find candy is bought a lot even when it is not 'best.'
context: Popularity is not quality. Sales rankings track marketing, sugar, and price as much as flavor. The 'best' label has to be earned with something more than 'most picked.'

question: A kid in math says, 'Most of us got the same answer, so it has to be right.' What did the kid skip?
choices: Checking the math itself — many students can make the same mistake and arrive at the same wrong answer.
Most kids in a class are correct by definition, so the answer that won the vote is mathematically right.
Voting on math is the most accurate way of doing it, so the agreement on the answer settles the problem.
Math answers are decided by majority rule, so the most popular answer in any class is right by vote.
answer: Checking the math itself — many students can make the same mistake and arrive at the same wrong answer.
context: Popular agreement is not proof in math (or anywhere). A whole class can share one error from one bad shortcut. Truth in math comes from showing your work, not from the vote.

question: Maya wore her lucky socks and aced her test. She says, 'The socks caused the score.' Where is the slip in her reasoning?
choices: Post hoc — Sock-wearing came BEFORE the score, but that does not show the socks caused it — studying is the lever.
Maya's socks are clearly magic, so any time she wears them her tests will always go better than before.
Maya is right because anything that happens just before a test must be the reason the test went well.
Maya should never wear other socks again, since once a sock works it will always work for any test.
answer: Post hoc — Sock-wearing came BEFORE the score, but that does not show the socks caused it — studying is the lever.
context: Post hoc fallacy — 'after this, therefore because of this.' Order in time is not the same as cause. Maya's study habits, sleep, and prep matter much more than her socks.

question: After Ben drank green smoothies for a week, he won the spelling bee. He says, 'Smoothies cause spelling wins.' What did Ben miss?
choices: Post hoc — Lots of other things were happening — study time, practice, sleep — any of which could be the real cause.
Smoothies always lead to spelling wins, so Ben has found the only secret to school spelling contests.
Ben is right because anything you drink in the week before a win is the real cause of how the win came.
Smoothies and spelling go together perfectly, so the link Ben has noticed is a real one beyond all doubt.
answer: Post hoc — Lots of other things were happening — study time, practice, sleep — any of which could be the real cause.
context: Post hoc. Many things happen before a win — picking ONE and crowning it the cause ignores all the others. Real causes are tested by changing one thing at a time.

question: Lila got a new haircut, then the team won the next three games. She says, 'My haircut caused the wins.' Where is the leap?
choices: Post hoc — Wins depend on many factors — opponents, plays, practice — not on what one teammate's hair looks like.
Haircuts always boost the team, so Lila should change her style every week to keep the win streak going.
Lila is right because what a player does in the week before a win is the real cause of the team's win.
Hair is the most important factor in team sports, so the wins are correctly tied to Lila's new haircut.
answer: Post hoc — Wins depend on many factors — opponents, plays, practice — not on what one teammate's hair looks like.
context: Post hoc plus sports superstition. The brain LOVES to invent causes for streaks. Real causes can be tested; superstitions can only be obeyed. Notice the difference.

question: After kids start using a new app, their grades drop. A parent says, 'The app caused the drops.' What might the parent be missing?
choices: Post hoc — Maybe kids were already struggling and turned to the app to escape — the drop could be cause, not effect.
The app is the only possible explanation, so the parent is right and the app must be banned by tomorrow.
Apps always cause grade drops, so the parent has logically pinned down the cause without more evidence.
Grades are simple to explain — whatever new thing kids do is automatically the cause of any drop or rise.
answer: Post hoc — Maybe kids were already struggling and turned to the app to escape — the drop could be cause, not effect.
context: Post hoc with reverse-cause possibility. The new thing came first, the grade dropped second — but the kids' struggles might have driven them to the app, not the reverse.

question: Teammate: 'If our QB were strong, we'd be winning. We ARE winning. So our QB must be strong.' Where does the logic slip in this argument?
answer: Affirming the consequent — Wins can come from many things; the win alone does not point back to a strong QB as the cause.
choices: Affirming the consequent — Wins can come from many things; the win alone does not point back to a strong QB as the cause.
The team is not really winning, so the teammate is wrong about the season's record this year in every case that comes up.

The team needs more data; once they reach ten wins in a row, the argument becomes a real proof in every case that comes up.
context: Affirming the consequent: 'If P then Q; Q; so P.' Q can happen for many reasons -- defense, schedule, luck. Mill's A System of Logic (1843) systematized these slips.

question: Online claim: 'If a product works, lots of people buy it. This shampoo sells tons. So it must really work on hair.' What is the slip in this argument?
answer: Affirming the consequent — Shampoos sell for many reasons -- ads, packaging, price -- so high sales do not prove the product works.
choices: Affirming the consequent — Shampoos sell for many reasons -- ads, packaging, price -- so high sales do not prove the product works.

context: Classic affirming the consequent. A working product MIGHT sell, but selling does not prove working. Ads, hype, and trends drive sales independent of whether the thing performs.

question: A kid says: 'If you studied, you'd get a good grade. Maya got an A on the quiz. So Maya must have actually studied for it.' What is wrong with this kind of reasoning?
answer: Maya might already know the material; an A does not prove she studied for THIS quiz at all.

The argument is solid because A grades only go to students who put serious time into their studying.

context: If P then Q; Q; so P. Studying is one path to an A; prior knowledge or easy material are others. The grade alone cannot point back to studying.

question: Sports debate: 'If a coach cares, players show up early. Our players showed up early today. So our coach must really care about us.' Where is the slip in this argument?
answer: Affirming the consequent — Players show up early for many reasons -- fear, habit, playing time -- not only because the coach cares.
choices: Affirming the consequent — Players show up early for many reasons -- fear, habit, playing time -- not only because the coach cares.

context: Affirming the consequent. The 'caring coach' is one cause of early attendance, not the only one. To support the claim, you would need to rule out the other paths.

question: A friend insists: 'If you liked me, you would text me first. You DID text me first today. So you must like me a lot.' What is the slip in the friend's reasoning here?
answer: People text first for many reasons-- a question, boredom, plans-- a single text does not prove they like you back.

context: Form: 'If P then Q; Q; so P.' Liking is one reason to text first; needing notes is another. The consequent alone tells you little about the antecedent.

question: An ad claims: 'If a phone is high quality, it costs a lot. This phone costs a lot. So it must be a high-quality phone.' Where is the trick in this kind of ad?
answer: Affirming the consequent — Phones cost a lot for many reasons -- brand, hype, scarcity -- so price by itself does not prove quality.
choices: Affirming the consequent — Phones cost a lot for many reasons -- brand, hype, scarcity -- so price by itself does not prove quality.

There is no trick at all because expensive phones always work better, so paying more is the smarter buy in normal use.
context: Affirming the consequent. Quality CAN drive price up. So can fashion, hype, and shortage. The high price tells you a phone is expensive, not that it is good.

question: YouTuber argues: 'If our team had chemistry, we would crush the rivals. We crushed them. So we have real team chemistry now.' What is the gap in this argument?
answer: Affirming the consequent — One blowout can come from many causes; the win alone does not point back to chemistry as the real reason.
choices: Affirming the consequent — One blowout can come from many causes; the win alone does not point back to chemistry as the real reason.

Chemistry causes wins, not blowouts, so the YouTuber used the wrong word, and that ruins the argument for most people.
context: Affirming the consequent. The win is the consequent; chemistry is one possible antecedent. Maybe the rivals were tired. The result does not prove the cause.

question: In a comment thread: 'If a song is good, it goes viral on TikTok. This song went viral. So it must be a genuinely good song.' What is the slip in this kind of comment?
answer: Affirming the consequent — Songs go viral for hooks, dance trends, or memes -- so virality by itself does not really prove quality.
choices: Affirming the consequent — Songs go viral for hooks, dance trends, or memes -- so virality by itself does not really prove quality.

The slip is that TikTok is the wrong app; only Spotify can really prove if a song is high quality here in normal use.
context: Affirming the consequent. Quality may drive virality, but so do hooks, trends, and timing. A viral song might be great. It might also just be catchy.

question: Hopeful says: 'If you make varsity, you get a jacket. I did not make varsity. So I will never get a jacket from this school for any reason.' Where is the slip in this argument?
answer: Denying the antecedent — Jackets get given out for many things -- band, debate, honor roll -- so missing varsity does not block all.
choices: Denying the antecedent — Jackets get given out for many things -- band, debate, honor roll -- so missing varsity does not block all.

context: Denying the antecedent: 'If P then Q; not P; so not Q.' Varsity is ONE path to a jacket. There can be others. Closing one door does not close them all.

question: A friend says: 'If she really cared, she would have invited me. She did not invite me. So she must not care about me at all anymore.' What is wrong with the friend's reasoning?
answer: Denying the antecedent — Caring shows up in many ways -- texts, talks, time -- so one missed invite does not prove caring is gone.

context: Denying the antecedent. The invite is one sign of caring, not the only one. Plenty of caring people forget invites. The 'if-then' line only flows one way.

question: Online: 'If you trained, your time would drop. Your time did not drop. So you didn't train for the race at all.' What is the flaw in this kind of online comment?
answer: Denying the antecedent — Times stay flat for many reasons -- illness, sleep, course -- flat times do not prove no training happened.

context: Denying the antecedent. Training is one cause of faster times. Hydration, weather, and rest also matter. The flat time tells you something, but not what.

question: A classmate argues: 'If a movie is great, it wins awards. This movie did not win any awards. So it cannot really be a great movie at all.' What is the slip in this argument?
answer: Denying the antecedent — Great movies miss awards for many reasons-- bad timing, weak campaigns, snubs-- loss does not prove poor.

question: Captain: 'If you wanted to play, you'd have shown up Saturday. You missed Saturday. So you don't want to play this season for sure.' What is wrong with the captain's reasoning?
answer: Denying the antecedent — Wanting to play and showing up on one date are not the same; jobs, family, illness can block a willing kid.

context: Denying the antecedent. Attendance is evidence of wanting to play, but it is not the only proof. A missed Saturday could be illness, work, family.

question: Peer review: 'If your story is good, the teacher loves it. The teacher did not love your story. So your story must not be good.' What is the slip in this kind of peer review?
answer: Denying the antecedent — Teachers miss good stories for many reasons-- taste, mood, fatigue-- reaction by itself does not settle quality.

question: Locker room: 'If you went to the gym, you'd have sore arms today. You don't have sore arms. So you must not have gone to the gym this week.' What is wrong with this kind of reasoning?
answer: Denying the antecedent — Soreness happens for many reasons; some workouts skip arms, no soreness does not prove no gym visit.

question: Captain: 'Our drills work because they are the best. How do we know they are the best? Because they work better than any other drill any team in this league has tried.' What is the slip?

question: A fan says: 'This team is amazing because they win games. They win games because the team is amazing at the sport they play every weekend in the league.' What is the trouble here?

question: Reviewer: 'The phone is high quality because the company makes good phones. How do we know they make good phones? Because all of their phones are very high quality.' What is the slip?

question: A friend says: 'You need to pass the entrance test to make the team. I passed the test. So I am definitely on the team for sure this season already.' What is the trouble here?

question: Classmate argues: 'You need to study to get an A. I studied hard last night for the test. So I am going to get an A on it tomorrow morning for sure no matter what.' What is the slip?
answer: Studying is needed for an A but might not be enough; the test could be hard, the timing tight, or the material unfamiliar.

question: A peer says: 'You need rest to play well in a game. I got eight hours last night. So I am going to play great this Saturday morning for sure no matter who we are facing today.' Trouble?

question: Creator: 'You need a good camera to make great videos. I just bought the best camera on the market. So my next video is automatically going to be great when I post it.' What is the slip?

question: Young scientist: 'You need water to grow plants. I am watering this seed every day this week. So the seed is absolutely going to grow into a healthy plant for sure pretty soon.' What is the issue?

question: Captain: 'You need to want to win to become a champion. Our team wants it badly this year. So we are going to win the championship for sure no matter what happens this season.' Slip?

question: A peer says: 'You need an interesting topic to write a great essay. My topic is very interesting. So my essay is automatically going to be a great one no matter what I write next.' Issue?

question: Driver in training: 'You need to know road rules to get a license. I memorized the whole book last night. So I am going to pass the driving test tomorrow for sure no matter what happens.' Slip?

question: Baker: 'You need flour to bake a cake. I bought the highest quality flour at the store. So my cake is going to taste amazing once I get it out of the oven a bit later today for sure.' Trouble?

question: A friend says: 'You need to apply to a college to get in. I submitted my application last week. So I am definitely getting in when decisions come out next month at the school for sure.' Issue?

question: Scout: 'Every player on this team is a great athlete individually. So this is going to be a great team that wins lots of games together all season for sure this year for the whole league.' Trouble?
answer: Composition fallacy — Great individual athletes do not always make a great team; chemistry, role fit, and shared strategy matter just as much.

question: Online claim: 'Each ingredient in this snack is healthy on its own. So the whole snack must definitely be healthy too, and you can eat it any time of the day every day this week of school.' Issue?
answer: Composition fallacy — Healthy ingredients do not always combine into a healthy product; sugar, salt, and quantity can ruin a mix from good parts.

question: Fan: 'Every song on this album is amazing on its own. So the album as a whole has to be one of the greatest albums of all time and a top pick for the year coming up in any list.' What is the slip?
answer: Composition fallacy — Great individual songs do not always make a great album; flow, theme, and order shape how an album works as one piece.

question: Captain: 'Every drill we use is excellent on its own. So putting them all together into a full practice plan must result in an excellent overall practice each week for our players this season.' Trouble?
answer: Composition fallacy — Excellent drills can crowd each other; without pacing, recovery, and balance, the full plan can exhaust or confuse players.

question: A fan: 'Our team is the best in the league. So every single player on our team must be the best player at his position across the entire league, no matter who you ask in the league.' What is the slip?
answer: Division fallacy — a team can be the best without each player being the best at his spot; balance, depth, and chemistry can carry a roster too.

question: Online review: 'This restaurant has an amazing menu. So every single dish on the menu must also be amazing, no matter which one you happen to order during your visit to the place at any time later.' Issue?
answer: Division fallacy — a restaurant can have a great menu without every dish being a winner; the average and the specifics are not the same thing.

question: A peer: 'This is the smartest class in the whole grade. So you, as a member of this class, must be one of the smartest kids in the grade by simple logic and basic math here for sure too in any way.' Slip?
answer: Division fallacy — a class can be the smartest on average while individuals vary widely; group ranking and personal ranking are not the same.

question: Online: 'This brand makes high-quality products in general. So every single item from this brand has to be high quality, no matter which specific product line they happen to be selling at the moment now.' Issue?

question: A podcast host says, 'Studies show meditators are calmer, so YOU should meditate.' What unstated step is needed to make this argument work?
answer: That being calmer is a goal that YOU actually have or that you should have personally.

context: Studies showing X causes Y don't automatically mean YOU should do X. The hidden premise is always 'and you want Y.' This is sometimes called the 'missing major premise' move.

question: A school newspaper editorial argues, 'Phones distract students, so the school must ban them.' What hidden assumption does the 'must' rest on?

context: Identifying the harm doesn't pick the response. The argument skips from 'X is bad' to 'this exact policy fixes it.' Other fixes (storage pouches, time limits) might do the job too.

question: An ad reads: 'Top athletes use this drink, so it will improve YOUR game.' What hidden step is the ad sneaking past you?

question: A guest on a podcast claims, 'Humans evolved to eat meat, so a meat-heavy diet is healthiest.' What is the buried assumption?

context: The argument skips from descriptive ('we evolved to do X') to prescriptive ('we should do X'). The hidden bridge — that evolution aimed at our flourishing — is itself a contested claim.

question: An op-ed says, 'Our school's test scores are below average, so we need a new principal.' What unstated step lets the writer jump to that conclusion?
answer: That the principal is the actual cause of the scores — and not curriculum, staffing, or students.

That below-average scores are a sign the school has no real teachers worth keeping on staff.
context: Naming a problem isn't the same as naming a cause. The argument assumes one variable (leadership) drives the outcome — without ruling out the others. This is a hidden causal premise.

question: A documentary narrator says, 'The empire fell shortly after its currency was debased, so debasement causes empires to fall.' What is the secret claim?
answer: Post hoc — that what came AFTER something must have been caused by it, not just connected to it in time.
choices: Post hoc — that what came AFTER something must have been caused by it, not just connected to it in time.
That every empire in human history has had a currency that could be debased somehow at will.
That historians always know the exact moment any empire formally decides to fall and collapse.
That debasement is something that has never once failed to bring down any nation in any era.
context: The hidden assumption is causal: 'A preceded B, so A caused B.' Latin name: 'Post hoc ergo propter hoc.' Many empires debased without falling soon; many fell without debasement.

question: A class essay claims: 'People in country X live longer, so their healthcare system is superior.' What is the buried premise?
answer: That lifespan is driven mainly by the healthcare system rather than by all the other factors.
choices: That lifespan is driven mainly by the healthcare system rather than by all the other factors.

That superiority is something that can only be measured by simply counting the years of life.
context: Lifespan reflects diet, genetics, climate, war, traffic, and dozens of other things. The argument assumes one cause without ruling out the others. This is hidden 'single-cause' reasoning.

question: An online review states: 'The book is short, so it can't be deep.' What unstated rule is the reviewer leaning on?
answer: That depth and length are reliably connected — that more pages always means more substance.
choices: That depth and length are reliably connected — that more pages always means more substance.

context: The hidden premise — length tracks depth — is testable and often wrong. The Tao Te Ching is short. Some 800-page novels are shallow. The argument needs the premise to survive — and the premise is shaky.

question: A workplace memo says, 'Our competitor just laid off staff, so we must do the same to stay ahead.' What is the unstated claim?
answer: That copying a competitor's move will always strengthen your own position somewhere in the market.
choices: That copying a competitor's move will always strengthen your own position somewhere in the market.
That competitors always make their decisions only by following us very carefully every quarter.

context: The argument assumes herd behavior is optimal — that what one company does is automatically right for another. Different companies have different cash, talent, and problems. The hidden premise is shaky.

question: A blog post argues, 'Humans are naturally aggressive, so violence in society is acceptable.' Where is the deepest move in this argument?
answer: It jumps from a fact about how we ARE to a claim about what we OUGHT to allow in society.
choices: It jumps from a fact about how we ARE to a claim about what we OUGHT to allow in society.
It assumes every human is just as aggressive as every other human, all day, every day.
It mistakes one form of violence for the only type ever observed by anyone in any era.
It pretends humans live entirely alone and never interact with each other in any way.
context: Going from 'is' to 'ought' without an extra step is one of the oldest moves in ethics — flagged sharply by Hume in 1739. Facts about human nature don't, by themselves, settle questions of right and wrong.

question: A magazine column says, 'People naturally prefer their own family, so favoring family in hiring is morally fine.' What's the deep problem in moving from 'is' to 'is okay'?
answer: Naturalistic fallacy — Showing that something IS done widely doesn't show that it OUGHT to be done by anyone at all.
choices: Naturalistic fallacy — Showing that something IS done widely doesn't show that it OUGHT to be done by anyone at all.
Showing that people prefer family means hiring is no longer a real activity for any firm in every case that comes up.
Showing that hiring exists is the same as showing hiring is the only morally perfect activity in every case that comes up.
Showing that favoring family is common means it must therefore be banned by all law-abiding firms.
context: This is the 'is-ought' gap. Plenty of natural tendencies (revenge, in-group bias, gluttony) are widespread AND morally questionable. The bridge from 'natural' to 'right' needs its own argument.

question: A speaker argues, 'Most cultures throughout history have practiced X, so X must be morally acceptable.' What is the hidden leap?
answer: Treating widespread practice as moral evidence — but 'is' doesn't yield 'ought' by itself, ever.
choices: Treating widespread practice as moral evidence — but 'is' doesn't yield 'ought' by itself, ever.
Treating culture as if it has no influence at all on what people end up doing daily in society.
Treating history as something nobody can really study or come to know about in detail any more.
Treating moral acceptance as a thing that only modern people are allowed to discuss in classrooms.
context: Slavery, torture, and child sacrifice were each widespread across many cultures. Frequency tracks human habit, not moral truth. To get from 'is' to 'ought' you need a separate moral argument.

question: A science writer claims: 'Brain scans show people feel pleasure when they cheat, so cheating must not really be wrong.' What is the gap in this reasoning?
answer: Naturalistic fallacy — the brain showing pleasure tells us what people FEEL, not what they SHOULD or should not do.
choices: Naturalistic fallacy — the brain showing pleasure tells us what people FEEL, not what they SHOULD or should not do.
The brain scans are simply wrong, because cheating cannot really be measured by scanning in normal use.
The brain is not a place where pleasure actually happens at all, so the entire claim falls apart in normal use.
The brain produces pleasure only when people happen to be doing things that are morally correct in normal use.
context: Pleasure is a fact about feelings. Right and wrong are normative claims. A pleasant feeling during a wrong act doesn't make the act right — bullies enjoy bullying. The 'is-ought' gap stands.

question: A textbook argues, 'Animals in the wild kill weaker members of their group, so the strong are right to dominate the weak among humans.' What's the deepest fault?
answer: It treats a description of nature as if that description by itself answered a moral question about humans.
choices: It treats a description of nature as if that description by itself answered a moral question about humans.

It treats nature itself as a place where killing has never actually happened to anyone in any species.
It treats domination as the only behavior that ever takes place in any wild setting anywhere on earth.
context: This argument has been used to justify cruelty for centuries. The fact that nature contains predation doesn't tell us how humans — who can reason, plan, and choose — should treat each other.

question: An ad claims, 'This herb is 100% natural, so it's safer than any medicine.' What is wrong with the deeper logic of 'natural = safer'?
answer: Plenty of natural things — arsenic, hemlock, snake venom, certain mushrooms — are dangerous or deadly.

Natural and unnatural are words that never really apply to anything that actually exists in the world.
Medicines are also natural, so the ad's distinction does not make any sense whatsoever to a chemist.
The herb in the ad was probably made in a factory, which makes it actually unnatural in any case.
context: The 'naturalness' heuristic is widespread in advertising. But nature contains both nourishment and poison. Safety is decided by evidence about a specific substance, not by whether something is 'natural.'

question: A creator argues, 'Cancer happens naturally in the body, so chemotherapy is unnatural and therefore wrong.' What is the underlying flaw?
answer: Appeal to nature — Calling something 'unnatural' doesn't make it wrong, and calling something 'natural' doesn't make it right.
choices: Appeal to nature — Calling something 'unnatural' doesn't make it wrong, and calling something 'natural' doesn't make it right.
Cancer doesn't really happen in bodies, so the entire claim has no real meaning anywhere in medicine in normal use.
Chemotherapy was first invented by ancient people, so it is actually a fully natural treatment too in normal use.
Doctors are part of nature themselves, so anything any doctor does is automatically natural also for most people.
context: Houses, vaccines, and eyeglasses are all 'unnatural' by this standard — yet they save lives. The natural-unnatural line doesn't track moral worth or medical value. This is the appeal to nature.

question: A wellness brand says, 'Humans evolved to walk barefoot, therefore wearing shoes causes most modern foot problems.' What is the deeper issue?
answer: 'We evolved to do X' doesn't tell us X is healthier than the alternatives developed since then.
choices: 'We evolved to do X' doesn't tell us X is healthier than the alternatives developed since then.
Humans did not actually evolve from anything, so the barefoot argument is a kind of joke.
Shoes were invented well before evolution started, so they are also a fully natural human product.
Foot problems do not really exist in modern humans, so the entire claim has no factual basis at all.
context: Evolution optimized us for ancestral environments, not for modern surfaces or distances. Many evolved tendencies — sugar craving, fight-or-flight on highways — work poorly today. 'Evolved for X' isn't 'best at X.'

question: An online creator argues, 'Hunting is natural because we have meat-eating teeth, so vegetarianism is going against our nature.' What's the deeper move?
answer: It uses anatomy as if it were enough to make a moral claim about how we should eat in our era.
choices: It uses anatomy as if it were enough to make a moral claim about how we should eat in our era.
It assumes hunting and vegetarianism are the same kind of activity in every way.
It treats teeth as if they were the only part of the human body that matters for choosing a diet.
It claims that meat-eating teeth never evolved at all in any human population over recorded history.
context: We also have appendixes, wisdom teeth that don't fit, and instincts to overeat sugar. Having a body part doesn't mean using it is morally required. The deeper move is treating biology as ethics.

question: An interviewer asks a politician, 'Have you stopped accepting bribes from foreign companies?' Whichever way she answers, what has she been forced to do?
answer: Loaded question — Concede that she WAS accepting bribes at some point — the question assumes guilt before any answer.
choices: Loaded question — Concede that she WAS accepting bribes at some point — the question assumes guilt before any answer.
Concede that foreign companies even exist as a thing in the world she is currently working within.
Concede that questions about money are always considered fair to ask political figures in public.
Concede that she has been interviewed by this exact interviewer at least once in some earlier year.
context: This is the classic 'loaded question' — a question with a buried premise the answerer can't reach. 'Yes' or 'no' both confirm the smear. The honest answer is to refuse the question's frame.

question: A comment under a video reads: 'Why does the author always lie to her readers?' What is wrong with this as a question?
answer: It assumes the author always lies, and treats that assumption as if it were already a settled fact.
choices: It assumes the author always lies, and treats that assumption as if it were already a settled fact.
It assumes authors are real people, which is usually true in the modern publishing world.
It assumes readers exist at all, which is something most authors take entirely for granted always.
It assumes videos have comments, which is true on most platforms where videos are shared by users.
context: Loaded questions sneak claims past the audience. The form 'why X?' acts as if X is already proven. Anyone responding must either accept the premise or refuse to engage with the form.

question: In a debate, one side asks: 'When will you admit your plan would destroy the economy?' What buried premise is making this a TRAP?
answer: The premise that the plan WOULD destroy the economy — treated as if it were a settled and proven fact.
choices: The premise that the plan WOULD destroy the economy — treated as if it were a settled and proven fact.
The premise that economies exist in any country that bothers to have any sort of political debate.
The premise that admitting things is something that any debater is even willing to do at any time.
The premise that the debate has rules forcing the speaker to answer every question entirely fairly.
context: The question pre-judges the very thing being debated. Loaded questions in debate aren't questions — they're accusations dressed as questions. Recognizing them is the first step in not falling for them.

question: A reporter asks a CEO: 'How long have you been hiding the company's safety problems?' What does the CEO need to do first if she's innocent?
answer: Reject the question's buried premise — that safety problems exist and that she has been hiding them.
choices: Reject the question's buried premise — that safety problems exist and that she has been hiding them.
Reject the reporter as someone who should never be allowed to ask any further questions in public.
Reject the very idea that companies can ever have any problems related to worker safety at all.
Reject the press conference and walk away without saying anything at all to anyone in the room.
context: Loaded questions force the target to either accept the smear or look defensive. A good response names the loading: 'You're assuming X, which I dispute. Let me address X first.' This is rare in practice.

question: A teacher asks a student in class: 'Why don't you ever do your reading carefully?' What hidden claim makes this a loaded question?
answer: That the student NEVER reads carefully — a sweeping accusation that is tucked inside the form itself.
choices: That the student NEVER reads carefully — a sweeping accusation that is tucked inside the form itself.
That reading is something that all students should do entirely at home rather than during class.
That the teacher has the right to know about all reading habits of every single student personally.
That carefully done reading is the only kind of reading that helps anyone learn anything important.
context: The form 'why don't you X?' acts as if 'not X' is established. A student answering 'I don't know' has just agreed. The fair version is: 'Are you having trouble reading carefully? If so, can we talk?'

question: An ad reads: 'Are you tired of being lied to by other car dealers?' What's the rhetorical trap baked into this question?
answer: It assumes other dealers HAVE been lying to you, without any evidence, in order to position itself as honest.
choices: It assumes other dealers HAVE been lying to you, without any evidence, in order to position itself as honest.
It assumes that you are tired right now, which is something only the actual customers themselves can know.
It assumes that cars exist in the modern world, which is a very safe assumption for any reader of an ad.
It assumes that ads are things that readers actually look at and pay close attention to in their lives.
context: Loaded questions in advertising create a frame: 'Others bad, we good.' Even if you've never been lied to, the question plants the idea. This is sometimes called 'preloading' the audience's beliefs.

question: A friend insists everyone in his class who shoplifts deserves expulsion, but when HIS little brother is caught, he says 'This case is different.' Without giving a principled reason, what is he doing?
answer: Special pleading — demanding an exception for his case without a principled reason that applies to others.
choices: Special pleading — demanding an exception for his case without a principled reason that applies to others.
Logical reasoning — applying the rule fairly and consistently across all the possible cases involved.
A category error — treating shoplifting as if it were something other than what it really and truly is.
A genetic fallacy — judging the action by who is doing it rather than by the actual nature of the act.
context: Special pleading is the move of asking for an exception without a principled reason. If you can't say what makes THIS case different in a way that applies generally, you're just protecting your team.

question: A pundit says every politician who takes money from corporations is corrupt — except the ones on her side, who 'have integrity that resists influence.' What's the fault in this claim?
answer: Special pleading — She invents a special category for her side without showing any principled difference that could be tested.
choices: Special pleading — She invents a special category for her side without showing any principled difference that could be tested.
She invents a category called integrity, which is actually something that does not really exist anywhere.
She invents a problem with corporations, which usually behave well and are very fair in all their dealings.
She invents the idea of taking money, which is something no politician has ever actually done in office.
context: Special pleading lets people apply rules to enemies while exempting allies. The question to ask: 'What testable property distinguishes the exempt cases?' If there isn't one, the exemption is unprincipled.

question: A blogger argues that one should never trust a study funded by industry — except for this one study funded by industry that supports his view. What is happening?
answer: Special pleading — keeping the general rule, but quietly making an exception for the study that supports him.
choices: Special pleading — keeping the general rule, but quietly making an exception for the study that supports him.
Methodological caution — examining each individual study on its actual merits before deciding to trust it.
Bayesian updating — adjusting his belief levels based on the strength of the new evidence as it appears.
Common sense — ignoring studies that come from sources that nobody trusts in modern scientific practice.
context: Skepticism applied to opponents but not to allies isn't skepticism — it's tribalism. If industry funding undermines a study in one case, it undermines it in the other. Consistency is the test.

question: A speaker says all psychics should be banned because they prey on people — except her sister, whose readings 'are different because she really cares.' What's wrong?
answer: Special pleading — Caring doesn't show the readings are accurate — the exception isn't justified by any principled reason given.
choices: Special pleading — Caring doesn't show the readings are accurate — the exception isn't justified by any principled reason given.
Caring is the only thing that has ever mattered in any kind of professional reading work in any culture in normal use.
Caring is something that all psychics share equally well, so the sister isn't really any different at all in normal use.
Caring is impossible to measure scientifically, so the sister's case cannot be fairly examined by anyone in normal use.
context: Special pleading often hides under appeals to character or intention. The original objection (psychics make claims they can't back up) applies to caring psychics too. The exemption isn't principled.

question: A coach insists that no excuse is acceptable for missing practice — but when his star player misses, he explains it as 'a unique family situation.' What move is this?
answer: Special pleading — protecting a favored case by inventing a category that conveniently only fits that case.
choices: Special pleading — protecting a favored case by inventing a category that conveniently only fits that case.
Pragmatic reasoning — adjusting team rules based on the talent levels of the player being judged that day.
Genetic fallacy — judging the player by his family background rather than by his actions on the practice field.
False analogy — treating practice attendance as if it were comparable to family situations in any sensible way.
context: If 'family situations' excuse the star, they have to excuse the bench-warmer too. Otherwise the 'no excuses' rule was never a rule — it was a way to discipline people the coach didn't favor.

question: A commentator says every law that limits free speech is tyranny — except the one she supports, which 'protects vulnerable groups, so it doesn't count.' What's the failure?
answer: Special pleading — She redefines her preferred exception out of the category instead of giving a principled reason for the exemption.
choices: Special pleading — She redefines her preferred exception out of the category instead of giving a principled reason for the exemption.
She defends her preferred exception by naming a vulnerable group that the law is officially supposed to protect.
She uses the strong word tyranny instead of just calling the other bad laws unfair, which is the very same thing.
She trusts only herself to know which speech limits are good and which are bad tyranny in our modern context.
context: Redefinition is the favorite trick of special pleading. If 'limiting speech' is tyranny in case A but not case B, the speaker owes a non-circular criterion. 'It's for a good cause' won't work — that's what everyone says.

question: A speaker says, 'No one has ever proven that ghosts don't exist, so ghosts must be real.' What's wrong with this line of thinking?
answer: Argument from ignorance — Not proving something false isn't the same as proving it true — absence of disproof isn't proof of anything.
choices: Argument from ignorance — Not proving something false isn't the same as proving it true — absence of disproof isn't proof of anything.
Ghosts have been proven not to exist many, many times in lab studies, so the speaker just doesn't know that yet in normal use.
Existence claims about ghosts cannot really be made one way or the other, in any era, in any way at all for most people.
Proving things is something impossible to do in modern science, so this kind of argument is always invalid here in normal use.
context: This is 'argument from ignorance' (ad ignorantiam). The burden of proof is on the claim-maker, not the doubter. Failing to disprove a claim leaves it where it started — unsupported.

question: A teen says, 'You can't prove I cheated on the test, so I didn't cheat.' Where is the reasoning faulty?
answer: Lack of proof of cheating doesn't establish innocence — it only shows that proof has not yet been found.
choices: Lack of proof of cheating doesn't establish innocence — it only shows that proof has not yet been found.
Lack of proof of cheating actually proves that the test was not really fair to the students taking it at all.
Lack of proof of cheating means the teacher should have written a much easier test for the whole class.
Lack of proof of cheating means that cheating itself doesn't really exist as a concept in modern schools.
context: The court standard 'innocent until proven guilty' is a legal rule about how to act under uncertainty — not a claim that lack of proof equals actual innocence. The two are easy to confuse.

question: A podcast host claims, 'Scientists haven't explained consciousness, so it must be supernatural.' What is the logical mistake?
answer: An unexplained thing is just unexplained — the gap by itself is not evidence FOR any one specific theory.
choices: An unexplained thing is just unexplained — the gap by itself is not evidence FOR any one specific theory.
An unexplained thing is automatically supernatural by definition, so the host is just being completely honest.
An unexplained thing has actually been explained already by many scientists who have studied it for years.
An unexplained thing means the scientists are not really doing their jobs properly at the moment at all.
context: Filling a knowledge gap with your preferred explanation is sometimes called the 'God of the gaps' move — but it works for any pet theory. 'We don't know X' supports 'we don't know X,' nothing more.

question: An online forum argues, 'Nobody has ever caught aliens, so aliens visit Earth secretly all the time.' What is the deep flaw?
answer: Lack of evidence of visits is being used to support a theory of secret visits — and that is exactly backwards.
choices: Lack of evidence of visits is being used to support a theory of secret visits — and that is exactly backwards.
Aliens have been caught by various governments, but the forum participants don't know about that fact at all.
Aliens do not exist anywhere in the universe, so the entire conversation on this forum is a waste of time.
Forums online cannot really discuss aliens because no one writing on them is an expert in the relevant field.
context: Lack of evidence is normally evidence AGAINST a claim, not for it. The forum is inverting the rule. This is sometimes called the 'argument from silence' when it concerns historical records.

question: A creator says, 'Doctors can't explain why my treatment works, so it must be working through energy fields they don't understand yet.' What's wrong with this reasoning?
answer: Doctor confusion about a result doesn't support any one specific alternative theory — it just leaves the question open.
choices: Doctor confusion about a result doesn't support any one specific alternative theory — it just leaves the question open.
Doctor confusion is impossible because all doctors everywhere agree on what energy fields exist and operate for the most part.
Doctor confusion is a clear sign that all of medicine is wrong about every illness in every patient ever for the most part.
Doctor confusion means the creator simply should have gotten the treatment from a more competent doctor.
context: There are usually many possible explanations for why a treatment seems to work — placebo, regression to the mean, confounders, observer bias. Picking 'energy fields' over these is filling a gap with imagination.

question: A book argues, 'Historians haven't found a record of Person X, so Person X never existed.' What's the gap in this logic?
answer: Absence of evidence and evidence of absence aren't the same — many old records have been lost over time.
choices: Absence of evidence and evidence of absence aren't the same — many old records have been lost over time.
Person X did not exist because no historian has ever existed who could properly record any individual.
Records of all people in all times are always perfectly preserved by careful historians in modern archives.
Historians don't really study individual people much anyway, so the absence of records is fully meaningless.
context: For ancient periods, the survival rate of documents is tiny. We have no records of most ordinary people who lived. Concluding non-existence from missing records works only when records SHOULD have survived.

question: An online creator says, 'No mainstream paper has ever published my theory, so the establishment must be afraid of it.' What's the fallacy?
answer: Lack of publication is being treated as evidence FOR the theory rather than as a probable sign against the theory.
choices: Lack of publication is being treated as evidence FOR the theory rather than as a probable sign against the theory.
Lack of publication proves that mainstream papers are biased against new ideas in general, no matter what.
Lack of publication is impossible to verify because mainstream papers are not really tracked by anyone.
Lack of publication means the creator's theory must be brand new and has never been seriously considered.
context: The simpler explanation — that the theory hasn't survived peer review because it doesn't hold up — is rarely considered. Treating rejection as proof of suppression is a hallmark of pseudoscience self-defense.

question: A debate club member argues, 'You couldn't show that my plan would fail, so my plan would work.' Where is the reasoning faulty?
answer: Failing to disprove a plan doesn't show the plan would succeed — it only leaves the case for the plan unmade.
choices: Failing to disprove a plan doesn't show the plan would succeed — it only leaves the case for the plan unmade.
Failing to disprove a plan basically proves the plan is the very best plan that has ever been proposed yet.
Failing to disprove a plan means the opponent didn't really try to disprove it carefully or fairly enough.
Failing to disprove a plan means all plans should be accepted unless proven false ahead of any real testing.
context: Burden of proof sits with the person making the positive claim. 'My plan will work' needs to be supported by reasons FOR it — not by the opponent's failure to demolish it. The default position is doubt.

question: A news article reads: 'Cities with more libraries have higher college graduation rates, so libraries cause people to graduate.' What might be going on instead?
answer: Wealthier cities tend to have BOTH more libraries AND more graduates — wealth is the actual driver of both.
choices: Wealthier cities tend to have BOTH more libraries AND more graduates — wealth is the actual driver of both.
Libraries are not really associated with graduation, so the reported correlation is a fake one.
Libraries cause college graduation only on days when current students actually visit them on a regular basis.
Libraries somehow make people smarter just by being nearby, even if those students never go inside any one of them.
context: Correlation between A and B can have several causes: A causes B, B causes A, both come from C, or pure coincidence. Confusing correlation with causation is one of the most common errors in popular science.

question: An ad claims that people who eat their cereal lose more weight than non-eaters. What is the simplest competing explanation that the ad ignores?
answer: Cereal eaters are people who care about their overall health, and that wider habit is what drives the weight loss.
choices: Cereal eaters are people who care about their overall health, and that wider habit is what drives the weight loss.
Cereal eaters are all the same person who happened to lose weight for completely unrelated reasons in the past.
Cereal eaters do not actually exist because all cereal in the world is consumed at restaurants instead of homes.
Cereal eaters lose more weight only on days when they also happen to consume large quantities of plain water.
context: Self-selection bias is everywhere in food research. People who eat any 'healthy' product tend to do other healthy things too. Disentangling the product's effect from the lifestyle's effect requires careful study.

question: A study notes that countries with more chocolate consumption per person have more Nobel Prize winners per person. What's the most likely real explanation?
answer: Both correlate with national wealth — rich countries can afford both chocolate and elite scientific institutions.
choices: Both correlate with national wealth — rich countries can afford both chocolate and elite scientific institutions.
Chocolate makes people smarter directly, which obviously improves their Nobel chances by quite a lot.
Nobel Prize winners are required to eat plenty of chocolate as part of their formal award acceptance.
Countries with chocolate factories produce Nobel winners as a kind of side product of their industry for the most part.
context: This is an actual published correlation that got popular press in 2012. The chocolate-IQ link is a textbook case of a 'lurking variable' — both metrics are downstream of GDP per capita.

question: A documentary says, 'Children who eat breakfast score higher on tests, so breakfast improves test scores.' What competing explanation should the viewer consider?
answer: Children with stable home lives tend to BOTH get breakfast AND do better on tests for several different reasons.
choices: Children with stable home lives tend to BOTH get breakfast AND do better on tests for several different reasons.
Children who eat breakfast do not really exist in the first place because all children always skip breakfast.
Children who score higher on tests are basically forced by all their teachers to eat breakfast every morning.
Children who eat breakfast cause the tests they take to magically become easier through some unknown method.
context: Many breakfast-and-grades studies fail to control for socioeconomic status. A kid with a calm morning routine has more than just food going for her. The 'eat breakfast' policy advice rests on shaky causal ground.

question: A study finds people who carry umbrellas have more rainy days. What's the actual direction of the cause?
answer: Rain causes people to carry umbrellas — not the other way around, as a quick or careless reading might suggest.
choices: Rain causes people to carry umbrellas — not the other way around, as a quick or careless reading might suggest.
Umbrellas somehow cause rain by a hidden mechanism that meteorologists have never been able to figure out yet.
Umbrellas and rain are not really related at all, so the correlation in this study is just a coincidence really.
Umbrellas are usually owned by people who happen to live in cities with lots of rainy weather across the year.
context: 'Reverse causation' is the error of getting the arrow backwards. The umbrella case is obvious because we KNOW rain comes first. In other cases (does happiness cause success, or success cause happiness?), it's harder.

question: A tabloid headline reads: 'Diet soda drinkers have more health problems, so diet soda must cause illness.' What's the most likely confounder being missed?
answer: People with health problems often switch TO diet soda — the illness usually comes first, not after the soda choice.
choices: People with health problems often switch TO diet soda — the illness usually comes first, not after the soda choice.
Diet soda drinkers are usually elite athletes who train extremely hard every single day of the entire year.
Diet soda drinkers do not really have any health problems at all when carefully examined in real medical studies.
Diet soda drinkers are forced by their doctors to drink diet soda only after they get sick from other causes.
context: This is reverse causation in disguise. People diagnosed with diabetes often switch from regular to diet soda. The diet soda then 'predicts' diabetes — but actually FOLLOWED it. Direction matters.

question: A book claims: 'Everyone in this town is friends with someone famous.' What are the two different things this could mean?
answer: Either each person has SOME famous friend (perhaps different), or there is ONE famous person whom everyone knows.
choices: Either each person has SOME famous friend (perhaps different), or there is ONE famous person whom everyone knows.
Either the town has famous people, or the book is wrong about whether anyone is friends with anyone there.
Either the people are friends with famous celebrities, or the townspeople are themselves all famous celebrities.
Either the town is small enough to have just one resident, or the town has many famous residents inside its limits.
context: Quantifier scope ambiguity is the source of many real-world misunderstandings. The reading 'each has some famous friend' and 'one famous person known to all' are very different claims with very different evidence.

question: A motivational speaker says, 'There is something everyone is afraid of.' How could a careful listener spot the ambiguity?
answer: It could mean each person has SOMETHING they fear, or it could mean ONE thing scares every person on earth alike.
choices: It could mean each person has SOMETHING they fear, or it could mean ONE thing scares every person on earth alike.
It could mean the speaker is just afraid of his own audience, who are clearly scaring him a lot.
It could mean the speaker has not really thought about what he is saying very carefully ahead of time.
It could mean that fear is something that actually exists outside of people and waits to scare them daily.
context: The difference is huge. 'Each has some fear' is uncontroversial. 'One fear common to all humans' is a strong claim that would need evidence. Spotting which reading is intended is an act of careful listening.

question: A scientist says, 'Every problem has a solution.' What two completely different things might she mean?
answer: Either each problem has SOME solution (perhaps a different one), or ONE solution can solve every problem (unlikely).
choices: Either each problem has SOME solution (perhaps a different one), or ONE solution can solve every problem (unlikely).
Either she means solutions are very easy to find quickly, or she means solutions are usually impossible to find.
Either she is talking about science problems specifically, or she is talking about life problems generally as well.
Either she has solved every problem herself by now, or she has not solved any problems that she has encountered.
context: Math has the same ambiguity. 'For every x, there is some y such that...' versus 'There is some y such that for every x...' is the difference between an obvious truth and a usually-false claim.

question: A teacher tells the class: 'Some assignment was completed by every student.' Two students argue what this means. Who is right?
answer: Both readings are possible — either each student did SOME assignment, or one particular assignment was done by all.
choices: Both readings are possible — either each student did SOME assignment, or one particular assignment was done by all.
The teacher meant only one of the readings, but listeners cannot easily figure out which one from the sentence.
The teacher is incorrect because no assignment is ever truly completed by every student in any class anywhere.
The teacher meant that every assignment was completed by some student, which is in fact a separate claim entirely.
context: Natural language is genuinely ambiguous on quantifiers. Formal logic uses notation (∀, ∃) to remove the ambiguity. When stakes are high (legal contracts, scientific claims), this ambiguity causes real disputes.

question: A senator says, 'I will vote yes on every bill that some constituent supports.' What's the careful reader's question?
answer: Does 'some' mean 'at least one constituent' (a very low bar) or 'a substantial group of them' (a much higher bar)?
choices: Does 'some' mean 'at least one constituent' (a very low bar) or 'a substantial group of them' (a much higher bar)?
Does 'every' mean every bill or only the bills that the senator personally finds politically appealing to her of course?
Does 'yes' mean an actual yes vote or just a vote of support without any actual recorded vote being cast?
Does 'constituent' refer only to people in the senator's state or to all people in the entire country also of course?
context: 'Some' in everyday English is famously slippery. A senator who says she'll vote for any bill 'some constituent' supports has either committed to almost every bill, or — by reinterpreting later — almost none.

question: A friend cites a famous physicist's views on dieting as proof of what to eat. When is appealing to authority a PROBLEM?
answer: When the cited authority is being relied on OUTSIDE their actual area of training and direct expertise.
choices: When the cited authority is being relied on OUTSIDE their actual area of training and direct expertise.
When the authority is still alive and could potentially answer questions from those who disagree.
