When the authority has written more than three books published by any kind of publisher anywhere worldwide.
When the authority is famous enough that most members of the general public have at least heard of them.
context: Citing a physicist on physics is reasonable; citing the same physicist on diet is a misuse. The rule is: 'Expertise is domain-specific.' This is sometimes called the 'misplaced authority' fallacy.

question: An article cites a Nobel laureate's view on a topic FAR outside her field. Why doesn't her Nobel prize make her opinion strong in that area?
answer: Expertise in one specialized field doesn't transfer to topics that require very different training and evidence.
choices: Expertise in one specialized field doesn't transfer to topics that require very different training and evidence.
Expertise is not really something any human being can ever fully achieve in a normal lifetime.
Expertise is a word that has no real meaning at all in any modern academic or scientific discussion.
Expertise outside one's actual field is actually MORE valuable because of its fresh and outside perspectives.
context: Linus Pauling won two Nobel prizes (chemistry, peace) — and was confidently wrong about vitamin C and cancer for decades. Famous people are still amateurs outside their expertise. Citing them mixes credentials and competence.

question: When IS citing an authority a reasonable form of argument? Consider what makes some appeals legitimate.
answer: Appeal to authority — When the cited person actually works in the field, agrees with mainstream experts, and shares their typical findings.
choices: Appeal to authority — When the cited person actually works in the field, agrees with mainstream experts, and shares their typical findings.
When the cited person is famous enough to be widely recognized by most members of the general public on sight in normal use in normal use.
When the cited person has stated their opinion many times in many different kinds of public settings already for most people.
When the cited person is being quoted accurately in a popular magazine that has many readers and subscribers for most people.
context: Appeal to authority is informal logic's nuance case: it's not always a fallacy. We rely on doctors, pilots, and engineers. The misuse is when expertise is misplaced or when one outlier expert is preferred over consensus.

question: A documentary cites ONE scientist who disagrees with the consensus in his field. When does picking the outlier mislead the audience?
answer: Cherry picking — When most experts in the field disagree with him but the film hides that and presents the outlier as the authority.
choices: Cherry picking — When most experts in the field disagree with him but the film hides that and presents the outlier as the authority.
When the outlier has not yet published their work in any recognized peer-reviewed scientific journals anywhere yet.
When the outlier is older than most of the other scientists working in the same field by several full decades.
When the outlier holds a position at a university that is not in the top ten most famous schools in the world.
context: Cherry-picking experts is how science denial dresses itself up. There's almost always SOME credentialed dissenter on any topic. The deception is in implying the outlier represents the field rather than a fringe.

question: A class essay quotes a popular celebrity on a difficult scientific subject. What is the writer's mistake?
answer: Confusing fame and recognition with the kind of specialized training that gives someone real authority on the subject.
choices: Confusing fame and recognition with the kind of specialized training that gives someone real authority on the subject.
Confusing famous people with non-famous people, which is something that hardly ever happens in any actual writing.
Confusing scientific subjects with subjects that are much easier and that require no special training to handle.
Confusing one celebrity with another celebrity who actually has scientific training and proper academic credentials.
context: Celebrities have platform but rarely have expertise on the topics they discuss. The 'celebrity authority' move treats visibility as evidence of competence. The two are very different things — fame is not knowledge.

question: A study on the health effects of soda is funded entirely by a soda company. What is a reasonable thing for a reader to notice?
answer: The funding doesn't disprove the study by itself, but it does raise real questions about study design and reporting.
choices: The funding doesn't disprove the study by itself, but it does raise real questions about study design and reporting.
The funding makes the study automatically true and trustworthy because companies pay only for accurate research.
The funding has no effect at all on what the study eventually finds because researchers are always perfectly fair.
The funding makes the study automatically false and entirely worthless to consider for any reader anywhere ever.
context: Industry funding is correlated with industry-favorable findings — a well-documented bias. The right response is heightened scrutiny: how were studies designed, were unfavorable findings published, were endpoints chosen carefully?

question: A pundit who profits from a TV show about UFOs argues that UFOs are real and important. What should a careful listener notice?
answer: Conflict of interest — the pundit's livelihood depends on UFOs being interesting, and that gives him a motive to overstate the evidence somewhat.
choices: Conflict of interest — the pundit's livelihood depends on UFOs being interesting, and that gives him a motive to overstate the evidence somewhat.
The pundit must be lying about everything because no one ever tells the truth about their own field of work or expertise in normal use.
The pundit is probably wrong because UFOs are something that nobody has ever spent any time studying carefully at all in normal use.
The pundit cannot be trusted at all because TV shows are not real sources of any kind of information for anybody in everyday life.
context: Conflict of interest doesn't prove someone wrong — but it's evidence about which way they're MOTIVATED to err. The honest move is to seek confirmation from sources with no financial stake in the answer.

question: A doctor recommends a treatment in which she invented and holds the patent for. What is the right reaction?
answer: Take her claim seriously, but also check it against doctors who DON'T have any financial stake in the answer.
choices: Take her claim seriously, but also check it against doctors who DON'T have any financial stake in the answer.
Reject her claim outright, because all doctors who hold patents end up dishonest about their treatments.
Accept her claim outright, because all medical doctors are equally trustworthy regardless of any other factors.
Ignore the patent entirely, because patents do not really tell us anything important about a doctor's honesty here.
context: Patents create incentive misalignment. The doctor may genuinely believe in her treatment AND be motivated to overstate its benefits. Independent verification is the cure for both honest bias and dishonest spin.

question: A creator tells viewers that a stock she owns is going to skyrocket. What kind of bias is in play?
answer: She personally profits if viewers buy and the stock rises, so she has a clear motive to overstate her certainty here.
choices: She personally profits if viewers buy and the stock rises, so she has a clear motive to overstate her certainty here.
She must be wrong about this stock because stocks never go up at all after creators say they will on social media.
She must be right about this stock because creators have access to financial information that most people do not have.
She has no real bias because creators always disclose every position that they hold in every public discussion ever.
context: 'Pump and dump' schemes use social media exactly this way. Even when the creator believes her own pitch, the financial stake creates motivated reasoning. Disclosure helps, but skepticism is the real shield.

question: A politician's family member runs a contractor company. He votes to give that company a large contract. Why is this concerning?
answer: His vote could be honest, but the financial benefit to his family creates a clear bias the public has no way to verify.
choices: His vote could be honest, but the financial benefit to his family creates a clear bias the public has no way to verify.
His vote is automatically corrupt because politicians never make any honest decisions in public office anymore.
His vote is automatically clean because politicians always fully disclose every conflict of interest publicly.
His vote is not really concerning because contractors are usually the best and most ethical people for public work.
context: Conflicts of interest are mostly judged by APPEARANCE rather than by proof — because proof is hard. The point of disclosure rules is to let the public weigh the bias risk, not to settle whether the act was corrupt.

question: A campaign ad shows three studies supporting its claim and never mentions the seven that contradict it. What is this rhetorical move called?
answer: Cherry picking — Cherry-picking — choosing only the evidence that fits the desired conclusion while ignoring the contrary evidence.
choices: Cherry picking — Cherry-picking — choosing only the evidence that fits the desired conclusion while ignoring the contrary evidence.
Strategic emphasis, which is generally seen as a normal honest way of presenting research data to most audiences.
Logical induction, which is the standard way that scientific evidence draws conclusions from large sets of studies.
Confirmation testing, which is the rigorous scientific method used to verify published claims by careful researchers.
context: Cherry-picking is a form of selection bias — but a deliberate one. Honest claims survey ALL the evidence, including contradicting studies, and explain why the overall picture leans one way.

question: A headline reads: '9 OUT OF 10 doctors recommend.' What missing information would change how you read this?
answer: How many doctors were actually asked, how those doctors were chosen, and whether the 10th doctor was simply ignored.
choices: How many doctors were actually asked, how those doctors were chosen, and whether the 10th doctor was simply ignored.
How many advertisements have used this exact same line of argument in any past advertising campaign anywhere before.
How many people have actually read the headline carefully before deciding whether to buy the product on offer.
How many doctors there exist in the country that has the advertised product on sale at the moment of the ad.
context: Statistical claims need DENOMINATORS and METHOD. '9 of 10' could mean 9 of 10 hand-picked friends or 9 of 10 randomly sampled doctors. The headline is meaningless until you know which.

question: A salesperson says, 'This couch was $3000, now only $1500.' Even if the original price was a fiction, why does the $3000 still influence what you'll pay?
answer: Anchor bias — the first number you happen to see shapes your sense of what a reasonable price for the item feels like.
choices: Anchor bias — the first number you happen to see shapes your sense of what a reasonable price for the item feels like.
Anchor bias — but only people who are very bad at math or have never bought any furniture before are actually affected.
Sales psychology, which actually works because every shopper carefully checks every price against the original list amount.
Memory effects, which happen because people always remember the first thing they hear about any product they buy.
context: Anchoring is one of the most robust findings in decision research. Even random, irrelevant numbers can shift estimates. The high 'original' price isn't there to inform — it's there to make $1500 feel reasonable.

question: An article reports: 'Crime rose 50% this year.' That sounds alarming. What context turns this into a less scary number?
answer: If crime went from 2 incidents to 3 in a tiny town, the percentage is technically real but tells you nothing important.
choices: If crime went from 2 incidents to 3 in a tiny town, the percentage is technically real but tells you nothing important.
If crime never really rose at all in that area, the article is just lying outright to its readers right.
If crime is impossible for the article to measure with any kind of real accuracy, the reported number is mere guesswork.
If crime statistics are kept by the local government in question, then the public has no real way of checking them anyway.
context: Percentage changes without BASE RATES are deceptive. 'Up 50%!' could mean 100 to 150 or 2 to 3. News stories often choose the framing that maximizes emotional impact — the careful reader asks for the absolute numbers.

question: An online creator says, 'My method has helped THOUSANDS of people.' What context completely changes this claim?
answer: Whether THOUSANDS more people weren't helped at all, and whether 'helped' was even tracked by anyone besides the creator.
choices: Whether THOUSANDS more people weren't helped at all, and whether 'helped' was even tracked by anyone besides the creator.
Whether the creator is famous enough on the internet to be widely recognized by the general public on social media platforms.
Whether the creator has thousands of followers on her social media accounts, which is something fairly easy to verify online.
Whether the creator's method is one that has been around for a great many years already without ever changing at all.
context: Anecdote at scale is still anecdote. A method that helps 1,000 and fails 10,000 has 'thousands of success stories.' Without a denominator and a definition of 'help,' the claim is unfalsifiable.

question: A magazine writes that a celebrity 'might be involved in a scandal.' What is the rhetorical trick in this kind of hedged claim?
answer: It plants the suggestion of guilt while keeping plausible deniability — the careful reader does the smearing for them quietly.
choices: It plants the suggestion of guilt while keeping plausible deniability — the careful reader does the smearing for them quietly.
It is a perfectly honest way to describe a situation that has not yet been fully investigated by anyone in the news media.
It is a kind of lazy form of writing that all magazine editors use just to fill the empty space in their own publications.
It is a strong sign that the magazine has not really discovered any actual information about the celebrity in question yet.
context: 'Might be' clauses let writers imply without committing. Tabloid headlines lean on this hard. The trick works because readers tend to remember the IMAGE (scandal) and forget the HEDGE (might).

question: Two different errors get confused: the 'naturalistic fallacy' and the 'appeal to nature.' What is the difference at root?
answer: Appeal to nature — Naturalistic is about ethics (jumping from 'is' to 'ought'); nature-appeal is about value (calling natural things good).
choices: Appeal to nature — Naturalistic is about ethics (jumping from 'is' to 'ought'); nature-appeal is about value (calling natural things good).
Naturalistic is something only philosophers worry about, while the nature-appeal is reserved for ordinary people only.
Naturalistic is an old term that almost nobody uses anymore, and the nature-appeal is brand new in modern philosophy too.
Naturalistic refers to wild animals in nature, while the nature-appeal is mainly about plants and other growing things only.
context: Coined by Moore in 1903, the 'naturalistic fallacy' is about defining 'good' in natural terms. The 'appeal to nature' is the marketer's slogan that natural products are better. Both errors, different shapes — easy to mix up.

question: Someone says aspirin is from willow bark and therefore 'natural.' Another person says we should follow our gut instincts because they 'evolved.' Which is which kind of error?
answer: Appeal to nature — the first is appeal to nature (origin equals good); the second is naturalistic-style (what evolved is what is right).
choices: Appeal to nature — the first is appeal to nature (origin equals good); the second is naturalistic-style (what evolved is what is right).
Both arguments are exactly the same kind of logical error and use exactly the same reasoning entirely in every case that comes up.
Neither argument is an error at all because both of them happen to follow the standard rules of formal logic we use.
The first is a basic logical error, while the second is just standard common-sense reasoning that most everyday people use.
context: The aspirin case is about the ORIGIN of a product being treated as a virtue. The instinct case is about a fact (we evolved it) being treated as a normative claim (we should follow it). Different errors, both common.

question: Saying 'this poison is natural, so it's healthy' is one kind of mistake. Saying 'humans naturally fight, so violence must be moral' is another. What's the second error doing?
answer: Appeal to nature — Sliding from a descriptive claim about how people behave to a normative claim about whether that behavior is right.
choices: Appeal to nature — Sliding from a descriptive claim about how people behave to a normative claim about whether that behavior is right.
Sliding between two factual claims about violence that genuinely have no logical connection to one another in every case that comes up.
Sliding into a description nearly nobody uses, so this kind of argument is not actually a real problem in every case that comes up.
Sliding into a basic misunderstanding of the word natural, which only happens with people who happen to dislike philosophy.
context: The first ('natural = healthy') is straightforward appeal to nature. The second ('we fight naturally, so fighting is moral') is the deeper 'is-ought' error. Mixing them up means missing exactly where the argument breaks.

question: A nutrition blog says, 'Wheat is natural, so eating bread is healthy.' A philosopher says, 'Survival is natural, so survival is morally required.' What's the structural difference?
answer: The first treats origin as evidence of health; the second treats descriptive nature as a binding moral command.
choices: The first treats origin as evidence of health; the second treats descriptive nature as a binding moral command.
The first is about food and the second is about ethics, but otherwise the two are exactly the same mistake.
The first is a small mistake while the second is a much bigger mistake, though they are basically the same kind of error.
The first uses the word natural and the second does not use it at all, so only the first one is really an error in formal logic.
context: Knowing the difference matters. The nutrition argument fails on FACTS (wheat is sometimes not healthy). The survival argument fails on STRUCTURE (you can't get an ought from an is without a moral premise).

question: A magazine writes that 'monogamy is natural for humans' to argue that other arrangements are wrong. Where are the TWO errors stacked here?
answer: First, a contested factual claim about what is 'natural'. Second, the leap that 'natural' settles what is morally right at all.
choices: First, a contested factual claim about what is 'natural'. Second, the leap that 'natural' settles what is morally right at all.
First, a logical claim about monogamy. Second, a purely emotional appeal aimed at non-philosophers in the audience.
First, an honest factual description of behavior. Second, a fair conclusion that follows directly from the factual description above.
First, a factual claim about humans. Second, another factual claim that is not at all connected to morality in any clear or careful way.
context: This is a common stack: the empirical claim is contested (humans show mixed patterns), AND the move from 'natural' to 'right' fails. Spotting BOTH errors is the mark of advanced argument analysis.

question: An op-ed argues 'All rich people are thieves.' Pressed, the writer says 'I just mean wealth is sometimes unjust.' Asked about policy, she returns to 'thieves.' What move is this?
answer: Motte and bailey -- the bold claim is advanced; a modest version is the bunker when challenged.
choices: Motte and bailey -- the bold claim is advanced; a modest version is the bunker when challenged.
Begging the question -- the conclusion is hidden in the premise of the original op-ed argument.
Slippery slope -- one mild concession will end up sliding to a much more aggressive position.
Equivocation -- the word 'thieves' is used in two different senses across the same argument.
context: Nicholas Shackel named the move (2005). The 'bailey' (aggressive, attractive claim) is what the writer really wants; the 'motte' (safe, defensible claim) is where she hides under fire. Counter-move: force the writer to pick one and stay there.

question: A podcaster says 'Science is just a social construct.' Pushed, he clarifies 'I mean scientists are humans with biases.' Later he is back to 'just a construct.' Spot the move.
answer: Motte and bailey -- modest claim shields the radical one; the radical one returns once cover is up.
choices: Motte and bailey -- modest claim shields the radical one; the radical one returns once cover is up.
Strawman -- the podcaster is misrepresenting what his critics actually believe about science.
Ad hominem -- attacking scientists personally rather than addressing their methods or claims.
Genetic fallacy -- judging a body of science by its social origins rather than by its content.
context: The motte ('scientists have biases') is uncontroversial; the bailey ('science is JUST a construct') is the radical thesis. Sliding between them lets the speaker claim both safety and bite.

question: A columnist writes that capitalism is inherently violent. Challenged, she narrows to 'all economic systems involve coercion.' In her next piece, she is back to 'inherently violent.' Name the maneuver.
answer: Motte and bailey -- the strong thesis is the goal; the weak retreat is the shield when challenged.
choices: Motte and bailey -- the strong thesis is the goal; the weak retreat is the shield when challenged.
False dilemma -- the columnist forces a choice between accepting her view or being a defender.
Composition fallacy -- properties of parts of the system are projected onto the whole of it.
Hasty generalization -- one or two cases of coercion are made to stand in for the whole system.
context: The structural test: does the writer treat the modest and aggressive versions as the same claim? If she retreats only under fire and advances when unopposed, the bailey is what she really wants.

question: An academic asserts 'mathematics is patriarchal.' In response to a critic, he says he just means 'fewer women have published in pure math historically.' Then he repeats the original. What pattern fits?
answer: Motte and bailey -- a historical observation becomes a shield for a sweeping cultural verdict.
choices: Motte and bailey -- a historical observation becomes a shield for a sweeping cultural verdict.
Appeal to authority -- the academic relies on credentials rather than offering any actual argument.
Red herring -- the historical observation is irrelevant to the question of math's true nature.
Tu quoque -- accusing the critic of the same bias he is leveling against the field of mathematics.
context: The aggressive thesis ('math itself is patriarchal') is what stings; the modest retreat ('fewer women published') is what defends. Most readers absorb the punch and forget the qualifier was ever offered.

question: A celebrity tweets 'religion poisons everything.' When pushed, he replies 'I just mean some religious institutions have done harm.' His next podcast is back to 'poisons everything.' What is happening?
answer: Motte and bailey -- a defensible historical claim is the bunker; the sweeping verdict is the goal.
choices: Motte and bailey -- a defensible historical claim is the bunker; the sweeping verdict is the goal.
Loaded question -- the original tweet smuggles in a contested premise as if it were settled fact.
Cherry picking -- the celebrity is selecting only harmful religious examples and ignoring the good ones.
Appeal to emotion -- the word 'poisons' is meant to provoke rather than to describe the situation.
context: Spot the asymmetry: the retreat happens in argument; the advance happens to an audience. The writer's actual position is whichever version is harder to attack at the moment.

question: A pundit declares 'Free speech is a myth.' Asked, she says 'I mean some voices get more reach than others.' Her column ends with 'free speech is a myth.' Which name fits?
answer: Motte and bailey -- the indefensible thesis is the agenda; the trivial truth is the safe retreat.
choices: Motte and bailey -- the indefensible thesis is the agenda; the trivial truth is the safe retreat.
Begging the question -- the column assumes free speech doesn't exist instead of arguing for it.
Bandwagon -- the pundit appeals to popular opinion among her audience rather than to evidence.
Appeal to consequences -- the pundit argues that free speech leads to harms, not that it is a myth.
context: Diagnostic question: does the modest claim, taken on its own, deserve any of the heat the strong claim generates? If 'some voices reach further' is the real thesis, no one would write the column.

question: A self-help guru says 'Thoughts create reality.' Pressed, he says 'I just mean your mindset affects outcomes.' His next book is titled 'Thoughts Create Reality.' Diagnose.
answer: Motte and bailey -- a bland psychological truism shields a metaphysical claim that sells books.
choices: Motte and bailey -- a bland psychological truism shields a metaphysical claim that sells books.
Equivocation -- the word 'reality' shifts between subjective experience and the external world.
Appeal to popularity -- the guru relies on the success of similar books rather than on evidence.
Composition fallacy -- effects on individual thoughts are extrapolated to the cosmos as a whole.
context: The retreat ('mindset matters') is something a stoic would have endorsed two thousand years ago. The advance ('thoughts literally create reality') is the marketable thesis. Spot the shift.

question: An activist insists 'Silence is violence.' Challenged, she clarifies 'I mean inaction in the face of injustice has costs.' At her next rally, she chants 'silence IS violence.' What is the move?
answer: Equivocation — Motte and bailey -- a contested moral claim hides behind a banal one about costs of inaction.
choices: Equivocation — Motte and bailey -- a contested moral claim hides behind a banal one about costs of inaction.
Equivocation -- the word 'violence' is stretched so broadly that it loses any real meaning.
Slippery slope -- the activist warns that silence will lead step by step to actual violence.
Appeal to emotion -- the slogan moves listeners without offering them a substantive argument.
context: Equivocation IS in play, but the move is broader. The activist actively switches between two claims and treats them as one. The diagnostic is the retreat under pressure, advance under cover.

question: A theologian writes 'all paths lead to God.' Asked about polytheism, he answers 'I just mean sincere seekers deserve respect.' His sermon next week returns to 'all paths.' Spot the move.
answer: Motte and bailey -- a respectful posture toward seekers shields a strong claim about religious truth.
choices: Motte and bailey -- a respectful posture toward seekers shields a strong claim about religious truth.
False equivalence -- the theologian treats radically different religious paths as comparable.
Genetic fallacy -- judging the truth of a religion by who happens to follow it, not by content.
Appeal to consequences -- arguing that all paths lead to God because it is the most peaceful view.
context: Religious-pluralism debates produce this constantly. The pluralist thesis is substantive and contested; the retreat to 'be respectful' is harmless. Each version smuggles cover for the other.

question: A tweet reads 'capitalism kills.' Asked, the user says 'I mean some business decisions cause harm.' Her bio still says 'Capitalism kills.' Which fallacy is the structural fit?
answer: Motte and bailey -- the bumper-sticker indictment is the message; the harmless retreat is the shield.
choices: Motte and bailey -- the bumper-sticker indictment is the message; the harmless retreat is the shield.
Hasty generalization -- a handful of harmful business decisions are projected onto a whole system.
Whataboutism -- the user deflects criticism by pointing at harms done under other economic systems.
Strawman -- the user attacks a caricature of capitalism rather than its actual defenders' claims.
context: The motte-bailey pattern is most visible in slogans designed to travel. The slogan is the bailey; the qualification offered to a critic is the motte. The slogan keeps its punch by ignoring the motte.

question: A debater dismisses a peer-reviewed study by saying 'one study doesn't prove anything.' Earlier she cited a single blog post to support her own view. What pattern is at work?
answer: Isolated demand for rigor -- the standard rises sharply when applied to the other side's evidence only.
choices: Isolated demand for rigor -- the standard rises sharply when applied to the other side's evidence only.
Cherry picking -- the debater selects studies that confirm her view and ignores contrary ones.
Genetic fallacy -- the debater rejects the study because of the journal that published it first.
Ad hominem -- the debater attacks the researcher rather than addressing the study's methodology.
context: Scott Alexander popularized the term. The fallacy isn't the demand for rigor; it's the ASYMMETRY. Any standard you apply to others, you must apply to yourself first. Spotting the asymmetry is the catch.

question: A podcast host says climate models can't predict the future, but trusts a single seasonal forecast from his weather app. What move has he made?
answer: Isolated demand for rigor -- skepticism is calibrated to which conclusion he wants to reach.
choices: Isolated demand for rigor -- skepticism is calibrated to which conclusion he wants to reach.
Appeal to common sense -- the host trusts everyday intuition over scientific abstraction here.
Hasty generalization -- the host's experience with one forecast colors his view of all models.
Genetic fallacy -- the host dismisses climate models because of who funded the original research.
context: Skepticism is a tool, not a posture. Selective skepticism -- demanding certainty from one model and trusting another with weaker credentials -- reveals motivated reasoning, not honest epistemic care.

question: A columnist refuses to credit any study unless it has a randomized trial, then cites observational data approvingly for his preferred conclusion in the same paragraph. Name the move.
answer: Special pleading — Isolated demand for rigor -- the methodological bar moves with the conclusion the columnist wants.
choices: Special pleading — Isolated demand for rigor -- the methodological bar moves with the conclusion the columnist wants.
Cherry picking -- the columnist selectively reports the studies that confirm his preexisting view.
Special pleading -- the columnist exempts his own evidence from criteria he applies to others.
Appeal to authority -- the columnist cites credentialed experts without examining their reasoning.
context: Special pleading is close but different. Special pleading exempts a CASE; isolated demand for rigor exempts an EVIDENTIARY STANDARD. Both reveal motivated reasoning. The cure is consistent standards.

question: An expert says folk remedies need double-blind trials to be taken seriously. She then recommends a new pharmaceutical based on a small open-label study. Which pattern fits?
answer: Isolated demand for rigor -- the standard for skepticism shifts depending on whose claim is at stake.
choices: Isolated demand for rigor -- the standard for skepticism shifts depending on whose claim is at stake.
Appeal to authority -- the expert relies on her credentials rather than on the underlying data.
Composition fallacy -- the expert assumes properties of a sample apply to all folk remedies broadly.
Genetic fallacy -- the expert rejects folk remedies because of their non-scientific cultural origin.
context: Folk remedies and pharma both deserve scrutiny; the fallacy is applying different bars to each. Real epistemic discipline says: state your standard, apply it to all candidates, follow the answer.

question: A scholar dismisses Christian historical sources as 'too biased to use,' then cites a Roman historian's hostile remarks as if they were neutral fact. What rhetorical move is operating?
answer: Isolated demand for rigor -- bias disqualifies one source but is invisible when it favors the scholar.
choices: Isolated demand for rigor -- bias disqualifies one source but is invisible when it favors the scholar.
Genetic fallacy -- the scholar judges Christian sources only by their religious origin and motives.
Appeal to antiquity -- the scholar trusts the Roman historian merely because the source is older.
Cherry picking -- the scholar selects whichever sources happen to support a preferred conclusion.
context: Every ancient source has perspective. The discipline is to weight bias consistently. Calling out bias only in your opponent's evidence is the move, not the conclusion that bias matters.

question: A journalist insists police statistics are unreliable unless audited by independent panels. She then quotes uncorroborated witness reports to back her own headline. Name the asymmetry.
answer: Isolated demand for rigor -- the journalist's bar for evidence depends on which conclusion it serves.
choices: Isolated demand for rigor -- the journalist's bar for evidence depends on which conclusion it serves.
Cherry picking -- the journalist selects only the police statistics that support her own narrative.
False equivalence -- treating audited statistics and uncorroborated witness reports as equivalent.
Ad hominem -- the journalist attacks the credibility of police rather than their actual statistics.
context: This is one of the most common moves in modern reporting. The catch isn't 'audit everything.' It's 'audit your own side at least as harshly as you audit the other.' The asymmetry is the diagnostic.

question: A talk show argues 'We can't trust corporate-funded studies on this drug.' The same host then cites a corporate-funded study to defend a different drug she likes. What is happening?
answer: Conflict of interest — Isolated demand for rigor -- the conflict of interest matters only when it points the wrong way.
choices: Conflict of interest — Isolated demand for rigor -- the conflict of interest matters only when it points the wrong way.
Appeal to motive -- the host attacks the funding source rather than engaging with the actual data.
Tu quoque -- the host turns a criticism back on her critics rather than addressing their point.
Composition fallacy -- the host generalizes from one corporate study to all corporate-funded research.
context: Appeal to motive is a related move, but the diagnostic for isolated demand is the inconsistency. Same evidentiary objection, two opposite verdicts -- the verdict is tracking the conclusion, not the evidence.

question: An academic rejects a colleague's data as 'too small a sample size,' then publishes her own paper with a smaller sample on a related claim. What fallacy is in play?
answer: Isolated demand for rigor -- sample size matters when the colleague invokes it, not when she does.
choices: Isolated demand for rigor -- sample size matters when the colleague invokes it, not when she does.
Cherry picking -- the academic selects research methods that favor her own published conclusions.
Special pleading -- the academic carves out an exception for her own paper from the general rule.
Appeal to authority -- the academic relies on her own credentials to immunize her smaller sample.
context: Once you see the move, you see it everywhere -- on cable news, in peer review, in casual argument. The cure is to articulate your evidentiary standard FIRST, then apply it without exception.

question: A debater stacks 15 quick claims in 90 seconds -- each shaky, none fully argued. His opponent addresses three; the audience concludes the opponent 'couldn't respond.' What is the pattern?
answer: Gish gallop -- volume of claims, not weight, is mistaken for the strength of the case.
choices: Gish gallop -- volume of claims, not weight, is mistaken for the strength of the case.
Appeal to the stone -- the debater asserts claims without offering any reasoning behind them.
Strawman -- the debater attacks misrepresented versions of his opponent's positions in turn.
Bandwagon -- the debater relies on audience reaction rather than on the substance of arguments.
context: Coined for creationist Duane Gish, who fired so many bad arguments that careful opponents lost on stage. The counter-move: pick the strongest two claims, demolish them, decline to chase the rest.

question: A tweet thread lists '20 facts that prove X.' Half are false, three are irrelevant, and seven are misleading. A reader replies to the strongest one and is mocked for 'ignoring' the others. Diagnose.
answer: Gish gallop -- the writer makes refutation impossible by stacking more claims than anyone can address.
choices: Gish gallop -- the writer makes refutation impossible by stacking more claims than anyone can address.
Cherry picking -- the writer selects only the data points that confirm her preexisting position.
Appeal to popularity -- the thread's virality is used as evidence that its content must be true.
Burden shifting -- the writer puts the onus on critics to disprove each item one by one in detail.
context: Burden shifting is related and often a follow-up move. The defining feature of gish gallop is the VOLUME meant to exhaust scrutiny. Twitter threads weaponized this pattern at scale.

question: An online essay piles 50 'reasons' against a policy. Most are recycled talking points, others are factually wrong, and a few contradict each other. What pattern is operating?
answer: Gish gallop -- the sheer number of objections is the persuasive device; quality is not the point.
choices: Gish gallop -- the sheer number of objections is the persuasive device; quality is not the point.
Contradiction -- the essay's main weakness is internal inconsistency among the listed reasons.
False equivalence -- the essay equates serious objections with frivolous ones in a single list.
Appeal to common sense -- the essay relies on intuitive reactions rather than careful analysis.
context: Internal contradiction is a feature, not a bug, of gish gallop -- the writer needed numbers, not coherence. The reader who tries to engage every item ends up burning hours on bad arguments.

question: A podcaster lists ten 'red flags' about her opponent in two minutes. Each is sourceless; addressing one takes an hour. The opponent looks evasive for not handling all ten. Diagnose.
answer: Gish gallop -- making the response burden so high that any refutation looks like a partial defense.
choices: Gish gallop -- making the response burden so high that any refutation looks like a partial defense.
Poisoning the well -- the host front-loads negative claims before the opponent can establish credibility.
Ad hominem cluster -- the host attacks the opponent's character on multiple grounds simultaneously.
Appeal to suspicion -- the host invites the audience to be suspicious without making any actual case.
context: Poisoning the well names a related move but doesn't capture the volume tactic. The gish gallop is ABOUT the asymmetry of effort: 30 seconds to make a claim, an hour to refute it carefully.

question: A research denier produces a 60-bullet PDF objecting to a study. Each bullet would take a graduate seminar to refute. The PDF circulates as 'devastating critique.' Which fallacy?
answer: Gish gallop -- accumulation of objections substitutes for engagement with the strongest one.
choices: Gish gallop -- accumulation of objections substitutes for engagement with the strongest one.
Appeal to authority -- the PDF relies on the credentials of its author rather than the substance.
Strawman -- the PDF attacks misrepresented versions of what the original study actually claimed.
Burden shifting -- the PDF transfers responsibility to defenders to refute each item separately.
context: The pattern is endemic to comment-section discourse and adversarial PDFs. The counter-move: identify the strongest three objections, refute those carefully, ignore the volume. Don't play the gallop's game.

question: A pundit lists 25 'questions' the other side 'won't answer.' Each question would require hours of work. The list is shared as proof of evasion. What rhetorical move is in play?
answer: Gish gallop -- impossible-to-process volume is reframed as proof the other side is hiding from the truth.
choices: Gish gallop -- impossible-to-process volume is reframed as proof the other side is hiding from the truth.
Loaded questions -- the questions contain hidden assumptions designed to be hard to answer fairly.
Appeal to silence -- unanswered questions are treated as evidence the other side has nothing to say.
Strawman questions -- the pundit asks about positions her opponents never held in the first place.
context: Each of these names is partially right -- the moves often co-occur. But the structural device is the VOLUME. Twenty-five questions and 24 hours of news cycle means most go unanswered, by physics alone.

question: A blogger writes a 5000-word post with 40 numbered claims. A critic tackles four. The blogger replies 'You didn't address 90% of my argument.' Where does the move sit?
answer: Gish gallop -- the post is structured so that meaningful engagement is mathematically impossible.
choices: Gish gallop -- the post is structured so that meaningful engagement is mathematically impossible.
Appeal to length -- the blogger treats word count as evidence that the position is well-supported.
False precision -- the blogger uses '90%' to suggest a quantitative analysis that wasn't actually done.
Burden shifting -- the blogger places the entire refutation burden on critics rather than himself.
context: The diagnostic is the asymmetry of effort and the substitution of breadth for depth. Recognize the pattern, refuse the implicit bargain. Engage the strongest claim, ignore the rest, name the move.

question: A news segment treats a fringe blog with 200 readers as 'one side' against a major university's research team as 'the other side.' Both get equal airtime. Diagnose.
answer: False equivalence -- the segment treats sources as comparable when their credentials differ massively.
choices: False equivalence -- the segment treats sources as comparable when their credentials differ massively.
Appeal to balance -- the segment confuses fairness with treating every claim as equally weighted.
Cherry picking -- the segment selects the fringe source rather than mainstream skeptics of the work.
Bandwagon -- the segment lets viewer reaction rather than evidence determine which side is correct.
context: Appeal to balance is the audience-facing label; false equivalence is the underlying structural move. Two 'sides' is a journalistic convention, not a description of evidence weight. Bothsiderism breaks here.

question: A pundit says 'Both candidates lied this week.' Candidate A made one minor factual error; Candidate B told ten direct lies under oath. The pundit weights them equally. Spot the move.
answer: False equivalence -- counting incidents without weighing magnitude treats unequal cases as equal.
choices: False equivalence -- counting incidents without weighing magnitude treats unequal cases as equal.
Cherry picking -- the pundit selects only the lies that fit her preexisting narrative for both candidates.
Appeal to fairness -- the pundit pretends to neutrality by treating sides as identical regardless of facts.
Strawman -- the pundit attacks misrepresented versions of what each candidate actually said and did.
context: False equivalence trades on the appearance of even-handedness. The defect is comparing things that differ in scale, evidence, or stakes as if they were the same. Magnitude matters in argument.

question: An op-ed says a regulatory failure that killed 12 people is 'just as bad' as a regulation that briefly inconvenienced commuters. What is the rhetorical move?
answer: False equivalence -- the writer treats incommensurable harms as comparable to score a rhetorical point.
choices: False equivalence -- the writer treats incommensurable harms as comparable to score a rhetorical point.
Cherry picking -- the writer selects only the worst regulatory outcomes from a much larger dataset.
Appeal to consequences -- the writer judges policy purely by outcomes rather than by procedures.
Loaded comparison -- the writer chooses examples designed to inflame rather than to illuminate facts.
context: Twelve deaths and a commute delay are not the same magnitude. The op-ed pretends they are. Spot the category error: comparison requires a shared scale. False equivalence smuggles in the scale.

question: A talking head says 'Both parties are extreme.' One has a platform a few points off the historical median; the other has rewritten its platform wholesale. Diagnose.
answer: False equivalence -- 'extreme' is applied symmetrically when the underlying distances are very different.
choices: False equivalence -- 'extreme' is applied symmetrically when the underlying distances are very different.
Appeal to centrism -- the head assumes the middle position is always correct regardless of facts.
Cherry picking -- the head selects only the most extreme statements from each side of the aisle.
Strawman -- the head misrepresents both parties' platforms to make them appear more extreme.
context: Bothsiderism in politics is a textbook example. The defect isn't the impulse to fairness; it's the willingness to use a SYMMETRIC label without doing the asymmetric work of measurement.

question: A historian writes 'every empire committed atrocities.' This is meant to show that the British and the Khmer Rouge are 'morally comparable.' Spot the move.
answer: False equivalence -- a true generalization shields collapsing distinctions that any honest history must hold.
choices: False equivalence -- a true generalization shields collapsing distinctions that any honest history must hold.
Tu quoque -- the historian deflects criticism of one regime by pointing at the crimes of another.
Appeal to relativism -- the historian rejects moral judgment in history by claiming all sides are guilty.
Hasty generalization -- the historian extrapolates from a few cases to a universal claim about empires.
context: The premise can be true and the conclusion still bogus. Magnitudes, evidence quality, ideology, and deliberateness all differ across cases. Lumping them under 'atrocity' erases the differences that matter.

question: A film critic argues a $200M action film and an independent documentary 'should be judged by the same metric.' What rhetorical defect does this comparison hide?
answer: False equivalence -- different works of art serve different purposes and resist a single shared metric.
choices: False equivalence -- different works of art serve different purposes and resist a single shared metric.
Appeal to standards -- the critic confuses uniform criteria with appropriate criteria for each work.
Cherry picking -- the critic selects metrics that happen to favor one film type over the other.
Composition fallacy -- the critic judges films by averaging metrics that don't combine meaningfully.
context: Comparison is fine; choosing the wrong axis is the problem. False equivalence in aesthetics asks 'By WHAT metric?' before it asks 'Which is better?' The metric is part of the argument.

question: A commentator argues that journalists making errors and politicians lying are 'basically the same problem.' What is the structural defect in the comparison?
answer: False equivalence -- mistake and deception are conflated; intent and frequency are erased from the picture.
choices: False equivalence -- mistake and deception are conflated; intent and frequency are erased from the picture.
Tu quoque -- the commentator deflects criticism of politicians by raising the press's failures.
Cherry picking -- the commentator selects only the worst examples of each profession in turn.
Appeal to fairness -- the commentator treats different categories of failure as deserving equal blame.
context: Mistakes and lies differ in intent. They also typically differ in scale and consequence. Collapsing them under 'inaccuracy' loses the moral information the comparison was supposed to deliver.

question: A debater argues that vandalizing a sign and bombing a building are 'both forms of protest' and should be discussed in the same terms. Spot the move.
answer: False equivalence -- the protest category is real, but the harms differ by orders of magnitude in scale.
choices: False equivalence -- the protest category is real, but the harms differ by orders of magnitude in scale.
Composition fallacy -- the debater treats the protest category as if all members shared properties.
Slippery slope -- the debater suggests sign vandalism will inevitably escalate to building bombing.
Appeal to definition -- the debater treats the shared category label as ending the moral question.
context: Sharing a category does not equalize cases. False equivalence weaponizes shared categories to flatten differences that the listener should hold onto. Diagnostic: ask what the comparison is FOR.

question: A reporter asks a senator about a scandal. The senator answers 'what about the other party's worse scandals last year?' and refuses to return to the original question. Diagnose.
answer: Whataboutism -- deflection through comparison shifts discussion away from accountability for one's own side.
choices: Whataboutism -- deflection through comparison shifts discussion away from accountability for one's own side.
Tu quoque -- the senator argues that the reporter is hypocritical for raising any question.
Red herring -- the senator introduces an unrelated topic to distract from the original question.
Strawman -- the senator misrepresents the reporter's question as broader than it actually was.
context: Whataboutism is a specialized form of red herring -- the redirection is to OTHER people's wrongs. Soviet propagandists made the move famous; it survives in podcasts, press conferences, and Twitter.

question: Asked about her company's data breach, an executive responds 'Didn't a competitor lose more records last year?' She never addresses her own breach. Spot the move.
answer: Tu quoque — Whataboutism -- comparison to another offender's worse act is offered in place of any actual accounting.
choices: Tu quoque — Whataboutism -- comparison to another offender's worse act is offered in place of any actual accounting.
Tu quoque -- the executive treats the reporter as hypocritical for asking only about her company.
Appeal to consequences -- the executive argues her breach matters less than the competitor's did.
Cherry picking -- the executive selects the worst comparable breach to make her own seem minor.
context: Tu quoque and whataboutism are cousins but not identical. Tu quoque attacks the opponent's standing TO ARGUE; whataboutism deflects by changing the subject. The former is personal; the latter, topical.

question: An op-ed defends a country's human rights record by writing 'critics should look at THEIR OWN country's history first.' What rhetorical move is the writer making?
answer: Whataboutism -- pointing at the critic's home record is offered as a substitute for engagement with criticism.
choices: Whataboutism -- pointing at the critic's home record is offered as a substitute for engagement with criticism.
Tu quoque -- the writer disqualifies critics by implying they are hypocrites without standing to speak.
Nationalism -- the writer assumes one's own country deserves uniform defense against any criticism.
Appeal to fairness -- the writer suggests the rules should be applied equally before any judgment.
context: There is a valid version: 'Remove the log from your own eye first.' The fallacious version skips that step entirely. If your country has its own record, address THIS criticism, not the comparison.

question: A celebrity accused of poor behavior responds 'Plenty of other celebrities did worse and got away with it.' He never addresses what HE did. What fallacy is operating?
answer: Whataboutism -- moving the lens away from the actor in question is offered as if it were a defense.
choices: Whataboutism -- moving the lens away from the actor in question is offered as if it were a defense.
Appeal to fairness -- the celebrity demands the same treatment others have received in past cases.
Cherry picking -- the celebrity selects only the worst other-cases to make his own seem moderate.
Genetic fallacy -- the celebrity dismisses the accusation by attacking who happens to be raising it.
context: The valid kernel: SOMETIMES inconsistency in application is itself an injustice. But that argument requires showing the inconsistency matters. Pointing at other cases without doing that work is the fallacy.

question: A diet book cites three studies showing a fat-loss benefit and quietly skips twelve that found no effect. The publisher calls the book 'evidence-based.' Spot the rhetorical move.
answer: Cherry picking -- evidence is selected to confirm the thesis; contrary studies are excluded from the case.
choices: Cherry picking -- evidence is selected to confirm the thesis; contrary studies are excluded from the case.
Appeal to authority -- the publisher relies on the author's credentials rather than the evidence.
Survivorship bias -- only successful diet outcomes are studied; failures aren't tracked in the data.
Hasty generalization -- a few studies are extrapolated into a strong claim about all populations.
context: Survivorship bias is a different defect (sampling on outcome). Cherry picking is the deliberate or negligent SELECTION of evidence. Diagnostic: ask what the writer didn't cite that's clearly relevant.

question: A stock-pick newsletter shows its three best calls of the year and presents them as evidence of the analyst's skill. The 47 losses go unmentioned. What pattern is operating?
answer: Cherry picking -- only the wins are shown; the losses, which dominate the actual record, are filtered out.
choices: Cherry picking -- only the wins are shown; the losses, which dominate the actual record, are filtered out.
Survivorship bias -- the newsletter only sells subscriptions to people who weren't burned last year.
Texas sharpshooter -- the newsletter draws the target around its wins after the fact has occurred.
Appeal to authority -- the newsletter relies on the analyst's reputation rather than on actual data.
context: Texas sharpshooter is close but distinct -- it's about drawing the target AFTER the shots. Cherry picking is about excluding contrary data from a fixed target. The full track record is the cure.

question: A documentary on a controversial topic features five experts who agree with its thesis and zero who disagree. The film advertises itself as 'balanced.' Diagnose.
answer: Cherry picking -- the experts are selected to confirm; the documentary calls a one-sided lineup 'balanced.'
choices: Cherry picking -- the experts are selected to confirm; the documentary calls a one-sided lineup 'balanced.'
Appeal to authority -- the documentary leans on credentials rather than examining the underlying evidence.
False balance -- the documentary creates the appearance of fairness without doing the actual work.
Sampling bias -- the documentary's expert recruitment process selected only one type of researcher.
context: Sampling bias and cherry picking overlap. The cleanest reading: sampling bias is unintentional, cherry picking is selective by design or by indifference. Either way, the missing experts are the catch.

question: A news article uses crime data from January-March to claim crime is falling. It omits the April-December numbers, which show the opposite trend. What is the move?
answer: Cherry picking -- a sub-period is selected because it supports the thesis; the full-year data tells another story.
choices: Cherry picking -- a sub-period is selected because it supports the thesis; the full-year data tells another story.
Texas sharpshooter -- the writer drew the analytic boundary after seeing where the numbers fell.
Misleading statistics -- the writer manipulates the visual presentation of accurate underlying data.
Composition fallacy -- the writer treats a part of the year as representative of the whole year.
context: When a time window is chosen after seeing the data, Texas sharpshooter is also present -- the moves co-occur. Cherry picking is the broader defect; the missing data tells you what should have been shown.

question: A scientist publishes one positive result and files away ten null results in a drawer. Reviewers see only the one paper. What is this practice called?
answer: Cherry picking via the file-drawer effect -- only the significant result enters the public record at all.
choices: Cherry picking via the file-drawer effect -- only the significant result enters the public record at all.
P-hacking -- the scientist runs many tests until one reaches significance and reports only that one.
Selection bias -- the journal's editor preferred a positive result over null findings during review.
Survivorship bias -- the field only studies the experiments that produced publishable conclusions.
context: The file-drawer effect is the structural form of cherry picking in science. P-hacking is related -- tweaking analyses until significance appears. Both bias the literature toward false positives over time.

question: A commentator argues that a policy works by citing the three best-performing cities that adopted it. The five worst-performing adopters are not mentioned anywhere. Spot the move.
answer: Cherry picking -- the success cases are foregrounded; the failures, equally relevant, are left out of the case.
choices: Cherry picking -- the success cases are foregrounded; the failures, equally relevant, are left out of the case.
Texas sharpshooter -- the commentator drew the criterion of success around the cases she preferred.
Composition fallacy -- the commentator extrapolates from three cities to a verdict on the policy.
Appeal to anecdote -- the commentator substitutes specific cases for the systematic empirical record.
context: Anecdote and cherry picking overlap; anecdote substitutes a story for data, cherry picking selects stories from data. The cure for both: what's the FULL record? What does the average adopter look like?

question: A self-help author cites the daily routines of successful CEOs. He never mentions the unsuccessful CEOs who shared those same routines. The book claims a proven formula. Diagnose.
answer: Cherry picking with a survivorship overlay -- only winners are studied; losers with identical habits are invisible.
choices: Cherry picking with a survivorship overlay -- only winners are studied; losers with identical habits are invisible.
Survivorship bias alone -- the author only sees the winners' habits and can't compare to the losers.
Texas sharpshooter -- the author drew the success target around the habits that happen to appear.
Hasty generalization -- the author extrapolates from a sample of CEOs to a universal life formula.
context: Two moves are operating: cherry picking (selecting examples) and survivorship bias (sampling on the dependent variable). Together they produce the 'morning routine of millionaires' genre of bad evidence.

question: A historian cites three letters where a king praised liberty and ignores fifty letters where the same king urged repression. The biography calls him 'a friend of freedom.' What is operating?
answer: Cherry picking -- a partial record is selected to fit the biographer's thesis; the bulk evidence is excluded.
choices: Cherry picking -- a partial record is selected to fit the biographer's thesis; the bulk evidence is excluded.
Confirmation bias -- the biographer notices and remembers letters that support his preexisting view.
Appeal to authority -- the biographer relies on the king's stated views rather than his actual deeds.
Anachronism -- the biographer imposes modern liberty concepts onto a historical figure unfairly.
context: Confirmation bias is the cognitive root; cherry picking is the practice it produces in argument. Real historiography weights the full corpus, including the letters that complicate the thesis on offer.

question: A pundit predicted the company would collapse by 2024. It didn't. He now writes 'I always meant by 2026 -- and the warning signs are even clearer.' What is the move?
answer: Moving the goalposts -- when a prediction fails on schedule, the schedule is quietly rewritten to fit reality.
choices: Moving the goalposts -- when a prediction fails on schedule, the schedule is quietly rewritten to fit reality.
Hindsight bias -- the pundit reinterprets past statements to align with what actually happened later.
Cherry picking -- the pundit selects only the data that supports his updated timeline going forward.
Strawman -- the pundit reframes his critics' challenge as a different claim than they actually made.
context: The pattern is structurally about UNFALSIFIABILITY. Each time the prediction fails, the prediction shifts. A theory that absorbs all evidence equally explains none of it. State the criterion FIRST.

question: A diet guru promised dramatic results in 30 days. Followers got modest results. She now writes 'real benefits require 90 days, and 30 was a soft target.' Diagnose.
answer: Moving the goalposts -- the failed promise is retroactively recast as a milestone toward the real target.
choices: Moving the goalposts -- the failed promise is retroactively recast as a milestone toward the real target.
Hindsight bias -- the guru reinterprets her own past claims through the lens of what occurred later.
Equivocation -- the term 'results' is used in two different senses across the original and new claim.
Burden shifting -- the guru asks followers to disprove the new 90-day timeline instead of supporting it.
context: Diet, fitness, and investment claims pull this move constantly. The diagnostic: did the original claim have a clear test, and was that test failed? If so, ANY revision is suspect until justified.

question: A predicted recession failed to arrive. The economist now writes 'technically, it's been a recession all along by a deeper definition.' The definition is new. Spot the move.
answer: Moving the goalposts -- a new definition is offered post hoc so the failed prediction can be called a hit.
choices: Moving the goalposts -- a new definition is offered post hoc so the failed prediction can be called a hit.
Equivocation -- the economist uses 'recession' in two different senses across the predictions.
Ad hoc rescue -- the economist invents an exception to save the theory from disconfirmation.
Special pleading -- the economist makes a unique allowance for her own theory's failure case.
context: Ad hoc rescue is closely related; both add a patch after failure. Moving the goalposts is the specific subspecies where the success criterion itself is redefined to absorb the unwanted result.

question: A predicted election outcome failed. The forecaster now says 'I predicted the direction, not the magnitude, and the direction was clearly there.' Originally she predicted both. Spot the move.
answer: Moving the goalposts -- two-part claim becomes one-part after one part fails; the surviving piece is retained.
choices: Moving the goalposts -- two-part claim becomes one-part after one part fails; the surviving piece is retained.
Cherry picking -- the forecaster selects only the part of her past claim that survived the result.
Equivocation -- the forecaster uses 'predicted' loosely so the failed half doesn't really count.
Hindsight reframing -- the forecaster recasts her original claim to fit the actual outcome better.
context: All three options are partially true. The structural diagnostic: the original criterion is replaced by a softer one, the soft one is met, and the failure is rebranded as a success. State the FIRST claim.

question: A movement leader promised 100,000 protesters. 15,000 showed. He now says 'I always meant impactful protesters, not raw numbers.' The impact metric was just invented. Spot the move.
answer: Moving the goalposts -- a quantitative claim becomes a qualitative one to absorb a clear empirical failure.
choices: Moving the goalposts -- a quantitative claim becomes a qualitative one to absorb a clear empirical failure.
Equivocation -- the term 'protesters' shifts between countable people and influential participants.
Ad hoc rescue -- the leader invents a new metric to spare the original prediction from refutation.
Strawman of self -- the leader recasts his own past claim as if it had been narrower than it was.
context: Move dissection: 100,000 is a measurable claim. 'Impactful' is not. The shift from one to the other is the goalpost movement. Demanding the ORIGINAL claim be evaluated on its own terms is the cure.

question: A debate club judge ruled against a team. The captain now says 'The criteria she used weren't the real criteria for this round.' The criteria were stated in advance. Diagnose.
answer: Moving the goalposts -- losing is reinterpreted as wrong criteria; the rules that bound everyone go unmentioned.
choices: Moving the goalposts -- losing is reinterpreted as wrong criteria; the rules that bound everyone go unmentioned.
Special pleading -- the captain demands an exception from the rules that applied to all teams equally.
Sour grapes -- the captain dismisses the judgment because it didn't go his team's way in this case.
Appeal to consequences -- the captain argues the criteria must be wrong since they produced a bad result.
context: Each label captures part of the move. The diagnostic for moving the goalposts: the criteria existed BEFORE the result, and the dispute over them starts AFTER. Stable criteria across cases is the cure.

question: A speaker shows that 'people born in October are 23% more likely to be famous athletes.' She tested 100 birth-month subgroups and reported only the one that hit. Diagnose.
answer: Texas sharpshooter -- the target was drawn around the shots that landed close together by chance alone.
choices: Texas sharpshooter -- the target was drawn around the shots that landed close together by chance alone.
Cherry picking -- the speaker selected only the subgroup that supported a striking conclusion.
P-hacking -- the speaker ran many tests until significance appeared and reported only the survivor.
Hasty generalization -- the speaker extrapolated from one subgroup to a claim about all athletes.
context: Named for the shooter who fires at a wall, then draws a bullseye around the densest cluster. The data didn't reveal a pattern; the analyst found one IN the data and called it a discovery.

question: A conspiracy theorist 'predicts' an event by retroactively finding seven specific cues in old broadcasts that 'pointed to it.' He had not flagged the cues in advance. Spot the move.
answer: Texas sharpshooter -- the cues were selected after the event; the prediction was drawn around the data.
choices: Texas sharpshooter -- the cues were selected after the event; the prediction was drawn around the data.
Hindsight bias -- the theorist reinterprets past data through the lens of an outcome already known.
Confirmation bias -- the theorist notices cues that fit the conspiracy and ignores cues that don't.
Pareidolia -- the theorist sees meaningful patterns in coincidental arrangements of unrelated cues.
context: Hindsight bias is the cognitive root; Texas sharpshooter is the argumentative practice that grows from it. The diagnostic: were the criteria for a 'hit' set BEFORE the event, or only after? Always ask.

question: A researcher tested 50 nutrients against a disease. One showed a correlation at p < 0.05. He published that one. Why is the published finding likely false?
answer: Texas sharpshooter -- with 50 tests at p < 0.05, you expect a couple of false positives by chance alone.
choices: Texas sharpshooter -- with 50 tests at p < 0.05, you expect a couple of false positives by chance alone.
P-hacking alone -- the researcher tweaked the analysis until a significant result appeared.
Confirmation bias -- the researcher only reports results that fit his preexisting hypothesis.
Sampling bias -- the researcher's nutrient subjects weren't randomly drawn from the population.
context: The multiple-comparisons problem. P < 0.05 means a 5% false-positive rate per test; with 50 tests, roughly 2.5 false positives are expected by chance. Pre-registering the hypothesis is the cure.

question: A historian argues a calendar date 'predicted' a famous event. He found the 'prediction' by scanning a million pages of writings post hoc. What is the move?
answer: Texas sharpshooter -- the prediction was drawn around the calendar date that happened to match the event.
choices: Texas sharpshooter -- the prediction was drawn around the calendar date that happened to match the event.
Cherry picking -- the historian selected the one passage that matches and ignored the millions that don't.
Pareidolia -- the historian sees meaningful patterns in coincidental textual arrangements by chance.
Hindsight bias -- the historian reinterprets old texts through the lens of an outcome we already know.
context: Given a million pages and a date, finding one match is a near-certainty by combinatorics. The match isn't a signal; it's a statistical artifact. Pre-specifying the prediction is the only valid version.

question: A test is 99% accurate. A rare condition strikes 1 in 10,000. A positive test comes back. The article reports there's '99% chance of disease.' Where is the article wrong?
answer: Base rate neglect — Base-rate neglect -- the prior probability of the condition isn't combined with the test's accuracy.
choices: Base rate neglect — Base-rate neglect -- the prior probability of the condition isn't combined with the test's accuracy.
Misleading statistics -- the article confuses the test's sensitivity with the test's predictive value.
Conjunction fallacy -- the article treats two events as more probable than one in the same population.
Appeal to precision -- the article uses '99%' to suggest a confidence that isn't really warranted yet.
context: With a 1-in-10,000 base rate, even a 99% accurate test will return MOSTLY false positives. The actual post-test probability is closer to 1%. The original prior matters; ignoring it is the structural error.

question: A news story reports that 80% of people in a class who got the flu had been vaccinated. The story implies the vaccine doesn't work. What is the article missing?
answer: Base rate neglect — Base-rate neglect -- if 95% of the class was vaccinated, 80% of cases being vaccinated is expected.
choices: Base rate neglect — Base-rate neglect -- if 95% of the class was vaccinated, 80% of cases being vaccinated is expected.
Cherry picking -- the article selects only the cases that fit the anti-vaccine framing of the story.
Misleading statistics -- the article presents accurate numbers in a way designed to mislead readers.
Composition fallacy -- the article treats a property of cases as if it were a property of the vaccine.
context: The denominator matters. If 95% of the population is vaccinated, then 80% of cases being vaccinated means vaccinated people are UNDER-represented among cases. The headline collapses without the prior.

question: A criminologist reports that 70% of arrested people had the new flagged trait. She concludes the trait predicts criminality. What part of the picture is missing?
answer: Base rate neglect — Base-rate neglect -- the prevalence of the trait in the general population isn't reported here.
choices: Base rate neglect — Base-rate neglect -- the prevalence of the trait in the general population isn't reported here.
Cherry picking -- the criminologist selects only the cases where the trait happened to be present.
Sampling bias -- arrested people aren't a representative sample of criminals in the population.
Confounding -- some unmeasured third variable causes both the trait and the arrest rate together.
context: If 70% of EVERYONE has the trait, then 70% among arrestees tells you nothing predictive at all. The base rate sets what 'striking' means. Without it, the percent is just a number floating in space.

question: An ad says 'Our customers report 90% satisfaction.' A skeptic notes only 2% of customers responded to the survey. What concept does the skeptic want the ad to address?
answer: Base rate neglect — Base-rate aware sampling -- the surveyed 2% is unlikely to represent the unsurveyed 98% of customers.
choices: Base rate neglect — Base-rate aware sampling -- the surveyed 2% is unlikely to represent the unsurveyed 98% of customers.
Selection bias -- the customers who chose to respond are exactly those most pleased with the product in normal use.
Survivorship bias -- the customers who left the company aren't part of the survey at all anymore in normal use.
Cherry picking -- the ad selects the metric that survives scrutiny and omits the response rate in normal use.
context: Selection bias and survivorship bias both name pieces of the problem. The base-rate-aware question is: 'What fraction of the relevant population is included?' Two percent of customers is not 'customers.'

question: A profiler says 'The suspect matches a profile shared by 1 in 1000.' The city has a million residents. The article reports a 'one in a thousand' match strength. What is missing?
answer: Base rate neglect — Base-rate awareness -- if 1000 people match the profile in the city, the match alone identifies no one specifically.
choices: Base rate neglect — Base-rate awareness -- if 1000 people match the profile in the city, the match alone identifies no one specifically.
Misleading statistics -- the article presents an accurate rate in a way that creates a false impression in every case that comes up.
Conjunction fallacy -- the article treats the match probability as if it were a conjunction of independent traits in every case that comes up.
Cherry picking -- the article selects the profile attribute that fits a preferred suspect among the matches in every case that comes up.
context: The 'prosecutor's fallacy' -- a textbook base-rate neglect. P(evidence | innocent) is not P(innocent | evidence). The pool of matches is what matters. One-in-a-thousand can mean a thousand matches in a city.

question: A profile describes Linda as outspoken on social issues. Asked which is more likely: 'Linda is a banker' or 'Linda is a banker AND active in social movements,' most pick the second. Why is the second wrong?
answer: Conjunction fallacy -- a more specific claim cannot be more probable than the broader one it implies.
choices: Conjunction fallacy -- a more specific claim cannot be more probable than the broader one it implies.
Representativeness heuristic -- the second option fits Linda's profile and feels more like 'her.'
Base-rate neglect -- the picker ignores the broader population frequencies of bankers in the data.
Anchoring -- the picker is too influenced by the specific details mentioned in Linda's description.
context: The classic Kahneman-Tversky case (1983). 'Banker AND active' is a SUBSET of 'banker.' Any subset is less probable than the superset. The representativeness heuristic generates a feeling that overrides logic.

question: Asked which is more likely: 'A flood will hit California' or 'a flood will hit California AND damage a major bridge,' people often pick the second. What is wrong here?
answer: Conjunction fallacy -- adding 'damage a major bridge' can only narrow the cases, not broaden them.
choices: Conjunction fallacy -- adding 'damage a major bridge' can only narrow the cases, not broaden them.
Representativeness -- the second event sounds more vivid and so more likely than the bare prediction.
Availability heuristic -- bridge damage is easier to picture than a generic flood with no detail.
Anchoring -- the bridge detail makes the prediction more concrete and so more emotionally credible.
context: Adding specifics makes a claim MORE compelling but LESS probable. The two move in opposite directions. Insurance ads and political predictions exploit this constantly. Always check: is the claim a subset?

question: A news anchor asks: more likely the firm 'has financial trouble' or 'has financial trouble AND the CEO is hiding it'? Many pick the second. Where do they go wrong?
answer: Conjunction fallacy -- the second claim is a special case of the first; it can be no more probable than the first.
choices: Conjunction fallacy -- the second claim is a special case of the first; it can be no more probable than the first.
Representativeness -- the second option fits a familiar story shape and feels more likely than the bare claim.
Anchoring -- the CEO detail anchors the listener on a specific scandal pattern they've seen elsewhere.
Availability -- the listener can vividly imagine a CEO cover-up but not generic financial trouble.
context: The cognitive trap: vividness makes us forget probability. A vivid story is RARELY more likely than a less vivid alternative. The conjunction is always at most as probable as either conjunct alone.

question: Asked which is more likely about an unknown firm: 'In legal trouble' or 'in legal trouble AND will be acquired this year,' most pick the second. Diagnose.
answer: Conjunction fallacy -- the acquisition detail narrows the cases that count; the conjunction must be less likely.
choices: Conjunction fallacy -- the acquisition detail narrows the cases that count; the conjunction must be less likely.
Representativeness -- the acquisition makes the scenario fit a familiar acquisition-after-trouble pattern.
Availability -- the acquisition detail is more vivid and so easier to imagine than the bare legal trouble.
Anchoring -- the specific detail anchors the listener on a pattern they have seen play out in news.
context: The conjunction-rule violation is one of cognitive science's most robust findings. Adding any detail makes a claim LESS probable, however much more 'storied' the detail makes it sound to the listener.

question: An article studies the habits of 100 billionaires and concludes 'these habits cause success.' It never studies the millions who tried the same habits and stayed poor. Spot the move.
answer: Survivorship bias -- only winners are examined; people with the same habits but no success are invisible to the study.
choices: Survivorship bias -- only winners are examined; people with the same habits but no success are invisible to the study.
Cherry picking -- the article selects only the billionaires who fit the preferred lesson on habits.
Sampling bias -- the article's sample of billionaires isn't a random draw from the population overall.
Hasty generalization -- the article extrapolates from 100 billionaires to a universal life formula.
