context: Famous WW2 example: armor planes where they returned shot, not where they didn't. The downed planes would have shown the real vulnerable spots. Survivorship bias means the dead can't speak in your data.

question: A finance influencer notes that hedge funds founded in 1995 have averaged great returns. He ignores the hundreds of funds founded in 1995 that closed before being tracked. Diagnose.
answer: Survivorship bias -- the surviving funds' returns aren't the whole picture; the closed ones aren't in the data.
choices: Survivorship bias -- the surviving funds' returns aren't the whole picture; the closed ones aren't in the data.
Cherry picking -- the influencer selects the funds with the best returns and ignores the worst ones.
Selection bias -- the funds in the database were chosen by a process that favored profitable ones.
Sampling bias -- the database of surviving funds isn't a random sample of all funds ever founded.
context: The hedge fund industry's average return looks better than it should because failed funds drop out of the database entirely. The 'average return of FUNDS IN THE DATA' is not 'average return of FUNDS.'

question: A startup blog studies founders who succeeded and finds they all 'took huge risks.' It doesn't study founders who took the same risks and lost. What is the structural defect?
answer: Survivorship bias -- the same risks taken by the losers go unstudied; the lesson reflects survivors only.
choices: Survivorship bias -- the same risks taken by the losers go unstudied; the lesson reflects survivors only.
Cherry picking -- the blog selects the founder stories that fit a preferred narrative about risk-taking.
Confirmation bias -- the blog notices risk-taking when it succeeded and forgets when it failed.
Sampling bias -- the blog's sample of founders is drawn only from a small pool of successful exits.
context: Survivorship bias is the defining trap of 'success literature.' To learn from outcomes, study WHO TRIED the strategy -- not just who succeeded. The losers are the missing half of the experimental data.

question: 'My homework is late, but Joey's was late LAST month — talk to him first!' What's wrong with this defense?
choices: Whataboutism — Joey's lateness was a different time and a different question.
Joey deserves all the blame for late homework everywhere in every case that comes up.
Late homework is allowed in every class with any late history in every case that comes up.
Teachers must investigate older lates before newer lates first in every case that comes up.
answer: Whataboutism — Joey's lateness was a different time and a different question.
context: Whataboutism. Each lateness is its own event. Pointing at Joey can't undo the question about TODAY's missing work.

question: 'I love my puppy SO MUCH that he MUST be the smartest dog ever.' Where's the wishful thinking?
choices: Wishful thinking — Loving the puppy doesn't make him the smartest — that's a separate question.
Affection makes dogs smarter than the dogs that get less daily love in every case that comes up.
Puppies become the smartest in the world when their owners adore them in every case that comes up.
Love is the official measure of dog intelligence used by all vets and trainers in every case that comes up.
answer: Wishful thinking — Loving the puppy doesn't make him the smartest — that's a separate question.
context: Wishful thinking mixes our feelings with facts about the world. The puppy's intelligence is one thing; how much we love him is another.

question: A central planner promises to give every citizen 'exactly what they need.' To do that, the planner has to know each citizen's needs, tastes, and circumstances. What problem does this immediately create?
choices: Local knowledge — what each person knows about their own life — can't be gathered into one mind fast enough to be useful.
Citizens will never give the planner an honest account of their own needs, even when politely asked to do so.
The planner inevitably picks favorites and ignores most people's reported needs in any large-scale system.
Modern computers have not yet been built powerful enough to process the daily requests at population scale.
answer: Local knowledge — what each person knows about their own life — can't be gathered into one mind fast enough to be useful.
context: This is Hayek's 'knowledge problem,' sharpened in 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945). Each person knows things no planner can know — tomorrow's plans, their child's allergies, which fix is good enough. Markets aggregate this through prices; central planning can't.

question: Argue with a central planner long enough and you'll hear: 'We just need better data and computers.' What's the philosophical mistake in this reply?
choices: Much of the relevant knowledge isn't articulated even in the people who hold it — it can't be sent or processed.
Computers are simply too expensive for any current government to afford at the necessary national scale.
Better data would actually make centralized planning more efficient than markets, which is a different objection.
The reply is correct, and only practical hurdles stand in the way of full-scale central planning ever working.
answer: Much of the relevant knowledge isn't articulated even in the people who hold it — it can't be sent or processed.
context: Hayek's deeper point: much of what each person 'knows' is tacit — they couldn't write it down if they tried. A farmer knows when soil is ready by feel. A barista knows which regulars want it strong. No data transfer fixes this.

question: Two cars line up at a stoplight. The driver of the red car would pay $5 to skip the wait; the driver of the blue car would pay $50. Without a price mechanism, what can't be known?
choices: Which driver values the time more — and so whose wait is the bigger cost overall.
Whether either driver is in a real hurry or just impatient about waiting at lights.
How many other drivers are also waiting at intersections elsewhere in the city.
Whether the stoplight system is well-calibrated to traffic patterns of the area.
answer: Which driver values the time more — and so whose wait is the bigger cost overall.
context: Without prices, comparing values across people is essentially impossible. Markets translate subjective value into a number anyone can compare. The economic-calculation problem (Mises, 1920) is the foundation of the Austrian critique of socialism.

question: A philosopher argues: 'Human history has moved through stages — slavery, feudalism, capitalism. So the NEXT stage WILL be a classless society.' What logical gap is the argument crossing?
choices: Naturalistic fallacy — going from a description of past trends to a guaranteed claim about the future — patterns don't prove inevitability.
The stages listed are not actually accurate historical descriptions of any society that has ever truly existed in normal use.
Classless societies have already existed many times throughout the past two thousand years of recorded history in normal use.
The argument forgets that all the stages of history are happening simultaneously somewhere in the modern world in normal use.
answer: Naturalistic fallacy — going from a description of past trends to a guaranteed claim about the future — patterns don't prove inevitability.
context: The is-ought leap and induction problem combined. Even if the trend description is accurate (debated), 'Next will be' doesn't follow. Marx claimed historical inevitability — Popper called this 'historicism' and devoted a book ('The Poverty of Historicism', 1957) to attacking it.

question: A theorist holds that history has a direction and that this direction will end in justice. Pressed on how he knows, he says, 'It's scientific.' What philosophical move is he making (or failing to make)?
choices: Claiming the authority of falsifiable science while making predictions no possible evidence could disprove.
Confusing a hypothesis with a theorem — predictions need premises and his premises are not given.
Mixing two different senses of 'science' that mean entirely different things in academic discourse.
Treating his own intuitions as if they were public observations available to everyone.
answer: Claiming the authority of falsifiable science while making predictions no possible evidence could disprove.
context: Popper's central charge in 'The Poverty of Historicism' (1957) and 'The Open Society and Its Enemies' (1945): Marxism dressed prophetic claims in the clothes of science. A theory unable to fail is not science — it's faith with a lab coat.

question: A slogan reads: 'From each according to ability, to each according to need.' A careful reader asks one practical question. What is it?
choices: WHO gets to decide what each person's ability and need actually are?
WHEN should the abilities and needs be reassessed during a person's life?
WHERE should this exchange of ability and need physically occur in the country?
HOW should each person's preferences be ranked in order of total importance?
answer: WHO gets to decide what each person's ability and need actually are?
context: The Marx slogan (Critique of the Gotha Program, 1875) sounds beautiful — until you ask who has the AUTHORITY to assess ability and assign need. That power is the whole question. Robert Nozick called this 'no self-ownership' (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974).

question: A revolutionary thinker calls for equality of all citizens AND insists on a vanguard party with extra power to direct the revolution. What internal contradiction lives inside this combination?
choices: Equality of all citizens cannot coexist with one group having permanent authority over the rest.
Vanguards are too small to actually direct the lives of an entire revolutionary population.
The revolution cannot succeed without a vanguard, so equality is a long-term ideal only.
Equal citizens would naturally elect a vanguard, so the contradiction is not real after all.
answer: Equality of all citizens cannot coexist with one group having permanent authority over the rest.
context: Lenin's 'vanguard party' theory (What Is To Be Done?, 1902) institutionalized exactly this contradiction. Every collectivist revolution has produced a ruling caste. The contradiction is structural, not historical accident — Milovan Djilas wrote 'The New Class' (1957) from inside Yugoslav communism.

question: A central planner says 'We will abolish coercion' and a moment later 'all production will be directed by the state.' What's incoherent about saying both?
choices: Directing all production REQUIRES coercion of anyone who would have done otherwise.
Production direction is too complex to plan, and so the central planner will fail anyway.
Coercion is already abolished by definition, so the second claim is redundant in practice.
The state cannot exist at the same time as central planning, so neither claim can hold.
answer: Directing all production REQUIRES coercion of anyone who would have done otherwise.
context: Bastiat ('The Law', 1850), Hayek ('The Road to Serfdom', 1944), and Nozick all sharpened this: planning the economy means forcing some people not to do what they would otherwise have done. There's no third option.

question: A defender of an ideology points to a long list of disasters in countries that tried it. He responds: 'But that wasn't REAL X.' Then in the next breath he proposes the same arrangement. What rhetorical move is happening?
choices: No true Scotsman — Defending a controversial claim by retreating to a softer one, then advancing the original.
Honestly distinguishing between theory and the corruption of theory in real practice in every case that comes up.
Pointing out that no one has yet implemented the ideology with proper safeguards in every case that comes up.
Reasoning that bad implementations don't bear on the question of the ideology's truth in every case that comes up.
answer: No true Scotsman — Defending a controversial claim by retreating to a softer one, then advancing the original.
context: Motte-and-bailey (Nicholas Shackel, 2005). When every attempt fails the same way, 'Not REAL X' becomes its own evidence — the failures aren't accidents, they trace to the theory. Also called the 'No True Scotsman' move when used to exclude counterexamples.

question: Every attempt to implement a particular political theory has produced famine, mass killing, and a tyrannical ruling class. The theory's defenders blame each failure on local conditions. What pattern should a careful thinker notice?
choices: When every implementation fails the same way, the failure mode is in the theory itself, not the conditions.
Every theory deserves more attempts before final judgment is made about whether it works.
Local conditions vary so much that no general claim about the theory can be made yet.
The defenders are probably correct, and unfortunate conditions explain the historical record.
answer: When every implementation fails the same way, the failure mode is in the theory itself, not the conditions.
context: This is induction applied to political theory. Twenty failures with the same character (gulag, famine, ruling caste) point to a structural cause. Sowell developed this argument across decades — see 'A Conflict of Visions' (1987) and 'Intellectuals and Society' (2009).

question: A philosopher argues for redistributing wealth to create equality. A questioner asks: 'Will you ASK people for their wealth, or take it?' The philosopher says, 'For the greater good — we will compel.' What philosophical claim has she now committed to?
choices: The greater good can justify violating individuals' consent — a position that needs its own defense.
Wealth is not actually owned by anyone in the first place, so taking is not compelling.
Compelling people to share is only temporary until they learn to do it voluntarily.
The questioner has misunderstood — compelled sharing IS asking, when framed correctly.
answer: The greater good can justify violating individuals' consent — a position that needs its own defense.
context: This is the heart of the libertarian critique. Nozick (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974) framed it sharply: 'Taxation of earnings from labor is on a par with forced labor.' He didn't say taxation is wrong — he said the analogy demands defense, and most arguments don't give it.

question: A teacher says, 'Sharing is voluntary. But you MUST share or you lose recess.' What is logically off about her claim?
choices: Sharing under threat is not voluntary — the two parts of her claim contradict each other.
Recess punishments are not strong enough to make any kid actually share their snacks.
Sharing is always voluntary regardless of what consequences follow from the action.
The teacher's two claims are both fine because students can choose either option freely.
answer: Sharing under threat is not voluntary — the two parts of her claim contradict each other.
context: This is a kid-level version of the coercion-vs-consent contradiction. The same shape appears in adult political claims about 'voluntary' redistribution backed by force. Words like 'voluntary' have to do the work they actually do — not the work the speaker hopes.

question: Reformers want to tear down old institutions and rebuild society from scratch using reason alone. A critic asks: how did the old institutions arise in the first place? What philosophical move is the critic making?
choices: Pointing out that surviving traditions usually encode hard-won knowledge their designers don't fully see.
Insisting that any reform of existing institutions is automatically wrong because the old ways must be sacred.
Arguing that humans are too dim to ever change a social arrangement for the better in any meaningful way.
Mocking the reformers for not having read enough scholarly history about previous social experiments first.
answer: Pointing out that surviving traditions usually encode hard-won knowledge their designers don't fully see.
context: Hayek's 'constructivist rationalism' critique ('The Constitution of Liberty', 1960) and Edmund Burke's much earlier 'Reflections on the Revolution in France' (1790). Chesterton's fence — don't tear down a fence until you understand why it was put up. The argument doesn't say 'never reform' — it says 'Beware confident demolition.'

question: A planner claims his blueprint will produce a more rational society than the messy one we have now. But the messy society is the product of millions of choices over centuries. What's the planner missing?
choices: The messy society contains information his blueprint hasn't seen and can't replicate.
Blueprints are always more rational than evolved systems because they were planned.
Centuries of choices were mostly mistakes that the new blueprint corrects directly.
The planner has chosen the wrong word — 'rational' should be 'reasonable' instead.
answer: The messy society contains information his blueprint hasn't seen and can't replicate.
context: Spontaneous order vs. designed order. Hayek argued cities, languages, and markets are 'results of human action but not of human design' — they carry more usable knowledge than any single designer can hold. Burke and Sowell made parallel points from different angles.

question: A policy is proposed because it INTENDS to help the poor. A critic asks what the policy will actually DO. The advocate replies: 'But it's MEANT to help.' What's the flaw in the reply?
choices: Intentions and effects are different — a policy meant to help can still harm.
Helping the poor is the only intention that matters in any social policy.
Critics of any well-intentioned policy are usually opposed to helping anyone.
The advocate is correct — intent is what we should evaluate, not effect.
answer: Intentions and effects are different — a policy meant to help can still harm.
context: Sowell's recurring theme across decades: rent control intends to make housing affordable; it produces shortages. Minimum wage intends to lift the poor; the most-disadvantaged lose hiring chances. Intent doesn't predict effect — outcomes do.

question: A reformer says the state should control the economy AND the press AND the schools to fix injustice faster. A critic warns: even if her cause is just, what danger has she set up?
choices: She has built a tool the next ruler will use for the next ruler's purposes.
Controlling all three at once is too much work for any government to do.
Concentrating power doesn't actually speed up the implementation of any reform.
The reformer is correct and the critic has not understood the urgency of the cause.
answer: She has built a tool the next ruler will use for the next ruler's purposes.
context: Hayek's argument in 'The Road to Serfdom' (1944): well-meaning concentration of power creates the machine an authoritarian will inherit. Lord Acton: 'Power tends to corrupt.' Bonhoeffer and Solzhenitsyn lived this from the inside.

question: Two people argue about equality. One means 'equal treatment under law.' The other means 'equal outcomes regardless of choices.' They keep using the same word and reach no agreement. What rhetorical trouble is in play?
choices: Equivocation — the same word is being used for two different concepts in one conversation.
Stubbornness — both speakers are refusing to actually listen to each other's positions.
Ignorance — one of them hasn't read enough about political philosophy to argue fairly.
Bad faith — at least one speaker doesn't actually believe what they're claiming to think.
answer: Equivocation — the same word is being used for two different concepts in one conversation.
context: Sowell ('A Conflict of Visions', 1987) traces this exact equivocation through modern political debate. 'Equality before the law' (procedural) and 'equality of outcomes' (results-based) are different demands with different costs — pretending they're the same word's natural extension is a trick.

question: A comment reads: 'She drove a sports car to the interview, so she clearly doesn't need this job.' What hidden assumption is doing all the work?
answer: That driving a particular car reliably tells you about a person's actual financial need or situation.
choices: That driving a particular car reliably tells you about a person's actual financial need or situation.
That sports cars are usually parked badly at every kind of job interview you might ever attend.
That interviewers cannot judge anyone fairly without seeing the actual cars driven by candidates.
That every sports car is bought outright with cash and never borrowed from a friend or family.
context: Snap judgments lean on hidden premises. A car could be borrowed, leased on credit, inherited, or owned despite money troubles. The 'visible signal = inner truth' assumption gets sneaked past.

question: Your friend argues your science homework is wrong because 'your handwriting is messy.' You spot the ad hominem. Does spotting it mean your science answer is RIGHT?
choices: No — spotting a flawed argument doesn't prove the underlying claim. Your answer still needs to be checked.
Yes — once you spot the fallacy, your original answer is automatically established as correct.
Yes — but only if the friend admits the ad hominem and stops criticizing your homework completely.
No — fallacies are always meaningless and have no relation to truth in any kind of situation here.
answer: No — spotting a flawed argument doesn't prove the underlying claim. Your answer still needs to be checked.
context: The 'fallacy fallacy' — concluding 'argument is bad, therefore conclusion is false.' Spotting a fallacy only shows that ONE argument fails. The conclusion may still be true; it just needs a better argument. Critical thinking has two steps: spot the bad form, then evaluate the claim on its own.

question: A pundit uses bandwagon reasoning to argue for a tax cut: 'Polls show 65% of voters support it!' A critic spots the fallacy. Does spotting the bandwagon mean the tax cut is a BAD idea?
choices: No — only that the pundit's argument doesn't work. The tax cut itself needs to be evaluated by its actual likely effects.
Yes — once a fallacy is identified, the underlying policy proposal is automatically refuted by that fact.
No — but the critic should propose a different fallacy that better fits the pundit's bandwagon argument here.
Yes — public support is the only valid measure of a policy, and the pundit's fallacy proves the opposite.
answer: No — only that the pundit's argument doesn't work. The tax cut itself needs to be evaluated by its actual likely effects.
context: Same 'fallacy fallacy' at adult-discourse level. Pollster numbers don't argue for or against policy MERITS. A bad argument for a policy is independent of whether the policy is good. Always: identify the fallacy AND then evaluate the underlying claim on real grounds.

question: An op-ed cherry-picks studies to argue X. A reader correctly identifies the cherry-picking. A second reader concludes: 'Therefore X is false.' What has the second reader done?
choices: Committed the 'fallacy fallacy' — assumed a bad argument for X means X itself is false, which doesn't follow.
Reasoned correctly — once a flaw is spotted, the conclusion of the flawed argument is automatically refuted in turn.
Reasoned correctly — cherry-picking is so severe that any conclusion drawn from it must necessarily be considered false.
Committed circular reasoning — assumed X's falsity to prove the cherry-picking was misleading.
answer: Committed the 'fallacy fallacy' — assumed a bad argument for X means X itself is false, which doesn't follow.
context: Also called the 'argument from fallacy.' Identifying a flaw in someone's argument doesn't establish the opposite of their conclusion. The claim X needs to be evaluated on independent grounds. The first reader was right; the second reader overreached.
